title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.

title: Diagnose Vercel CLI setup problems with vercel doctor
description:

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
description:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate.

Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings, or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later.

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: Ampersand from Humans& now available on AI Gateway
description:
Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026.

Ampersand is a model for group conversations. Humans& built Ampersand on Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 and trained it with reinforcement learning in simulated group conversations that run for up to months of simulated time. Most chat models are built for one person asking a question and the model answering it. Ampersand is trained to take part in a conversation between several people. It reads every message, including the ones not addressed to it, and after each one it decides whether to reply or stay quiet.

It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another.

For example:

Sam: Heads up, I'm out Friday, driving to my sister's. Alex: Have a good trip! Maya: Let's do the launch rehearsal Friday at 10 with all three of us. Ampersand: Quick flag, Maya: Sam said he's out Friday driving to his sister's, so a Friday 10am rehearsal with all three probably won't work. Might be worth picking a different time so everyone can make it.

Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools. send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results.

Call it through the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, or a coding agent. Use humansand/ampersand-v0.1 as the model name:

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
description:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground.

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
description:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log.

Encryption on self-hosted Worlds

Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams.

A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management. Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay:

More security work in v5

Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads.

You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0, inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability.

A redesigned trace viewer

The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development.

Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets.

Workflows in every region

In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1. Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress.

For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region. Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path.

By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration:

To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start(). That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay:

The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1.

Infrastructure reliability

Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover.

With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors.

As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug.

Agent-ready performance

In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today.

Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit.

In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes.

The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures.

Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers:

Fewer queue hops

In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout.

The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms.

Incremental replay

Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log: replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms. The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes.

WebSocket streaming

Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default. In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds.

Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression.

These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application.

Benchmark results and methodology

Measured October 8, 2026, on Vercel production in iad1, against the managed Vercel World. Each version uses a separate deployment of the same app. Steps take 1 KB of JSON in and out.

The full results, including tails, are in the performance documentation.

Worlds: the shared durability primitive

Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World: the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness, which adds durability to existing agent harnesses.

Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness.

Choose the integration around how you want to build:

  • Workflow SDK: write durable application logic with use workflow and use step.

  • WorkflowAgent: use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow.

  • fx: embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx.

  • durable-harness: keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it.

    • Supports Pi and OpenCode, with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox.

  • eve: build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds.

We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability.

Build with Workflow SDK 5

Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds:

  • In-flight cancellation with AbortController

  • Searchable run attributes

  • More framework integrations

  • And more

The v5 upgrade docs cover what changed. To start building a new workflow, install the SDK:

title: Parallel Decisions now available on AI Gateway for free

Use it to enrich CRM records, check eligibility, route leads, or verify claims against current sources. Citations include source URLs, optional titles, and evidence excerpts. They apply to the whole request, rather than mapping individual sources to each answer. Your application can use answer probabilities to act automatically above a threshold and send uncertain results for review.

AI Gateway tracks these requests in logs and spend budgets alongside other model requests. Read the decision model documentation for question types, learn what decision models are, or browse the model catalog.

title: Build cache size limit on Vercel increased to 5 GB
description:
The build cache size limit on all Vercel build machines has been increased to 5 GB. This allows projects to save more installed dependencies and framework files for reuse between deployments, which can reduce install and build times.

Build machines are the compute environments that install dependencies and build your project before deployment. Previously, caches were discarded if they exceeded 1.5 GB on Basic and Standard, 3 GB on Enhanced, or 4.75 GB on Turbo, leaving the next build without a cache.

The change applies automatically across all build machine types at no additional charge, with no configuration required.

Learn more in the build cache documentation.

title: Vercel Sandbox starts up to 4x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now initializes up to 4x faster outside the Washington, D.C. (iad1) region when reused image data is served from a regional cache.

Initialization now reads cached image data close to where the sandbox runs, avoiding round trips to origin image storage in iad1 on cache hits. Regional caching supports managed and custom images backed by Vercel Container Registry, including snapshots based on those images.

In internal end-to-end benchmarks with Vercel Managed Images, startup time fell about 75% in Paris and from about 3.5s to 1.05s in Seoul. Regions closer to origin storage generally see smaller improvements because requests already travel a shorter distance.

Learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.

Read more

title: Vercel Security Review no longer requires a linked Vercel project
description:
You can now scan code changes for vulnerabilities with Vercel Security Review in GitHub repositories that have not yet been linked to a Vercel project.

By default, Security Review covers all unlinked repositories the Vercel GitHub App can access in a connected GitHub account. You can limit coverage to selected connected accounts or individual repositories in Agent settings. Once enabled, each push to a covered repository automatically triggers a review of its code changes.

Security Review checks commits directly in repositories with Security Review enabled, without requiring a Vercel project or deployment. When a push creates a deployment for a linked project with Security Review enabled, the review uses the additional project and deployment context.

Connect the account in your team’s Git settings, then enable Security Review in Vercel Agent settings.

Get started with the Security Review documentation.

title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
description:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

Trial

Skipped quote, ordered at 24th St: $9.27

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:

Product

What a failed attempt costs the user

Metric to lead with

Order my morning coffee

Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust

Pass^k

Coding agent with a test suite

Extra time and model cost; the agent uses test feedback to revise its code and try again

Pass@k

Draft an email the user reviews

A quick edit before hitting send

Success rate

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally.

Variant

Success

Claude Code + Opus 5.5

65%

$0.22

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

Ready to run your first eval? Paste this prompt into your coding agent, and it’ll build and run one for your product on Vercel with you:

title: AI Gateway now supports Private Inference
description:
Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway.

Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs, and observability as catalog models, so every model your team uses is managed in one place.

Use Private Inference to:

  • Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID.

  • Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider.

  • Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

  • Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs, trace drains, and custom reporting. Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model.

  • Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails.

To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves.

You can also register the provider and model with the Vercel CLI, version 65.16.0 or later:

Call the model using its private/<slug> ID:

Private model requests appear in AI Gateway logs alongside requests to catalog models.

title: Introducing Vercel Board
description:
Software development is moving from individual agents completing tasks to teams of agents working on more complex projects.

A single agent can track its work in a Markdown file, but there isn't a purpose-built primitive for tracking tasks, delegation, statuses, logs, and completed work across many agents and subagents.

We ran into this coordination problem internally and started experimenting with a shared message board as a primitive on two key projects:

  • Our security agents: We deployed a swarm of agents to analyze our codebases for vulnerabilities, push fixes and updates, and now we keep track of their work via Board.

  • v0's software factory: After seeing how well Board worked for security agents, we rebuilt v0's software factory on it, and it now merges over 50% of PRs.

Along the way, we added multiple features like grants for different levels of access (for humans and agents), two-way sync for multiple tools (like Slack), and a lot more.

Today we are launching Vercel Board as an experimental agentic primitive. It packages what we've learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows.

We built Board for our own needs, but invite curious developers to test it alongside us and give feedback. It is harness agnostic and fits well into existing multi-agent reinforcement learning. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can collaborate as if they were a single harness.

How it works

Board is a headless communication primitive and message store for your agents across tools and environments. Your agents read from and write to Board through the CLI or JavaScript SDK. Install the Board skill to give your agent instructions for using it:

Each board is organized into channels and threads. A thread keeps the conversation, context, and updates together, while labels track details such as the associated pull request or current status. Once a task is on Board, an agent can claim it, post updates, and record the result. For example, a coding agent can use the CLI to find an open bug, claim it, and share a pull request for review:

The thread keeps the original report, findings, and pull request so another agent or person can review the work. Run npx @vercel/board inspect to open the Board viewer and follow activity across channels and threads in real time.

Wake agents and schedule follow-ups

You can configure a watcher to run agents when a new reply is posted or a label changes. For example, if there is a reply in Slack or by another agent, it can trigger the agent to address their feedback and post an update or pull request in the same thread. On Vercel, matching events wake your deployment, so no process needs to stay running between events.

Agents can also schedule follow-ups with vercel board schedule. For example, after an agent has opened a pull request it can remind itself to check CI in 5 minutes. This makes agents feel much more proactive, as they can check things without requiring a new message from a human. For a pull request tracked in Board thread 812, the agent would run:

Note that agents can keep internal notes and check-ins on Board with --no-sync, while sharing progress updates through connected tools.

Sync with existing tools

A task can be pushed directly to Board or synced from a connected tool like Slack or GitHub. The Board SDK handles two-way sync, mirroring replies, reactions, edits, and deletions between Board and your connected tools:

Share structured data

Messages in Board can also include structured data based on a schema you define. Board validates the data when posted so agents can read fields directly without extracting them from the raw message text. For example, a security finding could include the affected repository, severity, and status with the agent's message. Here is an example schema, security-finding@1 (where @1 is the version):

Control access to your board

A core part of why we built vercel board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability. Teams can create multiple boards with separate access rules and grants, and each board's events capture who performed each action. This is how you can use the CLI to set it up:

When working with Vercel Sandbox, use the SDK to give it board access with no credential inside the sandbox, limited to the channels and permissions you choose:

Use cases

We use Board to connect agents with our teams' existing workflows and coordinate across multiple agents. Here are the patterns we've implemented.

Coordinate work between people and agents

Your team may already be working in Slack, GitHub, Linear, etc. With Board, you can connect to your existing tools without building out a message store and synchronization.

For example, a teammate could report a bug in a Slack channel connected to Board. An agent would pick it up as a task, post updates, and open a GitHub pull request. Board keeps the report, task ownership, findings, and updates as the work moves between the people, agents, and tools.

We use this pattern for our internal software factory. Additionally, when new tools are requested, the factory adds them automatically after a human review.

Explore the Factory template →

Help agents work together

You can give agents running on different machines or in different harnesses a shared backlog, for example a set of security tickets or bugs to investigate. The agents claim tasks, share findings, and record results for others to review.

Board also supports dependencies between tasks. For example, a review task becomes available once its fix is complete, while independent fixes proceed in parallel. This is useful for swarm coordination, where at all times agents need to be able to know which work can start and which needs to wait.

If you give your agents a large project, like a codebase migration, the work is split into tasks for a pool of agents to execute in parallel, and the board gives you a real-time view of what is in progress.

Explore the Swarm template →

Get started

Liquid AI’s d1.2 and d1.2-ultra are now available on AI Gateway with audio input and bounding box support.

These decision models return structured answers instead of generating text. Ask Boolean questions for yes/no probabilities, Choice questions to select a category, or Score questions to rate an input against a rubric. Multiple questions can share the same input in one request.

d1.2 is the faster, lower-cost model. d1.2-ultra is Liquid AI’s most accurate decision model.

Use liquid/d1.2 or liquid/d1.2-ultra as the model name. Before running the examples, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY to an AI Gateway API key.

Classify a voicemail with AI SDK 7

Pass audio as a file part in state. This example reads voicemail.flac and returns the probability that the caller is requesting a refund. It requires ai 7.0.136 or later.

For image classification, pass image bytes with the matching media type, such as image/png.

Locate an object with the Decisions API

Box questions return top and bottom as fractions of the image height, and left and right as fractions of its width.

This Python example uses the Decisions API to locate a signature in form.png and print its bounding box:

Decision requests appear in AI Gateway logs and count toward budgets.

Learn more in the decision model documentation, or browse all decision models.

title: Vercel Billing CLI is now available
description:
You can now check your team’s billing overview, review and download invoices, and preview upcoming charges with the Vercel CLI. All billing commands, including usage and budgets, are now grouped under vercel billing.

Billing overview and invoice history are available on all plans, subject to your team’s existing billing permissions. Upcoming invoice estimates require an active paid subscription.

Billing overview

Check your team’s plan, billing status, billing cycle, balance due, and overdue invoices:

In CLI 65.17.0 and later, this overview also includes configured invoice details such as your billing address, tax ID, and purchase order.

Invoices and upcoming charges

Use vercel billing invoices to review invoices, download PDFs, and preview upcoming charges. For inspect and download, replace <INVOICE_ID> with a full invoice ID from the list output:

title: Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました
description:
（本記事は、英語版の就任発表の日本語訳に、花尾本人の就任のご挨拶を加えたものです。）

Vercel日本法人の代表に、花尾和成が就任いたしました（東京拠点）。今後、Vercelは花尾とともに国内のチームを拡充し、日本市場への投資をさらに進めていきます。

弊社が10年以上前に公開したNext.jsを、日本の開発者の皆さまはいち早く使い始めてくださいました。そして現在、日本では三菱商事、富士通、U-NEXT、ディー・エヌ・エーといった大企業から、SANUや令和トラベルといったスタートアップまで、幅広い企業にVercelをご利用いただいています。

花尾はこの10年間、日本でソフトウェア企業の運営にリーダーシップを発揮してきました。前職ではPendoの日本法人社長を務め、それ以前にはHashiCorpの日本事業を立ち上げ、Pivotalの東京オフィスで営業部門を統括しました。

就任にあたり、花尾から皆さまへのメッセージをご紹介します。

このたび、Vercelの日本法人代表に就任いたしました花尾和成です。私は20年以上IT業界に身を置き、そのうち10年以上は、開発者が開発そのものに集中できるようにするプロダクトに携わってまいりました。この経験を活かし、日本の開発者の皆さまと、その先にあるビジネスの価値を最大化することに貢献してまいります。

Vercelには、CEOのギシェルモ・ラウチを筆頭に、日本を好きなメンバーが数多くいます。こうした仲間の後押しを受けながら素晴らしいチームをつくり、Vercelが日本市場にとってかけがえのない存在となることを目指します。そして究極的には、直接的にも間接的にも、Vercelが日本のあらゆる場所で使われている世界を実現したいと考えています。

今後ともご指導ご鞭撻のほど、よろしくお願い申し上げます。

ここからは、私（Nick Bogaty, CRO）が聞き手を務めた花尾へのインタビューをお届けします。日本市場にどのような可能性を感じているのか、Vercelへの入社を決めた理由とあわせて伺いました。

Vercelが日本でさらに成長できるとお考えなのは、なぜですか？

日本のソフトウェア開発は、まさに転換期を迎えています。日本には革新的な企業が多く、高い技術力を持つ開発者の皆さまが活躍されています。一方で、多くの企業では既存のシステムが複雑になり、最先端のAIの導入がなかなか進んでいません。その結果、AIを十分に活用できていないケースもあります。

日本企業がAIのポテンシャルを引き出すには、AIを試す段階から本番運用へ進む必要があります。Vercelは、その一歩を後押しできると考えています。AIアプリケーションを大規模に、安全かつ安定して、効率よく運用できるよう支える。これはまさに、Vercelが強みを発揮できる領域です。

そして、AIにかかるコストをどう管理するか、どんなルールで運用するか、セキュリティをどう確保するか。いまやどれも技術部門だけでなく、経営陣にとっても優先課題です。最近お会いした経営幹部の方々も、こうした課題に取り組んでいると口をそろえておっしゃっていました。この点でも、Vercelは日本企業の力になれると考えています。

Vercelへの入社を決めた理由をお聞かせください。

複雑なことをシンプルにし、企業がもっとすばやく動けるようにする。以前から、そんなテクノロジーに魅力を感じてきました。Vercelなら、これまで私が取り組んできたことを、さらに大きな規模で実現できると思ったのです。いま、AIはソフトウェアの開発から運用まで、そのあり方を変えつつあります。そのなかで、Vercelは次世代のアプリケーションを支える基盤になれると考えています。

入社の決め手になったのは、Vercelのビジョンと、開発者の皆さまを第一に考える文化です。そして、日本で一から事業をつくっていけることにも惹かれました。私がやりがいを感じるのは、事業を立ち上げ、優れた人材を集め、チームが主体的に難しい課題に挑める環境をつくることです。Vercelでは、私自身が可能性を信じている技術を軸に、そうした仕事に取り組めると思いました。

グローバル企業の日本事業を立ち上げるなかで、何を学ばれましたか？

事業を軌道に乗せるには、売上を伸ばすだけでは足りません。まずは仲間を集め、同じ目標に向かって力を合わせることが大切です。お客様やパートナー企業の信頼を得ることも欠かせません。そして、チームの一人ひとりが当事者意識を持ち、みずから動ける文化をつくること。そうした積み重ねが、事業の土台になります。

世界で生まれる新しい技術を、日本で暮らす方々が日々使うサービスに活かし、身近な課題の解決につなげることの大切さも学びました。CEOのギシェルモと出会った頃、日本で使われる数えきれないほどのデジタルサービスがVercel上で動く未来について語り合いました。Vercelの名前を知らない人にも、日々使うサービスを通じて、私たちの技術の価値が届く。私が実現したいのは、そんな「Vercel Everywhere」の未来です。

2027年に向けた取り組み

2027年には、Vercelの代表的なカンファレンス「Ship」を初めて東京で開催します。Vercelの社員だけでなく、Vercelを活用してサービスを開発する日本企業の皆さまからも、それぞれの取り組みについて直接お聞きいただける機会となるよう準備を進めています。詳細は年明けにvercel.com/shipでお知らせいたします。

また、東京オフィスのチームも拡充します。営業、ソリューションエンジニアリング、パートナーシップの各分野で仲間を増やし、日本のお客様をより手厚くサポートできる体制をつくります。クラスメソッド、AWS Japan、Sitecore Japanといったパートナー企業との連携も、さらに深めていきます。日本での採用情報については、採用ページにて順次お知らせします。

title: Kazunari Hanao joins Vercel as Country Manager, Japan
description:
日本語版はこちら：Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました

Kazunari Hanao has joined Vercel as Country Manager for Japan, based in Tokyo. His appointment is part of our continued investment in the Japanese market, including plans to expand our local team.

Japanese developers were early adopters of Next.js. And today, Vercel's customers in Japan include Mitsubishi Corporation, Fujitsu Limited, U-NEXT CO., Ltd., and DeNA Co., Ltd., alongside startups like SANU Inc. and Reiwa Travel, Inc.

Kazunari has spent the last decade building and leading software businesses in Japan. He joins Vercel from Pendo, where he was President of Pendo Japan. Before that, he built HashiCorp’s Japan business and spent nearly five years in sales leadership at Pivotal in Tokyo.

I asked him about the opportunity in Japan and his decision to join Vercel.

Why are you optimistic about Vercel's future in Japan?

Japan is at a turning point in how software gets built. The country has innovative companies and talented developers, but complex enterprise IT environments are slowing the adoption of frontier AI to the point that businesses can’t capture its value.

Vercel’s opportunity is to help Japanese enterprises move from experimentation to production, and run AI applications securely, reliably, and efficiently at scale. Cost, governance, and security for AI have become business priorities, not just technical ones. Almost every CXO I've met recently is working through those questions.

What interested you in working for Vercel?

I've always been drawn to technology that simplifies complexity and helps businesses move faster. Vercel felt like a natural continuation of that, with bigger potential. AI is transforming the whole software development lifecycle, and Vercel has a real chance to become a foundational platform for the next generation of applications.

Ultimately what convinced me was the vision, the developer-first culture, and the chance to build something in Japan from the ground up. I enjoy building businesses, bringing talented people together, and creating an environment where teams feel empowered to take on hard problems. Vercel gives me the chance to do that with technology I believe in.

What have you learned building businesses in Japan for global companies?

Building a successful business is about much more than growing revenue. It starts with bringing together the right people, uniting them around a shared goal, earning the trust of customers and partners, and building a culture where every team member feels ownership.

I've also learned how much it matters to connect global innovation with the specific needs of Japanese customers. During our first meetings, Guillermo and I talked about a future where countless digital services in Japan run on Vercel, and people experience its value every day whether they realize it or not. "Vercel Everywhere" is the future I want to build.

What’s next in 2027

We're bringing our flagship conference, Ship, to Tokyo for the first time in 2027. It's a chance to hear directly from the Vercel team and from Japanese companies building on the platform. We'll share more details at vercel.com/ship in the new year.

We’re also growing our Tokyo team across sales, solutions engineering, and partnerships. A larger local team will help us support Japanese customers and deepen our partnerships with Classmethod, AWS Japan, and Sitecore Japan. Watch our careers page for upcoming opportunities in Japan.

title: Inkling 2 Mini now available on AI Gateway
description:
Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines is now available on AI Gateway. The small multimodal reasoning model is built for agentic coding, tool use, and knowledge work, with text and image inputs and text output.

Inkling 2 Mini has 26.4 billion total parameters and 3.4 billion active per token. The model runs its middle layers more than once for every token, which lets it reason further before writing anything down and often reach an answer with fewer reasoning tokens. Like Inkling 2 Small, it is strongest on long-running agentic tasks.

The model has a 1M-token context window, and reasoning effort can be set from none through max.

Use thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Inkling 2 Mini in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: Delete a run's data on demand in Workflow SDK
description:
The Workflow SDK now lets you delete a finished run's stored data on demand. This feature gives you the ability to quickly meet compliance and security requirements when sensitive data needs to be purged from run payloads.

Deleting a run's data deletes any inputs, outputs, hook payloads, and error traces for the run and its related entities. This does not delete the run's metadata: the run is still listed in observability. Attributes, hook tokens, and timings for steps and events can still be inspected.

You can delete a run's data from the Vercel Dashboard, or via the CLI:

You can also delete a run's data programmatically from your code:

Deletion applies to finished runs only, so a run that is still going is skipped and keeps running. If you want to delete a run's payload as soon as it finishes, use the retention settings instead.

Upgrade to workflow@5.7.0 or higher to use this feature. Learn more in the deleteRuns() reference.

Read more

title: Agents can now manage AI Gateway through Vercel MCP
description:
Your agent can now manage AI Gateway through Vercel MCP. Ask it in plain language to:

  • Manage virtual models: Create reusable model IDs with saved settings, then list, inspect, update, or restore them.

  • Configure routing rules: View, add, and update team-wide rules that redirect requests to another model or block them.

  • Set spending budgets: View and set budgets for your team, projects, and members, and configure defaults.

To create a virtual model, for example, ask your agent:

Create a virtual model named coding-agent that uses anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 with Zero Data Retention enabled.

Your apps and coding agents using AI Gateway can then use vmc/coding-agent as the model ID. You can change its model or settings later without updating those clients or redeploying your app.

To get started, connect your agent to Vercel MCP with team-level access and the required AI Gateway permissions. Your Vercel team permissions still apply.

title: Flags SDK now works on Vercel without FLAGS_SECRET
description:
With flags@4.5.0, projects on Vercel can use Flags Explorer and precompute without FLAGS_SECRET. That cuts out a setup step for new projects and removes the need to keep a shared secret in sync across microfrontends.

Vercel signs Flags Explorer discovery requests and overrides, and the SDK encrypts flag values shown in the Vercel Toolbar with Vercel’s public key.

Existing projects keep using FLAGS_SECRET while the environment variable is set or the secret is passed in code. Upgrading alone doesn't switch them to Vercel-managed keys. To use Vercel-managed keys for these features, remove the environment variable and any code that passes the secret explicitly. For local development, run vercel env pull.

Precomputed codes created without a secret work only in the deployment that created them. Precompute without a secret requires Vercel system environment variables, which are enabled by default. Prebuilt deployments and codes that must work across deployments still need a secret; use FLAGS_PRECOMPUTE_SECRET if only precompute needs one. If you use a build cache, see the precompute documentation for the required configuration.

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

Read more

title: AWS PrivateLink endpoints are now available on Secure Compute
description:
Enterprise teams using Secure Compute can now create and manage AWS PrivateLink endpoints directly from the Vercel dashboard.

Endpoints on Secure Compute live in your team's dedicated VPC and use the network's AWS region. They belong to the network and are shared by its connected project environments.

Vercel Functions, Vercel Sandbox, and builds connected to the network can reach AWS-hosted backends over the AWS private network. Before you add an endpoint in Vercel, the backend must already be exposed through a published AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. Examples include RDS, Aurora, Redshift, Snowflake, MongoDB Atlas, and internal services behind a Network Load Balancer.

In Team Settings → Networking, open your Secure Compute network and choose Add Endpoint from the PrivateLink tab.

Standard pricing for new endpoints:

  • Each Secure Compute network includes one AWS PrivateLink endpoint. Additional endpoints cost $30 per month each.

  • PrivateLink data transfer costs $0.04 per GB.

Read the Secure Compute PrivateLink documentation to get started.

description:
All Vercel Sandbox runtimes now use Vercel Managed Images (VMIs).

Legacy runtimes, such as node22, now use the open-source images in the vercel/sandbox repository, distributed through Vercel Container Registry (VCR). Sandboxes created with these now come with 64 GB of storage and use the same infrastructure as sandboxes powered by VCR.
