title: Death chest plugins for Paper 1.21 - what to look for (and why I wrote one)
description:
Running an SMP or lifesteal server on Paper 1.21? A death chest plugin is close to mandatory - players quit when they lose a netherite kit to lava. Here is what to look for, and why I ended up writing my own.

What a death chest plugin needs

  • Item + XP storage - most plugins forget the XP
  • Protection timer - the owner's grave should not be lootable instantly, but it also should not be permanent
  • Overflow handling - a player with a full inventory plus a shulker box can drop more than one chest holds. Items must never silently vanish
  • Findability - a hologram timer helps, a return compass is better
  • Configurability - protection time, hologram text, despawn behavior

Why I wrote GraveGuard

The free options I tried either dropped XP, had no overflow handling (items silently deleted - this is the bug that makes players furious), or were abandoned before 1.21. So I built one and open-sourced it:

  • Death spawns a grave chest with items + XP
  • Hologram countdown over the grave
  • Protection timer in config (default 5 minutes)
  • Return compass points the owner back
  • Excess items drop next to the grave instead of disappearing

It is MIT-licensed, tested on Paper 1.21.11 with automated bot clients.

Links

  • Download: https://hangar.papermc.io/SecondWindMC/GraveGuard
  • Source: https://github.com/SecondWindMC/GraveGuard
  • Docs + config reference: https://secondwindmc.github.io/docs.html

Happy to answer questions in the comments.

title: CCDV-P Exam: How I'm Preparing for the Claude Certified Developer – Professional
description:
Anthropic quietly added a fifth Claude certification in November 2026: Claude Certified Developer – Professional (CCDV-P). If you already build with the Claude API, this is the one that tests whether you can actually operate those systems once real users depend on them.

Here's what I've learned from the exam guide so far, and how I'm planning to prepare.

The CCDV-P exam in one table

Item Detail
Questions 70 (60 scored, 10 unscored)
Type Scenario-based multiple-choice / multiple-response
Time 120 minutes
Passing score 720 (scaled 100–1,000)
Fee $175
Delivery Pearson VUE, online or test centre
Validity 12 months, free renewal if on time
Eligibility Claude Partner Network companies

The 8 domains (and where I'll spend my time)

  1. Production integration, reliability and knowledge grounding – 20%
  2. Advanced agent architecture and orchestration – 17%
  3. Observability and production monitoring – 12%
  4. Evaluation engineering and quality assurance – 12%
  5. Runtime guardrails and production security – 11%
  6. Advanced debugging and incident response – 10%
  7. Agent fleet operations for software delivery – 10%
  8. Cost and latency optimisation at scale – 8%

Domains 3, 6 and 7 have no equivalent in Developer – Foundations (CCDV-F), so that's where I expect the biggest gap.

My hands-on plan

Instead of reading docs, I'm taking one small agent and "productionising" it step by step:

  • Reliability: retries with backoff, timeouts, idempotent tools, a fallback model
  • Observability: trace every model + tool call, log tokens, alert on error rate and p95 latency
  • Evals: a 30-case eval set that runs on every prompt change, plus a few LLM-as-judge checks
  • Security: prompt-injection test cases mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
  • Incident drill: break something on purpose and write a short postmortem
  • Cost: add prompt caching and compare model tiers on the eval set

I wrote a longer guide with the full domain breakdown, CCDV-F vs CCDV-P comparison and a 6-week plan here: CCDV-P Exam Guide 2026

Has anyone booked CCDV-P yet? I'd love to know whether the scenarios lean more towards debugging or architecture.

title: Checking Stainless Steel PREN from a Mill Certificate in Python
description:
If you buy or specify stainless steel for chloride service, sooner or later someone asks for a minimum PREN. The datasheet says 316L is "about 24" and 254 SMO is "about 43". The certificate that arrives with the material has its own numbers. They are not the same thing, and a few lines of Python make the difference easy to see.

What PREN is

PREN (Pitting Resistance Equivalent Number) is a quick ranking of how well a stainless steel resists pitting in chlorides. It is calculated from the chemistry, in weight percent:

PREN = Cr + 3.3 × (Mo + 0.5 × W) + 16 × N

Chromium builds the passive film, molybdenum and tungsten help it survive chlorides, and nitrogen adds a surprising amount for such a small number. Most specifications use 16 for nitrogen; some duplex specifications use 30, so check which one your document asks for.

PREN is a ranking tool, not a guarantee. Temperature, crevices, deposits and welding all matter. But it is the number that shows up in purchase specs, so it is worth calculating correctly.

The formula in code 

def pren(cr, mo, n=0.0, w=0.0, n_factor=16):
    """Cr + 3.3 * (Mo + 0.5 * W) + n_factor * N, all in wt%."""
    return cr + 3.3 * (mo + 0.5 * w) + n_factor * n

The standard gives a range, not a number

Each grade's standard allows a range for every element. Feed the minimums and maximums into the formula and you get the PREN range the standard permits:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Grade:
    name: str
    uns: str
    cr: tuple  # (min, max) wt%
    mo: tuple
    n: tuple = (0.0, 0.0)

    def pren_range(self, n_factor=16):
        low = pren(self.cr[0], self.mo[0], self.n[0], n_factor=n_factor)
        high = pren(self.cr[1], self.mo[1], self.n[1], n_factor=n_factor)
        return round(low, 1), round(high, 1)


GRADES = [
    Grade("316L", "S31603", cr=(16.0, 18.0), mo=(2.0, 3.0), n=(0.0, 0.10)),
    Grade("317L", "S31703", cr=(18.0, 20.0), mo=(3.0, 4.0), n=(0.0, 0.10)),
    Grade("904L", "N08904", cr=(19.0, 23.0), mo=(4.0, 5.0), n=(0.0, 0.10)),
    Grade("2205", "S32205", cr=(22.0, 23.0), mo=(3.0, 3.5), n=(0.14, 0.20)),
    Grade("254 SMO", "S31254", cr=(19.5, 20.5), mo=(6.0, 6.5), n=(0.18, 0.25)),
]

for g in GRADES:
    low, high = g.pren_range()
    print(f"{g.name:<8} {g.uns}  PREN {low:>5} - {high:<5}")

Output:

316L     S31603  PREN  22.6 - 29.5
317L     S31703  PREN  27.9 - 34.8
904L     N08904  PREN  32.2 - 41.1
2205     S32205  PREN  34.1 - 37.8
254 SMO  S31254  PREN  42.2 - 46.0

Two things stand out.

316L can legally be below 24. A heat that sits near the bottom of the chromium and molybdenum ranges is still 316L, but its PREN is closer to 23. If your spec says "316L, PREN ≥ 24", that is a real extra requirement, not a restatement of the grade.

The ranges overlap. A rich 904L heat can match a lean 2205 heat. Grade names are a good shortlist; the chemistry on the certificate is what you actually receive.

Check the heat, not the grade

So the useful check is against the actual heat analysis on the EN 10204 3.1 certificate:

def check_heat(heat_no, chem, required, n_factor=16):
    value = pren(chem["Cr"], chem["Mo"], chem.get("N", 0.0),
                 chem.get("W", 0.0), n_factor=n_factor)
    status = "OK" if value >= required else "BELOW"
    print(f"{heat_no}: PREN {value:.1f} (required >= {required}) -> {status}")
    return value


# Two 316L heats, both inside the standard
check_heat("Heat A", {"Cr": 16.6, "Mo": 2.02, "N": 0.03}, required=24)
check_heat("Heat B", {"Cr": 17.2, "Mo": 2.45, "N": 0.06}, required=24)

Heat A: PREN 23.7 (required >= 24) -> BELOW
Heat B: PREN 26.2 (required >= 24) -> OK

Both heats are valid 316L. Only one meets the project requirement. If you only checked the grade name, you would accept both.

Do not drop nitrogen

The second trap is missing data. Nitrogen is multiplied by 16, so a 6Mo grade such as 254 SMO gets around 3 PREN points from nitrogen alone. Handheld XRF analysers, the usual tool for PMI, cannot measure nitrogen (or carbon). If someone builds the PREN from a PMI reading, nitrogen silently becomes zero:

# A 254 SMO heat against a seawater-style requirement
check_heat("Heat C", {"Cr": 19.6, "Mo": 6.0, "N": 0.19}, required=40)

# Same heat, nitrogen left out (e.g. typed in from a handheld XRF reading)
check_heat("Heat C (no N)", {"Cr": 19.6, "Mo": 6.0}, required=40)

Heat C: PREN 42.4 (required >= 40) -> OK
Heat C (no N): PREN 39.4 (required >= 40) -> BELOW

Same metal, opposite verdict. PMI is good for confirming the grade (Cr, Ni, Mo), but the PREN should come from the certificate's heat analysis, where nitrogen is reported.

If you turn this into a real tool, make nitrogen a required field and raise an error when it is missing, instead of defaulting to zero.

A few practical notes

  • State the formula in the spec. "PREN ≥ 40 calculated as Cr + 3.3Mo + 16N from the heat analysis" leaves far less room for argument than "PREN ≥ 40".
  • Duplex grades: confirm whether the nitrogen factor is 16 or 30. The same 2205 heat can differ by more than 2 points depending on the factor.
  • Nickel alloys: you can run the formula on alloy 625 or C-276 and get big numbers, but PREN was developed for stainless steels. For nickel alloys, rely on corrosion data rather than PREN alone.
  • Welds: the weld metal and heat-affected zone usually pit before the base metal. A high base-metal PREN does not help if the filler metal is under-alloyed.

Wrap-up

The datasheet PREN tells you which grades to shortlist. The certificate tells you what you bought. Calculating from the actual heat analysis, keeping nitrogen in, and writing the formula into the spec avoids most PREN disputes before they start.

If you are looking at 6Mo grades for seawater or chloride-heavy process lines, here is a reference page with forms and specs for 254 SMO stainless steel (UNS S31254).

title: AI model failover that never failed back: 17 days on a local model
description:
My AI agents run on paid models through OpenRouter, with a local model on my own GPU as the safety net. A little script I call the canary checks every 3 hours that the paid model still works. If it doesn't, it moves the agents down to the local model so they keep running.

On 7 September 2026 it did exactly that. Then it sat there for 17 days saying everything was fine, while four of my agents ran on a slower local model for no reason at all.

Two bugs, stacked. One in the probe, one in the "come back" logic. Both are worth knowing about if you've built any kind of automatic failover.

How the canary works

Every 3 hours it does two things:

  • Checks the money. A model you can't pay for is still an outage. Below a floor it moves the agents to local and alerts. On a top-up it moves them back.
  • Checks the model. It sends a tiny tool-calling test: "What is the weather in Reykjavik? Use the tool." A healthy model calls get_weather with city set to Reykjavik. Anything else counts as a failure.

Transient stuff like a 429, a 5xx, a timeout or a DNS blip never counts. Only a "hard" failure does, like a wrong answer or a dead model id. And it needs 2 hard failures in a row before it does anything. Then it walks a ladder of other paid models from different vendors, and only if all of them fail does it drop to local.

I built the ladder vendor-diverse on purpose, because a fallback that fails the same way as the primary isn't a fallback. Keep that line in mind, it comes back.

7 September: everything fails at once

This is the canary's own log from that day. Nothing retyped, just the lines from the file, with my agent profile names swapped for placeholders:

Read the model replies. They're not broken. They're being sensible. The first one starts "It looks like you've left a placeholder".

Every model was seeing [ADDRESS] where my probe said Reykjavik. OpenRouter had PII redaction switched on for my account, and it decided a city name was personal data. So it swapped the city out before any model saw it.

The primary failed twice. Then the ladder: qwen/qwen3.7-flash called the tool with {'city': '[ADDRESS]'}, which is a fair attempt honestly, and google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite asked me which city I meant. Both "failed". So the canary concluded no OpenRouter model was usable and reverted four agent profiles to the local qwen3.5-64k.

That's the bit I keep coming back to. Three models from three different vendors all failed within a few seconds of each other, the same way. That isn't three models dying. That's my input being broken. Vendor diversity does nothing for you when the thing they all share is your probe.

The redaction caused other mess around the same time too. One of my ops agents built an SSH command with [IP_ADDRESS] where the IP should have been, because its own command got redacted. A brand name in a research task came back as [PERSON_NAME]. I turned PII redaction off on 15 September and checked that IPs, brand names, emails and phone numbers went through untouched after that.

Then 17 days of "nothing to watch"

Turning the redaction off should have fixed it. Next canary run, probe passes, agents move back. Except they didn't, and this is the second bug.

After the revert, every run logged this:

profiles are on local Ollama and no credit revert is pending -- nothing to watch

The canary only had a "come back" path for one kind of revert: running low on credit. When it moved agents to local because the money ran low, it set a flag, and every run after that checked the balance and moved them back on a top-up.

A revert because the models failed set no flag at all. So on the next run the canary looked around, saw no OpenRouter primary configured, saw no credit revert pending, and decided there was nothing for it to do. It exited cleanly. Every 3 hours. It logged that line 134 times between 7 September 18:00 and 24 September 09:00.

And money was never the problem. On the day it reverted the log shows $7.81 of $10 left.

Nothing alerted on it either. The revert itself posted to Discord once, on 7 September. After that the canary was "healthy" by every measure I had: it ran on time, it exited 0, its log was full of tidy lines.

The fix, 24 September

Small change, in the end. A failover revert now sets its own flag, reverted_for_failover, the same way a credit revert always did. Every run that finds a flag set probes the paid ladder again. The first model that passes gets the agents back, the flag is cleared, and Discord gets a "💚 OpenRouter back" message. If none pass, it stays local, logs "will retry" and tries again in 3 hours.

This is the actual check now, straight from the script:

if primary is None and (st.get("reverted_for_credit") or st.get("reverted_for_failover")):
    for model, ctx, pin, pout in PAID_LADDER:
        ok, kind, detail = probe(model, key)
        if ok:
            changed = switch_primary(model, ctx, "creditrestore")
            ...

I set the flag by hand, ran it, and all four profiles went back to qwen/qwen3.7-flash at 14:31 that day. The 15:00 run logged probe: qwen/qwen3.7-flash ok. While I was in there I also gave every profile the same chain: qwen/qwen3.7-flash, then deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 as a paid fallback from a different vendor, then local, then a free model last. One profile had no paid fallback at all before that.

Same silence, different door

There's a comment in that script now about a related bug. The canary used to work out the current primary by reading one agent's config, the coding agent. When I moved that agent to a different provider, the function returned "no OpenRouter primary", and the main loop read that as "everything's local, nothing to watch". Silent off-switch, again, for every other agent. It reads the top-level config now, which always stays on OpenRouter.

Two different routes to the same line in the log. I think that line is the real bug. "Nothing to watch" should be something you can only reach on purpose.

What I'd do differently

  • If every vendor fails the same way at the same time, suspect your probe. There's no guard for this in the canary yet. The obvious one is: if the whole ladder fails with the same kind of error, alert loudly and don't revert.
  • Every automatic "go down" needs an automatic "come back". And they should share one flag, not one per reason. I had a return path for the failure I thought of first and none for the one that actually happened.
  • Probe with something boring. A city name looked harmless. Anything that a privacy filter, a content filter or a moderation layer could touch will one day get touched. A made-up token is a lot less likely to look like personal data than a real place name.
  • "Healthy and idle" needs to look different from "healthy and busy". A log line that says nothing is wrong every 3 hours for 17 days is just noise. If a monitor has nothing to monitor for more than a day, that should be a message.

Does your failover ever fail back on its own? I'd check. Mine only did for one of the two reasons it could leave.

🤖 Drafted with AI assistance from my own homelab notes, logs and repos, and fact-checked against them before publishing.

title: 파이썬 자격증 종류와 공신력 비교: 초보자에게 적합한 자격증 선택 방법
description:
PCEP·PCAP·PCPP, COS Pro, 정보처리기사는 모두 Python 학습과 함께 언급되지만 시행기관, 평가 범위, 자격의 제도적 성격이 다릅니다. 2026년 9월 13일에 확인한 공식 범위와 편집자의 선택 기준을 분리해 비교합니다.

자격의 성격부터 구분합니다

Python Institute의 자격은 Python 역량을 단계별로 평가하는 국제 민간 자격 체계입니다. YBM의 COS Pro는 국내에 등록된 비공인 민간자격이며, 정보처리기사는 한국산업인력공단이 시행하는 국가기술자격입니다. 서로 다른 제도를 한 줄로 세워 공신력 순위를 매기기보다 필요한 증명 범위를 먼저 정해야 합니다.

자격 2026년 9월 13일 공식 상태 공식 평가 범위 자격 성격
PCEP PCEP-30-02 활성 자료형, 연산자, 입출력, 조건·반복, 컬렉션, 함수, 예외 등 Python 입문 Python Institute의 Entry 단계 자격, 선수 조건 없음, 유효기간 5년
PCAP PCAP-31-03 활성 모듈·패키지, 예외, 문자열, 객체지향, 리스트 컴프리헨션·람다·클로저, 파일 입출력 Python Institute의 Associate 단계 자격
PCPP1 PCPP-32-101 활성 고급 객체지향, 코딩 표준, GUI, 네트워크 통신, 파일·데이터 처리 Python Institute의 Professional 단계 1 자격
PCPP2 공식 로드맵에서 개발 중 현재 활성 시험 범위 없음 접수 가능한 활성 자격으로 취급하면 안 됨
COS Pro Python 1·2·3급 운영 프로그램 이해·설계, 구현, 검사·수정 중심의 실기 YBM 발급 등록 비공인 민간자격
정보처리기사 2026년 기사 시험 운영 필기 5과목과 정보처리 실무: 소프트웨어·DB·프로그래밍 언어·정보시스템 전반 과학기술정보통신부 관련, 한국산업인력공단 시행 국가기술자격

Python Institute 공식 자격 로드맵은 PCEP, PCAP, PCPP1을 활성 상태로 표시하고 PCPP2는 개발 중으로 표시합니다. 따라서 현재 선택표에서 PCPP2를 취득 가능한 심화 자격처럼 추천하지 않습니다. 2026년 10월 18일 다시 확인한 PCPP2 시험 안내도 시험과 출제범위를 개발 중으로 표시합니다. 같은 날 YBM COS Pro 안내에서는 Python 1·2·3급을 등록 비공인 민간자격으로 안내했습니다.

Q-Net이 안내하는 정보처리기사 필기 과목은 소프트웨어 설계, 소프트웨어 개발, 데이터베이스 구축, 프로그래밍 언어 활용, 정보시스템 구축 관리이며 실기는 정보처리 실무입니다. Python만을 평가하는 시험이 아니므로 Python 문법 인증과 국내 국가기술자격이라는 목적을 분리해야 합니다.

사실 비교와 선택 기준을 분리합니다

위 표의 시행기관·활성 상태·공식 범위는 각 기관 자료에서 확인한 사실입니다. 아래 판단표는 그 사실을 바탕으로 한 Briefold 편집자의 선택 기준이며, 채용 가점이나 합격을 보장하는 기준이 아닙니다. 실제 우대 여부는 지원하려는 학교·회사·기관의 공고에서 확인해야 합니다.

목표 현재 수준 국내 활용 목적 먼저 검토할 선택지 판단 이유
Python 기초 범위를 점검합니다 조건문·반복문·함수를 학습하는 단계 특정 국가자격 요건이 없습니다 PCEP 또는 COS Pro 3급 Python 입문 범위나 기초 실기 문제에 집중할 수 있습니다
Python 프로그램 구조를 점검합니다 모듈·예외·객체지향을 사용합니다 Python 역량을 별도로 제시합니다 PCAP 활성 시험 범위가 다중 모듈과 객체지향까지 이어집니다
고급 Python 범위를 점검합니다 객체지향·네트워크·파일 처리를 실습했습니다 국제 민간 자격 경로를 따릅니다 PCPP1 현재 활성 Professional 단계이며 PCPP2는 아직 개발 중입니다
코딩 실기를 점검합니다 제한 시간 안에 문제를 구현합니다 국내 교육·평가 자료로 활용합니다 COS Pro의 수준별 샘플 문제 확인 후 급수 선택 등록 비공인 민간자격이고 급수별 평가 수준이 다릅니다
IT 전반의 국가기술자격이 필요합니다 Python 외에 DB·설계·시스템도 준비합니다 응시 자격이나 우대 요건을 공고에서 확인했습니다 정보처리기사 Python 전용 시험이 아니라 IT 전반의 필기와 실기를 평가합니다

선택 순서는 세 질문으로 정합니다

  1. 지원 공고나 학습 과정에 특정 자격이 명시돼 있습니까? 명시돼 있다면 그 자격의 공식 응시 조건과 최신 출제기준을 먼저 확인합니다.
  2. Python 자체의 범위를 증명하려 합니까? 입문이면 PCEP, 모듈·객체지향까지 다루면 PCAP, 고급 객체지향·네트워크·파일 처리까지 준비했다면 PCPP1의 현재 syllabus를 비교합니다.
  3. 국내 코딩 실기나 IT 전반의 국가기술자격이 목적입니까? 코딩 실기 중심이면 COS Pro 샘플 문제와 급수를, IT 전반이면 정보처리기사의 응시 자격과 2026년 출제기준을 확인합니다.

어느 경로든 자격증만으로 구현 능력을 모두 보여주기는 어렵습니다. 시험 범위와 같은 수준의 작은 프로그램, 테스트 결과, README를 함께 남기면 자신이 실제로 다룬 범위를 구체적으로 설명할 수 있습니다.

입문 코드의 실행 여부를 확인합니다

아래 예시는 average 변수에 점수를 저장한 뒤 조건문으로 통과 여부를 판정하는 최소 코드입니다.

scores = [72, 85, 91]
average = sum(scores) / len(scores)

if average >= 80:
    print("기초 문법 학습 완료")
else:
    print("반복 학습이 필요합니다")

이 코드를 실행하면 기초 문법 학습 완료가 출력됩니다. 이 예시는 자격별 난이도를 판정하지 않습니다. PCEP와 COS Pro의 입문 범위에서 변수, 리스트, 산술 연산, 조건문을 설명할 수 있는지 확인하는 최소 실행 예시입니다.

2026년 10월 18일 네트워크가 없는 격리 컨테이너의 Python 3.11.17에서 위 목록을 실행해 같은 출력을 확인했습니다. 입력을 빈 목록 []으로 바꾸면 len(scores)가 0이어서 ZeroDivisionError가 발생했습니다. 실제 프로그램에서는 평균을 계산하기 전에 목록이 비어 있는지 확인하고, 값이 없을 때 안내하거나 입력을 다시 받아야 합니다. 이 확인은 예제 코드에 한정되며 시험 문제를 실행한 결과는 아닙니다.

Python 예제 실행 순서

  1. 입력: 점수 72·85·91
  2. 계산: 합계 248을 3으로 나눔
  3. 판정: 평균이 80 이상인지 확인
  4. 출력: 기초 문법 학습 완료

접수 전 공식 페이지를 다시 확인합니다

시험 버전, 일정, 응시료, 유효기간은 바뀔 수 있습니다. Python Institute는 각 시험 페이지의 활성 버전과 syllabus를, YBM은 COS Pro 급수·일정·민간자격 정보를, Q-Net은 정보처리기사의 응시 자격·일정·출제기준을 각각 안내합니다. 이 글의 확인 날짜 이후에는 접수 직전 해당 기관 페이지를 다시 확인합니다.

Python 입문 범위 확인은 PCEP나 COS Pro의 해당 급수부터 비교하고, 모듈과 객체지향까지 학습했다면 PCAP을 검토합니다. PCPP1은 고급 범위를 준비한 뒤 선택하며, PCPP2는 2026년 10월 18일 재확인 당시에도 개발 중이므로 활성 시험처럼 계획하지 않습니다. 국내 국가기술자격이 필요한 경우에는 Python 전용 자격과 목적이 다른 정보처리기사를 별도로 검토합니다.

관련 글

  • 인공지능·데이터 분야 진입을 위한 컴퓨터자격증과 함께 준비할 실무 역량

이 글의 원문은 파이썬 자격증 종류와 공신력 비교: 초보자에게 적합한 자격증 선택 방법 에 있습니다. (Originally published on Briefold)

title: Building a Public Site with Astro: A Step-by-Step Guide
description:
Understanding the Challenge

Creating a public-facing website that is both performant and scalable is a significant challenge for developers. As users increasingly demand faster load times and seamless interactions, the need for efficient web technologies has never been more critical. A performant site not only enhances user experience but also positively impacts search engine rankings and conversion rates. In this context, selecting the right technology stack is crucial to achieving these goals.

One of the primary challenges is ensuring that the site can handle varying levels of traffic without compromising on speed. A static site generator like Astro can be a game-changer in this regard. By pre-rendering pages at build time, static sites deliver content swiftly, reducing server load and latency. This approach is especially beneficial for sites that serve content primarily to the public, where page views can spike unpredictably.

Consider a scenario where a site features a rich library of articles or resources. As the number of articles grows, so does the complexity of delivering them efficiently to users worldwide. In such a case, a static site generator can cache content across a content delivery network (CDN), ensuring that users access the nearest server, thereby reducing load times and improving overall site performance.

An edge case to consider is when a site requires dynamic content, such as user-specific data or real-time updates. While static sites excel in speed, they traditionally struggle with dynamic content. However, modern static site generators often provide solutions like serverless functions or client-side JavaScript to fetch dynamic data when necessary, allowing developers to maintain performance without sacrificing interactivity.

In summary, building a public site that is both performant and scalable requires a careful balance of technology choices. Static site generators like Astro offer a compelling solution by combining speed and efficiency, making them an attractive option for developers aiming to deliver high-quality user experiences.

Why Choose Astro?

Astro is an exciting choice for developers looking to build performant and scalable static sites. Its unique approach to web development focuses on delivering optimized, minimal JavaScript and static HTML, which significantly enhances page load times and performance. This is particularly beneficial for public sites that need to handle a high volume of traffic efficiently.

One of the standout features of Astro is its ability to render pages at build time, ensuring that users receive fully static HTML when they access the site. This approach reduces the need for client-side JavaScript, leading to faster initial page loads. For developers, this means less worry about performance bottlenecks caused by heavy JavaScript bundles. Instead, they can focus on crafting engaging content and user experiences.

Astro's component-based architecture also makes it a versatile choice. Developers can seamlessly integrate components from popular frameworks such as React, Vue, or Svelte, all within the same project. This flexibility allows teams to leverage existing components and libraries without being locked into a single framework. For example, a team might use React for complex interactive elements while employing Svelte for lightweight, performant components on the same page.

An edge case where Astro shines is in handling large content sites. Traditional static site generators might struggle with thousands of pages due to lengthy build times. Astro, however, employs a partial hydration strategy, ensuring only critical parts of the page are hydrated with JavaScript. This results in faster builds and efficient runtime performance, crucial for sites with extensive content.

The public site of Hamdosh is built with Astro, leveraging these capabilities to ensure a fast and reliable experience for users seeking to consolidate their family's health records. By utilizing Astro, Hamdosh can deliver structured data and Open Graph images efficiently, providing a seamless experience whether users are accessing the site directly or through shared links on social media. This strategic choice underlines the importance of selecting a framework that aligns with the site's performance and scalability goals.

Step-by-Step Implementation

Implementing a site using Astro involves a few straightforward steps that allow you to harness its power for building fast, modern web experiences. Here's a step-by-step guide to getting started:

1. Setting Up Your Development Environment

Before diving into the code, ensure you have Node.js installed on your machine. Astro requires Node.js, so having the latest stable version is recommended. Begin by setting up a new Astro project:

npm create astro@latest

Follow the prompts to name your project and select a template. The starter templates provide a solid foundation for building your site.

2. Configuring Your Project

Once your project is initialized, navigate into the project directory. Astro projects come with a src directory where you'll place your components and pages. Open the astro.config.mjs file to configure site-specific settings like the base URL or build options.

3. Creating Pages and Components

Astro uses a file-based routing system, meaning that any .astro or .md file placed in the src/pages directory becomes a route. For instance, creating src/pages/about.astro will automatically generate a /about route.

Here's a simple example of an about.astro page:

---
export const prerender = true;
---

<html>
  <head>
    <title>About Us</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Welcome to Example.com</h1>
    <p>Learn more about our mission and values.</p>
  </body>
</html>

4. Leveraging Astro Components

Astro components allow you to encapsulate reusable parts of your site. Create a src/components directory, and within it, define components like headers or footers. Use these components across multiple pages to maintain consistency.

For example, a simple header component might look like this:

---
const siteTitle = "Example Site";
---

<header>
  <h1>{siteTitle}</h1>
  <nav>
    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about">About</a>
  </nav>
</header>

5. Integrating Data Sources

Astro supports various data-fetching methods, allowing you to pull in data from APIs, markdown files, or even databases. You can use JavaScript or fetch API directly within Astro components to load dynamic data.

For example, to fetch data from a hypothetical API:

---
const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/items');
const items = await response.json();
---

<ul>
  {items.map(item => <li>{item.name}</li>)}
</ul>

6. Building and Deploying

After developing your site, it's time to build it for production. Run the following command to generate static files in the dist directory:

npm run build

These files can then be deployed to any static hosting provider, such as Vercel, Netlify, or GitHub Pages. Ensure that your hosting service supports static site deployment for optimal performance.

By following these steps, you can effectively set up and deploy a performant site using Astro. This approach offers a streamlined process for building modern web applications with a focus on speed and efficiency.

Pitfalls

When building a site with Astro, developers may encounter several common pitfalls that can hinder the performance and maintainability of the site. Understanding these challenges and knowing how to address them can save time and frustration.

One frequent issue is improper handling of image optimization. While Astro supports image optimization, it's crucial to ensure that images are appropriately sized and formats like WebP are used where possible to reduce load times. Failing to optimize images can lead to slow page loads, particularly on mobile devices. To tackle this, make sure to use Astro's built-in Image component to automate format conversions and responsive behavior.

Another challenge is managing dependencies. Astro's ecosystem is vast, and it's easy to inadvertently bloat your project with unnecessary packages. This can slow down build times and increase the bundle size. Regularly audit your package.json file to remove any unused dependencies and consider using tools like npm dedupe to clean up redundant packages.

A less obvious pitfall involves the use of dynamic content. While Astro excels at static site generation, integrating dynamic features without careful planning can lead to unexpected complexity. For instance, if client-side interactivity is required, ensure that only essential JavaScript is shipped to the browser. Utilize Astro's partial hydration feature to load JavaScript only for specific components that need it, reducing the overall footprint.

Lastly, watch out for SEO pitfalls. Astro makes it easy to inject metadata into pages, but overlooking structured data can impact search engine rankings. Always include JSON-LD structured data to enhance search visibility and Open Graph metadata to improve social media sharing previews.

By anticipating these pitfalls and implementing best practices, developers can create robust, high-performance sites that leverage the full potential of Astro.

Conclusion and Your Experience

Building a public-facing site with Astro offers a unique blend of performance and simplicity, making it an appealing choice for developers focused on creating modern web experiences. Throughout this tutorial, we've navigated the steps needed to set up a site using Astro, explored its benefits, and identified common pitfalls to avoid. The modular architecture of Astro allows you to integrate various JavaScript frameworks without compromising on speed, which is crucial for a site that demands quick load times and a seamless user experience.

One of the core advantages of using Astro is its ability to produce static HTML during build time, reducing the need for client-side JavaScript and enhancing performance. This is particularly beneficial for sites like our public site, which is built with Astro to ensure fast and efficient delivery of content. By pre-rendering pages, Astro minimizes the load on the server and improves the overall user experience, especially on mobile devices where performance is often a critical factor.

Astro's support for partial hydration further optimizes the delivery of interactive elements by only loading JavaScript when necessary. This feature can be a game-changer for sites that require dynamic content without sacrificing speed. Additionally, Astro's straightforward setup and flexible configuration make it easy to tailor the build process to your specific needs, ensuring that your site remains scalable as it grows.

As you embark on your own journey of building with Astro, consider the unique requirements of your project. How do you balance the need for interactivity with the demand for speed? What strategies have you employed to ensure your site remains performant and scalable? Share your experiences and insights with us!

title: LLM-as-a-Judge Position Bias: Claude Flipped 103 of 400 Verdicts
description:
My new prompt won 63% of the time. I had the Slack message half-typed. Then I swapped which answer went first, ran the exact same 400 comparisons again, and the new prompt won 43%.

Same judge. Same pairs. Same rubric. The only change was which answer appeared under "Response A". That is LLM-as-a-judge position bias, and it had been quietly deciding my A/B tests for weeks.

TL;DR

  • I ran 400 pairwise comparisons with Claude as the judge, then ran all 400 again with the answer order swapped. 800 judge calls total.
  • 103 of 400 verdicts (25.75%) flipped when I swapped the order. 92 of those flips went to whichever answer was shown first.
  • The new prompt looked like a 63% winner. Counting only verdicts that survived the swap, it won 160 to 137, about 54%. A small edge, not a landslide.
  • On a blind sample I labeled myself, most flipped pairs were ones I'd call a tie. A flip is the judge's way of saying "I can't tell."
  • Fix: always judge both orders, treat disagreement as a tie, and give the judge an explicit TIE option.

What was I actually testing?

I was A/B testing two versions of a report-writing prompt. The system takes an interview transcript and writes a feedback report: what went well, what was weak, what to practice next.

This is the report generator inside Preterview, an interview prep tool I built and run (full disclosure: I built it). It runs voice mock interviews with three interviewer styles, scores a resume or portfolio, and ends with a written report, which is the part I was trying to improve. If you want to see what the reports look like, it's at preterview.com/en.

Prompt v2 was supposed to make reports more specific: quote the candidate's actual words, tie every criticism to a moment in the transcript. I generated reports from v1 and v2 for the same 400 transcripts, then asked Claude to pick the better one.

The obvious setup: new report in slot A, old report in slot B, ask "which is better?" One order, one verdict per pair. That single fixed order is exactly why v2 looked so good.

What is LLM-as-a-judge position bias?

LLM-as-a-judge position bias is the tendency of a model acting as an evaluator to prefer an answer because of where it appears in the prompt, not because of what it says. In pairwise comparisons, the judge favors slot A or slot B more often than the content justifies. It's a well-documented effect in the LLM evaluation literature, and I still walked straight into it.

The nasty part is that each individual verdict looks reasonable. The judge writes a confident paragraph explaining why Response A is more specific. You read it and nod. Nothing in a single output tells you the reasoning was built after the slot already won.

How did I measure it?

I ran every pair twice: once with v2 in slot A, once with v2 in slot B. Same system prompt, same rubric, forced choice between A and B. Here's the core of the harness:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

JUDGE_PROMPT = """You are grading two interview feedback reports
written for the same transcript. Judge on: specificity (quotes
the candidate's words), accuracy (claims match the transcript),
and actionability (clear next steps).

<transcript>{transcript}</transcript>
<response_a>{a}</response_a>
<response_b>{b}</response_b>

Reply with exactly one line: WINNER: A or WINNER: B"""

def judge(transcript, a, b):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model=JUDGE_MODEL,
        max_tokens=20,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": JUDGE_PROMPT.format(
            transcript=transcript, a=a, b=b)}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text.strip().split()[-1]  # "A" or "B"

def judge_both_orders(transcript, old, new):
    first = judge(transcript, a=new, b=old)    # new in slot A
    second = judge(transcript, a=old, b=new)   # new in slot B
    new_won_1 = first == "A"
    new_won_2 = second == "B"
    if new_won_1 and new_won_2:
        return "new"
    if not new_won_1 and not new_won_2:
        return "old"
    return "flip"

Each call carried a transcript excerpt plus two full reports, roughly 5,200 input tokens. 800 calls came to about 4.2M input tokens. Not free, but cheap next to shipping the wrong prompt to every user.

How many verdicts flipped when I swapped the order?

103 of 400 verdicts flipped, a 25.75% flip rate. One in four comparisons gave a different winner depending only on which report was printed first.

Here's the full breakdown:

Outcome Pairs
v2 wins in both orders 160
v1 wins in both orders 137
Flipped toward slot A 92
Flipped toward slot B 11
Total 400

So the flips weren't random noise. 92 of 103 went to whoever sat in slot A. If the judge were just uncertain and guessing, you'd expect something close to a 50/50 split between the two flip directions. 92 to 11 is a thumb on the scale.

Now look at what that did to the headline numbers:

  • Run 1 (v2 in slot A): v2 won 252 of 400. That's 160 consistent wins plus 92 slot-A flips. 63%.
  • Run 2 (v2 in slot B): v2 won 171 of 400. That's 160 plus the 11 slot-B flips. 42.75%.
  • Swap-consistent only: v2 won 160, v1 won 137. 53.9% of decided pairs.

My first run happened to put v2 in slot A. I was about to announce a 63% win rate for a prompt whose real edge was closer to 54%. If I'd randomly done it the other way around, I would have thrown out a prompt that was actually slightly better.

Are flipped verdicts just ties in disguise?

Mostly, yes. I took 50 random pairs, hid which prompt produced which report, and picked the winner myself before looking at any judge output.

  • 13 of the 50 had flipped verdicts, which tracks the 26% overall rate.
  • On the 37 pairs with a swap-consistent verdict, the judge agreed with me on 31 (84%).
  • Of the 13 flipped pairs, I marked 9 as "honestly, these are about the same."

That changed how I read the whole result. Position bias doesn't mostly override clear quality differences. It fills the vacuum when there isn't one. When two reports are close, the judge needs some tiebreaker, and the tiebreaker it reaches for is "the first one I read."

Which means a forced-choice prompt is lying to you twice. It hides ties, and then it resolves those hidden ties in a biased direction.

Does adding a TIE option fix position bias?

It helps a lot but doesn't eliminate it. I changed the output line to WINNER: A, WINNER: B, or WINNER: TIE and reran all 400 pairs in both orders.

  • 88 pairs got a TIE in at least one order.
  • Strict flips, where one order said A and the other said B, dropped from 103 to 31.

31 is still 31. The judge is still nudged by order on close calls, it just has a more honest exit now. That's why I don't trust a tie option by itself. The swap is the part that does the real work.

How should you run pairwise LLM evals now?

Here's my current setup, and it's the one I'd recommend to anyone A/B testing prompts with a model as the grader:

  1. Always judge both orders. It doubles the cost. Pay it. A single-order pairwise eval tells you about slot preference as much as about quality.
  2. Count a flip as a tie. Only swap-consistent verdicts go in the win column. Report the tie count next to the win rate so nobody reads 54% as 54-out-of-100-decisive.
  3. Offer an explicit TIE. It catches the close calls before they become flips.
  4. Hand-label a small blind sample. 50 pairs took me under an hour and told me more than the other 750 calls about what the judge's disagreement meant.
  5. Track the flip rate as a metric. If it jumps after you edit the judge prompt, your judge got worse, even if the win rates look exciting.

The thing I keep coming back to: none of this showed up in any single output. Every verdict came with a tidy justification. The bias only appeared when I ran the same question twice and compared.

So how bad is LLM-as-a-judge position bias with Claude?

In my setup, bad enough to flip a decision. Swapping answer order changed the winner on 103 of 400 pairwise comparisons (25.75%), and 92 of those flips favored the answer shown first. It turned a real 54% edge into either a 63% win or a 43% loss depending on which slot the new prompt landed in. The flips clustered on pairs that were close in quality, so the fix is cheap and mechanical: run every comparison in both orders, count disagreements as ties, give the judge a TIE option, and spot-check a blind sample by hand. If your LLM-as-a-judge eval only runs one order, your win rate is partly measuring position.

title: I built a time machine for a diamond factory, spec-first with Kiro
description:
I built a time machine for a diamond factory, spec-first with Kiro

Kiroween 2026, Frankenstein category. Live demo ·
3-minute video · Code

In a diamond factory, a rough packet takes about seventeen days to reach dispatch. The people who work on
it spend hours on it, not weeks. Every manager has a theory about the fix: more people, another shift, a faster
machine. Nobody can test a theory on last week and see what would actually have happened.

So I built RealityCheck. It replays what really happened in a factory, lets you stop at any recorded
moment, change one decision, and simulates the other future beside the one that happened. In the
demonstration, halving the time packets sit parked finishes the work about 30% sooner. Hiring three more
inspectors changes nothing but the cost, because that stage was never waiting for people.

The hard part wasn't the simulation. The hard part was keeping every number honest. This post covers how Kiro
helped with that.

A Frankenstein of five parts

RealityCheck is five parts that were never meant to share a body:

  • Skeleton: an append-only history in PostgreSQL. A database trigger refuses any edit to the past.
  • Heart: a discrete-event simulation engine in plain Java, with no framework and no randomness.
  • Blood: patterns from one real factory's month of data, published only as rounded aggregates.
  • Voice: an AI analyst (Claude) that explains results but is forbidden to calculate.
  • Face: a React app where every number is tagged Actual, Simulated or AI interpretation.

Stitching those together is where projects like this usually go wrong. The AI makes up a percentage, or the
simulation quietly uses a random seed. Or a chart shows a number nobody can trace. I wanted rules that
couldn't drift, and that's what Kiro gave me.

Steering: write the rules down once

Before any code, I wrote four steering documents in .kiro/steering/, about 560 lines in all. Kiro loads them
into every piece of work:

  • product.md: every number shown comes from the engine or recorded data. AI explains and never calculates. Simulation never alters recorded history.
  • simulation-rules.md: thirteen sections the engine must obey, covering determinism, event ordering, units, calendars and work in progress at the fork, plus the properties its tests must hold.
  • architecture.md: module boundaries, enforced by ArchUnit tests.
  • tech.md: the stack, and what not to add.

The surprise was how often these settled a design question before it became an argument. I needed per-stage
handling delays, and the obvious answer was a random number generator. But the steering says the engine is
deterministic: same input, same result, to the second. So the delay comes from a hash of the batch id
instead. That's realistic variation with no randomness, and every run reproduces exactly.

Specs: eleven features, requirements to tasks

Every feature has a spec in .kiro/specs/:

  • requirements.md, in WHEN/THE SYSTEM SHALL form;
  • design.md;
  • tasks.md.

There are eleven specs, 83 requirements and over 120 tasks. Each task names the requirements it satisfies
and the test that proves it.

Day to day, I worked task by task. I opened a spec's task list, asked Kiro to implement the next task against
its requirements, then checked the result against the acceptance criteria.

The best moment was spec 11, calibrating against a real factory. My first offline backtest showed that queues
on capacity couldn't explain how long packets sat in a department. Workers hold packets in parcels, so a packet
waits a day or two while the stage runs well below capacity. I updated the design in the spec first, adding
calibrated handling delays with a dated note explaining why. Only then did I change the engine. The spec
stayed the source of truth even when the data proved my first idea wrong.

When the build departed from a design, the spec was updated instead of left stale. Every tasks.md ends with
implementation notes recording what changed and why.

Hooks: checks on save

Five hooks in .kiro/hooks/ run on save, each scoped to a narrow file pattern:

  • the touched backend module's unit tests;
  • frontend lint and type-check;
  • an API contract check against docs/api.md;
  • a simulation-engine review, which checks engine changes against simulation-rules.md and decides whether the algorithm version must change;
  • an architecture-docs sync when migrations or Compose change.

The engine review hook was my favourite. Changing the engine without bumping its version would make old
results look comparable with new ones when they're not. The hook catches that at the moment of saving.

Custom agents and property-based tests

Five custom agents in .kiro/agents/ act as specialists:

  • simulation engineer;
  • database designer;
  • Java backend architect;
  • React UI/UX;
  • QA and testing.

Each is loaded with only its own steering and spec, so the UI agent never wanders into engine code.

Spec 07 requires the engine's correctness properties to be verified with property-based tests. There are
29 jqwik properties across 8 test classes. They cover:

  • determinism;
  • stone and carat conservation at every stage;
  • stage order;
  • capacity that never goes negative;
  • termination.

My favourite is property 10: adding capacity never increases completion time. It holds only in the
single-stage case. With several stages sharing pools, adding capacity can occasionally make the schedule
longer, which is a known scheduling anomaly. The steering says so plainly, and the engine reports it rather
than hiding it.

An AI that refuses to invent

The analyst is Claude, and the steering rule "AI never calculates" shaped all of it:

  • Claude sees only evidence keys from stored simulation results.
  • Every number it writes is checked against those results.
  • If an answer contains a figure the evidence can't support, it's replaced by a built-in analyst, and the screen says so.

In the demo, Claude says the evidence does not isolate a cause, and refuses to invent one. That's the answer I
wanted.

Honest accuracy

A simulator you can't check is just a story. RealityCheck has a backtest: it simulates past dates with no
changes and compares the result with what was recorded. On one real factory, imported privately, it's within
about a fifth on packets finished over a week. We publish exactly where it's wrong.

Our first real-data backtest actually looked better than that. The extract held only pieces that finished,
which flattered the result. We fixed the comparison window and published the less flattering numbers.

What I'd tell someone starting with Kiro

Write the steering first. The rules you'd normally keep in your head ("never fabricate a number", "the
engine is deterministic") become context for every task. That's what turned "AI on top of a simulation" into
something I can trust.

Try it at https://3-106-245-39.sslip.io, and the code, including the whole .kiro directory, is at
https://github.com/DRishu070501/RealityCheck.

title: Local vs Cloud Apps: What Quicken's Two Products Teach Us
description:
AI Mode Answer
Quicken sells two different kinds of product: Quicken Classic, an installed desktop app that stores data locally and works offline, and Quicken Simplifi, a cloud app that needs an internet connection. They aren't interchangeable, and Classic has no data sync between its Windows and Mac versions. The split shows the usual trade-offs: local apps give you offline use and control but make sync and migration your problem, while cloud apps give you access anywhere but depend on a server. Old versions also show what happens when a vendor's servers drop support, and why backups before irreversible migrations matter.

Quick Answer

  1. Local apps: offline, user-controlled data, but sync and migration are hard.
  2. Cloud apps: access anywhere, but they depend on a server.
  3. Server dependencies age: old Quicken versions lose bank connections when servers stop supporting them.
  4. Migrations can be one-way, so back up first.

Disclosure: I'm part of the team at Quick Advisors Hub, an independent resource for accounting software users. We're not affiliated with Quicken or Intuit. Details are as of April 2026 from our own published guide, and Quicken changes products from time to time.

If you build software, a personal finance product is a surprisingly clean case study. Quicken sells both ends of the local-versus-cloud spectrum under one brand, and the differences between them are the same ones we argue about in architecture reviews.

Two products, two architectures

Quicken Classic is installed on your computer. It stores data locally and works offline. It comes in tiers (Deluxe, Premier and Business & Personal) that differ mainly in features, not in architecture.

Quicken Simplifi is cloud-based and needs an internet connection. It's US only, and it's not the mobile version of Classic. The two aren't interchangeable.

What the local model costs

A local-first app gives users offline access and direct control of their data. But look at what that implies:

  • Sync is your problem. A Classic subscription covers Windows and Mac, yet data sync between the two platforms isn't currently available. Users have to pick one machine as the home of their data.
  • Migrations are heavy. Our guide notes that some version upgrades involve an irreversible data format conversion. When the data is a single file on a user's disk, the safe move is a full manual backup before every upgrade.

What the cloud model costs

A cloud app removes those problems but adds a different one: it depends on a server someone else runs. Which brings us to the interesting part.

The server dependency ages out

Quicken 2017 and earlier are a good example. According to our guide, Quicken's servers no longer support bank connections for those versions. The installed program still opens, and the data is still there, but a feature that depended on the vendor's backend is gone. Versions from 2018 to 2022 may see more frequent bank connection errors.

That's the quiet cost of "local" apps that still lean on a service: the part that lives on the vendor's side can age out under software you still own.

Practical lessons

  • Design the export path early. Users will leave, upgrade or switch machines.
  • Make destructive migrations explicit. If a conversion can't be undone, say so before it runs.
  • Treat backups as a feature. A full manual backup before an irreversible change is cheap insurance.
  • Be honest about which features need a server. Users don't always know which parts of a "local" app will stop working.

A caveat

I'm describing two products from the outside, using our own published summary of them. I can't speak to Quicken's internal architecture, and specifics change over time, so check quicken.com for current details.

Over to you

  • Have you shipped a local-first app? How did you handle sync?
  • How do you handle irreversible migrations for users?
  • When a backend dependency is retired, how do you tell users what still works?

If you'd like the non-developer version of this, with a full feature comparison, it's in our Quicken versions guide (a link to our own website).

About the author: This article is written by the team at Quick Advisors Hub, an independent resource that publishes practical guidance for accounting and tax software users. We aim to explain things in plain language so you can decide what help you need, whether or not you ever work with us.

Disclaimer: This article is independent and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Quicken Inc. or Intuit Inc. Quicken, Simplifi and Intuit are trademarks of their respective owners, used here for identification only. It is general information, not official Quicken support, and not tax, legal or financial advice. Product names, features and availability change, so verify current details at quicken.com.
