title: Fixing "SQLite package has not been found installed" — When npm Errors Lie to You
description:
Earlier this week I installed a globally distributed Node.js tool — n8n, via npm install -g — on Windows. It crashed on startup with this:

Initial database connection attempt 1 failed: SQLite package has not been
found installed. Try to install it: npm install sqlite3 --save.
Retrying in 1000ms

Five retries. Then it gave up for good:

Error: There was an error initializing DB
DriverPackageNotInstalledError: SQLite package has not been found installed.
Try to install it: npm install sqlite3 --save
    at SqliteLibrary.loadLibrary (...\@n8n\typeorm\dist\driver\sqlite-pooled\SqliteLibrary.js:30:19)

Now, here's the part that still annoys me: sqlite3 was installed. Twice, in fact. Once globally, once nested inside the tool itself. The error message was lying — and the lie cost me a full hour, because I kept believing it.

This post is that debugging session, plus the method I walked away with. The method generalizes: it works for any native module that "cannot be found" when you know perfectly well it exists.

Prerequisites

  • Windows, Node v22, npm 10
  • A globally installed CLI tool that vendors sqlite3 as a nested dependency
  • A terminal, so you can fire off node -e one-liners

Step 1 — Symptom: verify the package before touching anything

The error tells you to run npm install sqlite3 --save. Don't. Not yet. First find out what actually exists:

npm ls -g sqlite3
# └── sqlite3@6.0.1

Installed. So why does the tool insist otherwise?

The answer sits in the throwing code. I opened SqliteLibrary.js and found this:

loadLibrary() {
    try {
        const sqlite = this.options.driver || require('sqlite3');
        this.sqlite = sqlite.verbose();
    }
    catch (e) {
        throw new DriverPackageNotInstalledError('SQLite', 'sqlite3');
    }
}

That catch swallows everything. Any failure inside require('sqlite3') — including "the native binary that lives inside the package is missing" — gets relabeled as "the package is not installed." A loading failure and an installation failure produce the exact same misleading sentence.

Lesson 1: when a wrapper catches require() and translates it into "package not installed," the package is rarely the problem. The loader is.

Step 2 — Hypothesis: two ways this can be true

Suppose the package exists but require fails anyway. Only two explanations are possible:

  1. Resolution picks a different copy than the one that works — nested node_modules shadowing.
  2. The resolved copy exists, but its native binary doesn't — a .node file that never made it down at install time.

One command distinguishes them. Ask Node what it would load, from the perspective of the code that's failing:

node -e "console.log(require.resolve('sqlite3', {
  paths: ['C:/path/to/the/tool/node_modules/@n8n/typeorm']
}))"

Out comes:

C:\...\node_modules\n8n\node_modules\sqlite3\lib\sqlite3.js

There it is. The tool ships its own nested sqlite3 (5.1.7) inside its node_modules, and Node's resolution walks the ancestor chain starting from the failing file — so it hits the nested copy before my global 6.0.1. The global copy I confirmed in Step 1? Never even a candidate.

Hypothesis 1, dead. Everything now points at hypothesis 2.

Step 3 — Verify: load each copy directly

Load both copies in isolation and compare:

# global copy — loads fine
node -e "require('C:/.../node_modules/sqlite3'); console.log('OK')"

# nested copy — the real failure, finally speaking for itself
node -e "require('C:/.../node_modules/n8n/node_modules/sqlite3')"

The nested copy's error is nothing like what the tool reported:

Error: Could not locate the bindings file. Tried:
 → ...\sqlite3\build\node_sqlite3.node
 → ...\sqlite3\build\Debug\node_sqlite3.node
 → ...\sqlite3\build\Release\node_sqlite3.node
 → ...\sqlite3\out\Release\node_sqlite3.node
 → ...\sqlite3\lib\binding\node-v127-win32-x64\node_sqlite3.node
 ...

No build/Release/node_sqlite3.node anywhere. The nested package shipped without its native binary.

Why? Because sqlite3's install script downloads a prebuilt binary from GitHub Releases at install time — and I was on a corporate network where that download failed silently. npm install -g reported success. The missing binary only surfaced hours later, at runtime, wearing a disguise.

Lesson 2: a silent network failure during install becomes a misleading error at runtime. The farther apart those two moments are, the harder the debugging gets.

Step 4 — Fix: fetch the prebuilt binary manually

I tried three shortcuts before the real fix. Keeping them in — each one is a trap worth knowing.

Trap 1 — prebuild-install doesn't fix it:

cd .../n8n/node_modules/sqlite3
npm_config_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7890 npx --yes prebuild-install
# warn install Client network socket disconnected before secure TLS
# connection was established

The binary fetcher needs GitHub access itself, and its proxy configuration refused to cooperate. Same wall, different tool.

Trap 2 — guessing the release URL 404s:

The prebuilt binaries live on the project's GitHub Releases. I guessed the asset name using the old Node ABI convention:

https://github.com/TryGhost/node-sqlite3/releases/download/v5.1.7/node-v127-win32-x64.tar.gz

What that downloads is a 9-byte file containing Not Found. Modern sqlite3 builds are N-API builds, so the assets are named napi-vX, not node-vXXX:

  • node-v127-win32-x64.tar.gz (my guess — doesn't exist)
  • sqlite3-v5.1.7-napi-v6-win32-x64.tar.gz (real asset)

N-API binaries are ABI-stable across Node versions — which is exactly why the Node version disappeared from the filename. Guess the old convention and you'll 404 every time.

Trap 3 — the GitHub API may be rate-limited:

The obvious next move is listing release assets through the API:

curl https://api.github.com/repos/TryGhost/node-sqlite3/releases/tags/v5.1.7

If your proxy exit IP is shared — and on any corporate proxy or VPN, it is — you can inherit some stranger's exhausted rate limit:

{"message":"API rate limit exceeded for 203.190.x.x. (But here's the good
news: Authenticated requests get a higher rate limit...)"}

The workaround that actually worked: scrape the release page's asset list, which carries no rate limit:

curl -sSL "https://github.com/TryGhost/node-sqlite3/releases/expanded_assets/v5.1.7" \
  | grep -o 'href="[^"]*"' | grep -i "win32-x64"

Real asset names, no API involved.

The fix itself (through a proxy that works):

cd .../n8n/node_modules/sqlite3   # the NESTED copy, not your global one

curl -sSL -x http://127.0.0.1:7890 -o binding.tar.gz \
  "https://github.com/TryGhost/node-sqlite3/releases/download/v5.1.7/sqlite3-v5.1.7-napi-v6-win32-x64.tar.gz"

tar -xzf binding.tar.gz -C .

One more trap hides in that last line. The tarball already contains build/Release/node_sqlite3.node — so if you extract with -C build/Release (which felt perfectly logical to me for about thirty seconds), you end up with build/Release/build/Release/... and the same "could not locate bindings" error. Extract to the package root.

Then verify — no need to launch the whole tool:

node -e "require('./lib/sqlite3.js'); console.log('fixed')"
# fixed

The next n8n start ran to completion.

Step 5 — Generalize: a checklist for lying "package not found" errors

Any time a native module — anything that loads a .node binary: sqlite3, bcrypt, canvas, sharp, node-pty... — claims it isn't installed:

  1. Don't reinstall. Check npm ls -g <pkg> (or the lockfile) first. If it's there, the error is lying, and you're debugging a loader, not an installer.
  2. Ask what resolution actually picks — require.resolve(pkg, { paths: [dir-of-the-failing-code] }). Nested copies shadow your global/parent install; you need to know which copy is losing.
  3. Load each candidate copy directly with node -e "require(...)". The direct error ("Could not locate the bindings file") beats the wrapper's relabeled one.
  4. If a native binary is missing, the install-time download failed silently. Fetch it manually from the project's GitHub Releases — remembering that assets are napi-vX (N-API) today, not the node-vXXX ABI names older guides mention.
  5. On restricted networks, the binary fetcher (prebuild-install) may fail where a plain curl -x proxy succeeds. Don't fight the tool. Use curl, place the file yourself.
  6. Read the throwing code when an error smells wrong. Ten lines of try/catch explained the whole mystery at a glance.

Takeaways

  • "Package not found" from a wrapper's catch block is a category of failure, not a diagnosis.
  • Node resolves modules along the ancestor chain from the requiring file — nested copies always shadow yours, and npm install -g <pkg> will never fix a nested copy.
  • Silent install-time failures on restricted networks surface later as runtime lies. The gap between cause and symptom is what makes them hard.
  • When the GitHub API rate-limits you behind a shared proxy IP, the expanded_assets HTML page is your friend.

The meta-lesson I'm keeping from this one: when an error tells you a package is missing, the package is rarely the problem — the loader is. Verify before you reinstall.

title: Debugging PrestaShop SEO: When Crawlability, Indexability, and Canonical Signals Conflict
description:
A PrestaShop product page can have a well-written description, optimized metadata, relevant keywords, and valid structured data while still failing to appear in Google Search. From a merchant's perspective, this may look like an SEO optimization problem. From a developer's perspective, however, it may be a problem with HTTP responses, application routing, crawler access, or inconsistent indexing signals.

The distinction matters because ecommerce platforms generate URLs through multiple application layers. Product combinations, category filters, language prefixes, routing configurations, and third-party modules can introduce alternative URLs that do not necessarily represent independent pages.

Auditing these URLs requires more than checking whether SEO fields have been completed. It requires investigating how the application exposes its content and whether search engines receive signals consistent with the intended page architecture.

Start with the intended behavior of each URL

Before investigating individual SEO warnings, establish what each type of URL is supposed to do. An ecommerce store may expose thousands of accessible URLs, but only a subset of them should represent independent search results.

Consider the following illustrative PrestaShop URLs:

URL Intended behavior
/12-trail-running-shoe.html Original product URL
/trail-running-shoe.html Preferred product URL after a URL migration
/trail-running-shoe.html?utm_source=email Tracking variation of the same product
/running-shoes Indexable category page
/running-shoes?q=Size-42 Filtered category variation requiring evaluation
/search?s=running Internal search page, generally not intended for indexing

These URLs should not automatically receive identical SEO treatment. A tracking variation may represent the same content as the preferred product URL, whereas a filtered category may or may not have independent search value.

The first task is therefore to define the desired behavior of each URL group. Without this information, a developer cannot reliably determine whether a redirect, canonical annotation, indexing directive, or sitemap entry is correct.

Separate crawler access from indexing eligibility

One of the most common diagnostic mistakes is treating every missing search result as an indexing problem.

A crawler must first discover and retrieve a URL before evaluating its content and indexing directives. If retrieval fails because of an application error, firewall restriction, or redirect loop, modifying the product's metadata will not resolve the underlying issue.

Start by inspecting the HTTP response using a normal GET request:

URL="https://example.com/trail-running-shoe.html"

curl -sS -D headers.txt -o page.html "$URL"

This saves the response headers and HTML separately, allowing you to inspect what the application actually returns.

grep -iE '^(HTTP/|location:|x-robots-tag:|content-type:|link:)' headers.txt

Different responses lead to different investigations.

Response Diagnostic direction
200 OK Inspect content, canonical annotations, and indexing directives
301 or 308 Verify the permanent redirect destination
302 or 307 Determine whether temporary redirection is intentional
403 Forbidden Investigate access restrictions, firewall, or bot protection
404 Not Found Investigate routing, deleted content, or outdated links
500 Internal Server Error Investigate application execution and server logs
503 Service Unavailable Investigate maintenance, overload, or service availability

A successful HTTP response is necessary for an ordinary product page to be considered for indexing, but it is not sufficient. A page returning 200 OK could still contain an error message, an unintended indexing directive, or content that does not represent the requested product.

Also, a successful request from your terminal does not prove that Googlebot can retrieve the same page. CDN rules, bot protection, and request-dependent application behavior can produce different responses for different visitors. Use Google Search Console's URL Inspection tool alongside server-side investigation when crawler-specific behavior is suspected.

Google's technical requirements for Search provide a useful reference for distinguishing accessibility from indexing eligibility.

Inspect indexing directives in the actual response

After confirming that the page is accessible, inspect the HTML returned by the application:

grep -inE 'canonical|robots|googlebot' page.html

This is a quick diagnostic search rather than a complete HTML parser. Review the matching elements in their actual HTML context, and inspect the rendered document if JavaScript modifies the page.

For example, an important product page might contain:

<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">

The URL may load correctly, appear in the XML sitemap, and receive internal links. Nevertheless, the noindex directive tells supporting search engines not to include it in their search results.

An equivalent restriction can also be delivered through an HTTP response header:

X-Robots-Tag: noindex

Checking only the page's HTML can therefore miss restrictions introduced by server configuration or another application layer.

Another common mistake is attempting to prevent indexing by blocking a URL in robots.txt. Blocking crawling does not reliably prevent the URL itself from appearing in search results. It can also prevent Google from retrieving a page-level noindex directive.

Crawler access and indexing policy should be investigated separately because they solve different problems.

Diagnose conflicting canonical, sitemap, and redirect signals

URL changes are particularly sensitive in PrestaShop because they can affect product links, category routes, internal navigation, and previously indexed addresses at the same time.

Removing numeric IDs from URLs is one example. Although the resulting URLs may be easier to read, the change creates a URL migration that must be handled across all relevant layers.

Imagine that a store replaces:

https://example.com/12-trail-running-shoe.html

with:

https://example.com/trail-running-shoe.html

After deployment, the old URL correctly redirects to the new address. However, the new page still contains a canonical annotation pointing to the old URL:

<link rel="canonical"
  href="https://example.com/12-trail-running-shoe.html">

Meanwhile, the sitemap lists the new URL, and some category pages continue linking to the original address.

Each component may appear functional when inspected independently. Together, however, they communicate inconsistent URL preferences.

The redirect identifies the new address as the destination, the canonical annotation identifies the original address as preferred, and the internal links continue exposing the outdated route. Search engines must reconcile these signals rather than receiving a clear indication of which address represents the product.

Google treats canonical annotations as signals rather than absolute commands. Its canonicalization documentation explains why consistent signals across redirects, canonical elements, sitemaps, and internal links are important.

Align the signals around one preferred URL

For the example above, a consistent implementation would look like this:

Component Expected configuration
Original product URL Permanent redirect to the new URL
New product URL 200 OK with the correct product content
Canonical annotation Points to the new product URL
XML sitemap Contains the new preferred URL
Internal product links Link directly to the new URL
Tracking variations Canonicalize to the preferred URL when the content is equivalent

The final product page should contain a self-referencing canonical:

<link rel="canonical"
  href="https://example.com/trail-running-shoe.html">

You can inspect the old URL's complete redirect path with:

curl -sS -L --max-redirs 10 \
  -D - -o /dev/null \
  "https://example.com/12-trail-running-shoe.html"

For this illustrative migration, the expected result is a direct permanent redirect followed by a successful response:

HTTP/2 301
location: https://example.com/trail-running-shoe.html

HTTP/2 200

If the request passes through several outdated URLs before reaching the product, investigate whether those intermediate redirects can be eliminated.

Importantly, a URL migration should not be initiated solely because the existing URL contains a numeric ID. Established URLs may already have backlinks, organic traffic, and external references. Changing them introduces maintenance work and potential search visibility risks that should be justified by an actual requirement.

Identify which application layer owns the problem

PrestaShop SEO behavior is not necessarily controlled by a single component. Depending on the installation, URL generation and metadata may be influenced by core configuration, custom modules, theme templates, class overrides, web server rewrite rules, and caching infrastructure.

A canonical problem, for example, may originate in a page-level SEO setting. It may also be caused by a theme outputting its own canonical annotation while an SEO module generates another one. Similarly, a broken product URL could originate in a routing configuration, an outdated internal link, or an incorrectly deployed server rewrite rule.

The following diagnostic mapping helps narrow the investigation:

Observed symptom Layer to investigate
Friendly URLs consistently return 404 Routing and server rewrite configuration
Multiple canonical annotations Theme templates and SEO modules
Old canonical remains after configuration changes Metadata generation and cached output
Browser works but crawler access fails CDN, firewall, bot protection, or server behavior
Sitemap contains outdated URLs Sitemap generation and URL generation logic
Product links still use an obsolete route Link generation, templates, and cached navigation
Incorrect behavior occurs in only one language or shop Language-specific or shop-specific configuration

The purpose of this mapping is not to assign a definitive cause from a symptom alone. It is to identify which component should be investigated next.

When a configuration value appears correct in the PrestaShop back office but the storefront returns different HTML, compare the configured value with the actual application output. If caching is involved, invalidate the relevant cached content and repeat the request before concluding that the configuration change has failed.

The back office represents the intended configuration. The storefront response represents what visitors and crawlers actually receive.

Prioritize fixes according to their dependencies

A large catalog can generate thousands of SEO warnings, but the number of warnings is a poor measure of their technical importance.

Suppose an audit identifies missing image ALT attributes on hundreds of products, duplicated metadata across several categories, and an unintended noindex directive affecting an entire product page type. Although the missing ALT attributes may account for most of the warnings, the indexing directive deserves immediate investigation because it conflicts with the visibility objective of every affected product.

A practical prioritization model is:

Priority Problem class Examples
P0 — Critical Accessibility and indexing blockers Widespread server errors, blocked important routes, unintended site-wide or page-type-wide noindex
P1 — High Inconsistent URL and discovery signals Incorrect canonicals, broken redirects, important orphan pages, outdated sitemap URLs
P2 — Medium Content and metadata deficiencies Duplicate titles, generic descriptions, insufficient product information
P3 — Enhancement Non-blocking search appearance improvements Missing eligible structured data enhancements

These priorities are contextual rather than universal. A structured data implementation exposing incorrect product prices, for example, may require more urgent attention than a missing optional schema property.

The principle is to resolve problems that invalidate downstream optimization before investing in improvements that depend on those problems being fixed.

This is also why an on-page SEO score should not be treated as a search engine ranking score. Rule-based analysis can identify content and metadata deficiencies, but it cannot establish whether a crawler successfully retrieved the page, whether Google selected its preferred canonical, or whether the content deserves to rank for a particular query.

For broader audit coverage beyond this debugging workflow, see the PrestaShop SEO audit guide.

Turn SEO verification into a deployment regression check

Technical SEO issues often appear after application changes rather than during the initial store configuration. A theme upgrade, module installation, routing change, catalog migration, or cache configuration update can alter the behavior of URLs that previously worked correctly.

Instead of treating SEO verification as an occasional manual activity, maintain a representative set of storefront URLs with explicitly defined expectations.

The sample should include important products, category pages, CMS pages, migrated URLs, tracking variations, filtered pages, and language-specific routes where applicable.

After a relevant deployment, verify the following:

  • Important indexable pages return successful responses and the expected content.
  • Migrated URLs redirect to their intended replacements without loops or unnecessary intermediate steps.
  • Canonical annotations identify the correct preferred URLs.
  • Neither HTML nor HTTP headers introduce unintended indexing restrictions.
  • Sitemap entries and internal links use the intended current URLs.
  • Language and shop contexts remain correct.
  • Structured data continues to represent the actual page content without contradictory values.

For pages that previously had indexing problems, compare the current storefront response with Google Search Console's live inspection and indexed information. These represent different observations: a successful live test indicates current accessibility or eligibility, while indexed information reflects Google's previously processed version.

A technically successful deployment can therefore be verified immediately at the application level, even though search engines may require additional time to recrawl and reassess the affected URLs. A successful verification does not guarantee indexing or improved rankings.

The most useful outcome of a PrestaShop SEO audit is not a dashboard with every warning marked as resolved. It is a storefront whose HTTP responses, routing behavior, indexing directives, canonical annotations, and discovery mechanisms consistently reflect the intended information architecture.

Once that foundation is reliable, content optimization, metadata improvements, internal linking, and structured data become meaningful parts of a long-term search visibility strategy rather than attempts to compensate for unresolved technical problems.

title: I built a GitHub Action that runs your Windows game under Proton on every pull request
description:
I kept seeing the same story from indie game devs. They ship a patch on Steam and a week later they find out from Valve's review or from a Steam Deck player that the game no longer starts under Proton.

Nobody did anything wrong. They just don't own a Deck and Valve only reviews the build after you submit it. By then the bad patch is already out.

So I built Protonaut. It's a GitHub Action that runs your Windows game build under Proton on every pull request, on a normal GitHub runner. If a change breaks the game on Linux, the PR goes red before it ever reaches players.

GitHub: Mahan-Imanian/protonaut · Demo PR: protonaut-demo/pull/1

The problems it catches

These are the ways a Windows game breaks under Proton that you'd normally only hear about from players:

  • The game crashes on start. Protonaut catches the crash and pulls the exact line out of Wine's log, like wine: Unhandled division by zero at address ..., so you don't have to dig through thousands of lines.
  • It runs, but the screen is black. Every run is captured, and black or empty frames are flagged.
  • It shows an error instead of the game. OpenTTD, run without its graphics files, keeps going while it displays "Missing graphics: OpenTTD requires graphics to function" inside its own window. A crash check would call that a pass. Protonaut reads the game window and flags error text like that.
  • An extra window or dialog pops up, like an "unsupported hardware" box, a launcher or a fatal error dialog.
  • The build itself has a problem: a DLL the game imports that nothing provides, files that only differ by letter case, or anti-cheat and launcher files worth a closer look.

What you get on the pull request

This is the comment Protonaut left on a build that crashes on start:

You get the failed checks, the crash line, screenshots and logs as an artifact, and a single command that reproduces the run on your own Ubuntu machine. See it live on the demo pull request.

Setup

It's one step after your build, on ubuntu-24.04:

- uses: Mahan-Imanian/protonaut@v0
  with:
    build: dist/Windows
    exe: MyGame.exe

The step fails the PR on any failure, writes the report to the job summary, and uploads the screenshots and logs. If you're on Godot, Unity or Unreal, there are ready-made workflows to copy in the recipes.

How it runs without a Deck or a GPU

A GitHub runner has no screen and no GPU, so Protonaut brings its own:

  1. A virtual display. It starts a headless display at 1280x800, the Deck's resolution.
  2. Rendering on the CPU. It draws with Mesa's software Vulkan driver, so any runner works.
  3. A pinned GE-Proton. Your build runs under a GE-Proton release checked against its SHA-256 before use.
  4. A sandbox. The game runs as a separate user, with no network and no access to your CI secrets.

Proven on real games every week

CI runs real open-source games through the action every week:

  • OpenTTD 15.3 (OpenGL)
  • Godot's 3D platformer demo, exported for both Vulkan and Direct3D 12
  • Chocolate Doom 3.0.1 with Freedoom (32-bit)

Every result with screenshots is in real-games.md.

Try it

If you ship a Windows game on Steam, add the step to your workflow and open a pull request. You'll know in a few minutes whether your build still runs under Proton.

It's open source, written in Rust under Apache-2.0. If it catches something or misses something, tell me in the comments or open an issue.

What's broken on Proton that you only found out about from players?

Protonaut is an independent project, not affiliated with Valve.

title: Tracekit: a tamper-evident flight recorder for coding agents
description:
Tracekit

An agent can edit its own log, so a log alone proves very little. Tracekit is a tamper evident flight recorder for coding agents. Hooks route each tool call through a policy checking signer before it runs, and every call and decision lands in a signed hash chain. The run exports as one .tkb file, and tracekit verify checks it offline and fails at any edited record. A transcript cross check also flags calls the signer never saw, because hooks can be skipped. Setup is tracekit init. It now sits at v1.7.3, released 24 November 2026, and the repo now has 876 stars under the MIT license. The same team has a companion runtime, Tracekit Box, that runs each agent job in its own micro VM.

Repo: https://github.com/Cygnux-Labs/Tracekit

What you get

  • A signed hash chain of every tool call and decision, verifiable offline with tracekit verify
  • A policy checking signer that approves each call before it runs, not after
  • A transcript cross check that catches calls the signer never saw, because hooks can be skipped
  • One .tkb export per run, and a companion micro VM runtime in Tracekit Box for isolating agent jobs

A log your agent can edit proves very little. Verify the record before you trust the run.

Quick poll

What would you use Tracekit for first?

  • Auditing a coding agent's tool calls
  • Verifying a signed trace with tracekit verify
  • Trying tracekit init on a real project
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found Tracekit interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: 12 Best AI Test Automation Tools in 2026: Features, Pricing, Pros and Cons
description:
Choosing an AI test automation tool in 2026 is considerably more complicated than it was a few years ago.

Almost every major test automation vendor now offers artificial intelligence in some form. Some use AI to identify elements, some generate automation scripts, some repair broken tests, and others employ autonomous agents that interact with applications without predefined instructions.

These approaches are fundamentally different. A tool that generates Playwright scripts solves a different problem from one that independently explores an application. A visual AI platform solves a different problem from a no-code enterprise automation solution.

This guide compares 12 AI test automation tools based on their architecture, AI capabilities, supported testing environments, maintainability, enterprise readiness, pricing considerations, and suitability for different types of teams. It also includes a practical framework for evaluating these tools against your own application.

Key takeaways

  • Endtest is a strong overall candidate for enterprise teams looking for AI-powered test automation, no-code test creation, real-browser execution, and flexible deployment.
  • Applitools specializes in AI-powered visual regression testing.
  • ACCELQ focuses on codeless automation for complex enterprise business processes.
  • TestMu AI KaneAI offers natural language test authoring combined with cross-browser testing infrastructure.
  • Alumnium provides an open-source approach to integrating AI into existing automation frameworks.
  • Maestro is particularly relevant for mobile teams that want AI-assisted authoring with predefined execution flows.
  • Testkube addresses test orchestration rather than replacing existing testing frameworks.
  • Autonomous testing agents offer significant potential for exploratory testing, but predictable execution remains important for critical regression scenarios.
  • The best AI testing platform is not necessarily the one that uses AI most extensively. It is the one that delivers reliable coverage with the lowest sustainable maintenance effort.

The best AI test automation tools at a glance

Tool Best for Primary approach
Endtest Enterprise AI and no-code automation Hybrid AI and predefined automation
testers.ai CARBON Testing within AI coding workflows Agent-assisted testing
Amikoo AI-assisted QA engineering QA workflow assistance
Applitools Visual regression testing Visual AI
ACCELQ Enterprise business process testing Codeless automation with AI
Testkube Kubernetes-native test orchestration AI-assisted orchestration
Perfecto Enterprise web and mobile testing Agentic testing
TestMu AI KaneAI Natural language test authoring AI-generated automation
Alumnium Open-source AI testing AI layer for existing frameworks
Thunders.ai Business-oriented autonomous testing Goal-based agents
QA.tech Autonomous application verification AI testing agents
Maestro Mobile application testing AI-assisted predefined flows

How the tools were selected

The comparison considers AI-assisted test creation, autonomous testing capabilities, execution consistency, human-readable test assets, maintenance and self-healing, cross-browser and mobile testing, complex workflows, failure diagnostics, security and deployment flexibility, development integrations, pricing, total cost of ownership, portability, suitability for non-technical testers, and vendor maturity.

This is a research-based comparison using public product information, published benchmarks, and technical analysis. It should not be interpreted as a claim that all 12 products were independently tested under identical conditions. Vendor-reported performance figures are identified as such.

What is AI test automation?

AI test automation is the application of artificial intelligence to software testing activities that would otherwise require substantial manual effort, predefined rules, or custom automation code.

Common applications include generating automated tests from natural language, identifying interactive elements, repairing tests after interface changes, detecting visual regressions, generating test data, analyzing failures, suggesting coverage, exploring applications autonomously, converting manual test cases, and evaluating behavior using contextual assertions.

An AI test automation tool does not necessarily require a language model during every test execution. Some of the most practical implementations use AI only when contextual reasoning is valuable, while retaining conventional automation for operations that require precision.

The five types of AI test automation tools

1. AI-assisted test generation

These tools transform natural language requirements, manual test cases, or application observations into automated tests. The generated output may consist of JavaScript, Python, YAML, or editable no-code test steps. Once generated, the test can execute without requiring AI to make decisions during every run. This approach is particularly useful for regression testing. Examples include Endtest, KaneAI, and AI-assisted Maestro workflows.

2. AI-powered test maintenance

These tools focus on reducing the work required to keep existing automated tests operational. A common example is self-healing. When an element locator stops working because an application has changed, the platform attempts to identify the intended element using other available information. Effective self-healing should distinguish between superficial interface changes and actual application defects. Otherwise, the automation might silently adapt to incorrect behavior.

3. Visual AI testing

Visual AI tools evaluate application appearance rather than relying exclusively on DOM properties or pixel-by-pixel comparisons. They can help detect layout changes, missing interface components, overlapping content, and unexpected rendering differences. Applitools is a prominent example. Visual AI is particularly relevant for responsive applications, design systems, and e-commerce websites.

4. Autonomous AI testing agents

Autonomous agents receive objectives and interact with applications to achieve those objectives. They typically observe the application, determine the next action, execute it, inspect the result, update the plan, and continue until the objective is achieved or a stopping condition is reached.

These systems are particularly promising for exploratory testing and applications that change frequently. However, repeated executions may produce different sequences of actions. This makes execution constraints, evidence collection, and repeatability important evaluation criteria.

5. AI-assisted test orchestration

Some AI tools do not primarily create tests or interact with application interfaces. Instead, they help determine which existing tests should run, coordinate executions, analyze failures, and provide release-readiness information. Testkube and testers.ai illustrate different approaches to this part of the lifecycle. These capabilities can be useful when an organization already maintains substantial Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, or API testing infrastructure.

Deterministic vs. agentic vs. hybrid test automation

Characteristic Predefined automation Autonomous AI agent Hybrid automation
Execution path Predetermined Dynamically selected Predetermined with selected AI decisions
Repeatability Generally higher Can vary between runs Depends on AI usage
Adaptation to unfamiliar interfaces Limited Potentially high Selective
Model usage during execution Not required Usually required Optional
Cost predictability Generally higher May vary Depends on configuration
Human review Inspect predefined steps Inspect objectives and traces Inspect steps and AI operations
Best use case Regression testing Exploratory testing Mixed enterprise workloads

Consider a banking application that transfers money between two accounts. A conventional automated test can explicitly verify that transferring $100 reduces one account balance by exactly $100 and increases the other by exactly $100. There is little benefit in asking a language model whether the mathematical result appears correct.

However, AI might be useful for generating the initial test, identifying an element whose locator has changed, or explaining why an execution failed. That is the appeal of hybrid automation. It applies AI where reasoning or interpretation provides value, without introducing unnecessary uncertainty into straightforward operations.

1. Endtest: Best for enterprise AI-powered test automation

Website: endtest.io

Endtest combines no-code test automation, AI-assisted test generation, autonomous testing agents, and conventional browser automation within a single platform. It is particularly relevant to organizations that want to introduce AI without replacing every existing testing practice. The platform has been available since 2016, predating the recent generative AI testing market.

AI Test Creation Agent

The Endtest AI Test Creation Agent can generate automated tests from natural language instructions. Unlike tools that produce source code requiring subsequent maintenance by developers, Endtest generates structured test steps that users can inspect and edit directly within the platform.

For example, a manual test case might contain these instructions:

  • Navigate to the registration page.
  • Register using a unique email address.
  • Open the verification email.
  • Follow the verification link.
  • Log in using the newly created account.
  • Confirm that the account is active.

The generated test can be reviewed and modified before becoming part of the regression suite. This is particularly useful for organizations with substantial collections of manual test cases stored in spreadsheets or test management systems.

AI Assertions

Traditional automated assertions generally compare predefined values or conditions. AI Assertions allow testers to express validations that require contextual understanding.

For example:

Verify that the displayed product image is consistent with the product description.

Or:

Determine whether the page contains a meaningful error message explaining why the transaction could not be completed.

These assertions are useful when the expected outcome cannot easily be expressed as a simple text or numerical comparison. For precise financial values, identifiers, and other deterministic conditions, conventional assertions remain preferable.

AI Variables

AI Variables allow users to extract, transform, or generate information using natural language. Potential applications include extracting information from page content, interpreting execution logs, or generating values according to specified requirements. This can reduce the need for custom processing scripts in certain testing workflows.

AI-powered failure analysis

When a test fails, determining the cause can take longer than fixing the underlying problem. Endtest provides AI-assisted analysis of execution evidence to help identify potential causes and suggest corrective actions. This is particularly useful when investigating failures across large regression suites. The suggested explanation should still be validated against the actual execution evidence.

Self-healing tests

Endtest includes self-healing capabilities intended to reduce maintenance caused by changing element locators. Teams evaluating self-healing should pay particular attention to whether repairs are transparent and whether the original test objective remains intact. A test that clicks the wrong button successfully is not a reliable test.

Endtest Bot

Endtest Bot extends the platform into autonomous application exploration. Instead of relying entirely on manually specified scenarios, it can explore an application and create tests based on its observations. This makes the platform relevant to both conventional regression automation and agentic testing. Organizations can maintain reviewed, predefined test suites while also using autonomous agents to identify additional coverage opportunities.

MCP integration

Endtest provides a Model Context Protocol integration that allows compatible AI assistants and coding agents to interact with the testing platform. This is increasingly relevant as organizations adopt AI-assisted development processes. A coding agent can potentially participate in a workflow where application changes trigger test creation, execution, result inspection, and subsequent investigation. The permissions granted to these agents should be configured according to the organization's security requirements.

Real-browser execution

One of Endtest's more important differentiators is its support for real browser environments. For enterprise web applications, the browser engine is only part of the testing environment. The operating system, browser version, device configuration, and native browser behavior can also affect the outcome.

Endtest supports browser execution on Windows and macOS, including actual Safari browsers. This matters because testing against WebKit is not identical to testing against Apple's distributed Safari application. Organizations supporting Safari users should evaluate whether their automation infrastructure reproduces the environments their customers actually use.

Complex end-to-end scenarios

A basic login test tells relatively little about the functional limits of an automation platform. Endtest supports testing scenarios involving email verification, SMS verification, PDF documents, multiple browser tabs, iframes, API requests, and dynamic interface elements. These capabilities are especially relevant to fintech applications, insurance platforms, healthcare portals, e-commerce websites, and enterprise SaaS products.

Published performance benchmarks: how Endtest compares

Three published comparisons by Endtest's founder provide quantitative evidence for shortlisting the platform. They evaluate different aspects of automation and should be interpreted separately, not as independent confirmations of a universal ranking.

AI-powered test automation: functional coverage and execution speed

The comparison of 10 AI-powered test automation tools reports results for nine end-to-end scenarios, including external verification messages, embedded frames, multiple tabs, document extraction and API-to-UI validation.

Tool Scenarios passed without workarounds
Endtest 9/9
mabl 6/9
Functionize 6/9

How to evaluate AI test automation tools: A practical benchmark

For existing code-first suites, the Selenium alternatives comparison offers a reference for setup, intermittent failures and repair effort. For teams moving toward visual or natural-language authoring, the no-code tools comparison offers a reference for measuring code-free coverage, AI authoring and recovery from interface changes. Both are vendor-published studies; use their evaluation dimensions as inspiration rather than assuming their results will transfer to your application.

The most useful benchmark is one that reproduces the application behavior your organization actually needs to verify. A simple login demonstration is insufficient. The following scenarios provide a more demanding evaluation framework.

Scenario 1: Email verification

Create an account, receive the verification email, extract the verification link, open it, and confirm account activation. Evaluate whether the tool requires custom scripts or external email services.

Scenario 2: SMS verification

Trigger an authentication code, receive it through an approved test number, extract the code, enter it, and confirm authentication. Evaluate support for external services and asynchronous delivery.

Scenario 3: Nested iframes

Interact with a credit card field embedded inside nested iframes. Verify that the tool can identify the correct browsing context and return to the main page afterward.

Scenario 4: Multiple browser tabs

Initiate an external authentication or payment flow that opens another browser tab. Complete the interaction and verify the result in the original tab.

Scenario 5: Dynamic application content

Test an interface containing changing element identifiers, asynchronous loading, and dynamically rendered components. Measure how often test maintenance is required.

Scenario 6: PDF extraction

Download an invoice and verify that the order identifier, customer information, and financial totals match the expected values.

Scenario 7: API-to-UI validation

Create a record through an API request and verify that the record is displayed correctly in the user interface.

Scenario 8: Contextual assertion

Verify that generated application content satisfies a requirement that cannot easily be reduced to a conventional exact-match assertion. For example, determine whether a customer support response addresses the customer's original request.

Scenario 9: Reusable authentication

Create an authentication sequence that can be reused across multiple test cases. Modify the authentication process and measure the effort required to update dependent tests.

Scenario 10: Cross-browser consistency

Execute equivalent scenarios on Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari. Record the actual browser versions, operating systems, and execution environments.

Scenario 11: Controlled application changes

Introduce a harmless change to an element locator, followed by a genuine functional defect. Evaluate whether self-healing repairs the harmless change without concealing the defect.

Scenario 12: Failure diagnosis

Introduce a known application error and evaluate how quickly the tool produces sufficient evidence to identify its cause.

Recommended benchmark procedure

  1. Use the same application and test data for every tool.
  2. Define success criteria before testing begins.
  3. Record test authoring time separately from execution time.
  4. Record all custom scripts, external services, and workarounds.
  5. Repeat successful executions under comparable conditions.
  6. Introduce identical application changes.
  7. Measure maintenance effort.
  8. Capture logs, screenshots, and execution evidence.
  9. Record licensing and infrastructure costs.
  10. Publish unsuccessful outcomes alongside successful ones.

Thirty repeated runs per scenario provide a useful initial sample for observing execution consistency, although larger samples may be necessary for low-frequency failures. Do not classify a capability as verified solely because it appears in product documentation.

Criterion Suggested weight
Functional coverage 20%

Enterprise AI testing: Security questions most comparisons overlook

AI test automation platforms may interact with sensitive application information, including credentials, customer records, financial transactions, medical information, page source, browser cookies, screenshots, API responses, and execution logs. This creates security considerations beyond those associated with conventional automation frameworks.

Where is application information processed?

Determine whether screenshots, page source, and other execution artifacts are processed within the vendor's infrastructure or transmitted to external AI providers.

Can individual AI features be disabled?

Organizations may approve AI-assisted test generation while prohibiting AI processing of production-like customer information. A platform that supports selective AI usage provides more flexibility for these requirements.

Does the vendor offer on-premises deployment?

On-premises deployment can help organizations control where test execution and storage occur. However, installing a testing platform internally does not automatically establish that every AI operation is performed internally. Verify the complete data flow.

How are AI agent permissions restricted?

Autonomous agents should not automatically receive unrestricted access to administrative interfaces. Evaluate role-based access, credential isolation, tool permissions, allowed environments, execution limits, approval requirements, audit logs, and network restrictions.

How does the platform handle prompt injection?

A testing agent may encounter application content containing instructions designed to influence its behavior. Application content should be treated as untrusted data rather than authoritative instructions. Include controlled prompt-injection scenarios in the evaluation, particularly when agents have access to external tools or sensitive application actions.

Is human approval available?

Some activities should require approval before execution. Examples include deleting records, modifying account permissions, or initiating real financial transactions. Testing environments, synthetic data, and restricted accounts should be used wherever possible.

What happens when the agent cannot complete an objective?

Determine whether the system supports execution limits, timeouts, retries, clear stopping conditions, and inspectable failure states. An agent should not continue indefinitely simply because it has not achieved its objective.

Testing applications built with AI coding agents

The growth of AI-assisted software development creates a new challenge for software quality. A coding agent can generate application code and corresponding tests, but both may share the same misunderstanding of a requirement.

For example, an agent might implement a discount calculation incorrectly and then generate a test that expects the same incorrect result. Both the implementation and test can agree while the application remains wrong. Independent verification is therefore important.

A practical workflow might involve:

  1. A coding agent implements a feature.
  2. Conventional unit tests verify implementation details.
  3. A separate testing process derives scenarios from business requirements.
  4. Browser-based tests verify actual user-facing behavior.
  5. Failure evidence is returned to the development process.
  6. A human reviews significant changes in expected behavior.

Tools such as Endtest, testers.ai, Alumnium, and Maestro offer different ways to participate in AI-assisted development and verification workflows. The important architectural principle is to avoid treating agreement between AI-generated implementation and AI-generated tests as sufficient evidence of correctness.

Common mistakes when adopting AI test automation

Mistake 1: Measuring test generation speed instead of long-term reliability

Generating 100 automated tests in an afternoon is not particularly valuable if half require substantial maintenance the following week. Measure ongoing reliability and maintenance effort.

Mistake 2: Assuming AI eliminates the need for testing expertise

AI can assist with implementation and exploration, but somebody still needs to understand business requirements and determine whether the application behaves correctly.

Mistake 3: Using AI for every assertion

An exact numerical comparison generally does not benefit from a language model. Reserve AI-based assertions for situations where contextual interpretation is genuinely useful.

Mistake 4: Ignoring self-healing risks

A repaired locator should still identify the intended element. Automatically preserving a passing test result is not the same as preserving the original test objective.

Mistake 5: Evaluating only simple demonstrations

Require vendors to automate scenarios involving actual application complexity. Email verification, nested iframes, external payment providers, PDF extraction, and asynchronous interfaces are useful starting points.

Mistake 6: Ignoring test portability

Determine what happens if the vendor changes its pricing, discontinues the product, or fails to meet future requirements. Investigate export capabilities and migration options before purchasing.

Mistake 7: Treating headless execution as complete browser coverage

Headless browser environments provide useful automation capabilities. However, they do not necessarily reproduce every operating system integration, browser-specific behavior, or real-device condition.

Mistake 8: Ignoring agent execution costs

An autonomous agent that repeatedly observes an application and invokes a language model may have different operating costs from a predefined automated test. Measure the cost per successfully completed objective.

Mistake 9: Confusing autonomous exploration with regression coverage

An agent exploring an application may discover useful behavior. It does not automatically guarantee that every important business requirement has been verified. Maintain explicit coverage for critical functionality.

Which AI test automation tools support real Safari?

Endtest supports actual Safari execution on macOS. Other cross-browser platforms should be evaluated according to their documented browser and operating system configurations. Do not assume that WebKit execution and Safari execution are identical.

Can AI generate Selenium or Playwright tests?

Yes. General-purpose coding agents and specialized AI testing products can generate Selenium and Playwright scripts. The main challenge is ensuring that the generated code remains reliable, maintainable, and aligned with business requirements.

Is AI test automation better than Playwright?

AI test automation and Playwright are not mutually exclusive. Playwright is a browser automation framework. AI can be used to generate, maintain, or extend tests written with Playwright. Alternatively, organizations can adopt higher-level testing platforms that manage automation infrastructure and expose human-readable test workflows. The better option depends on the team's technical expertise and operational requirements.

Can AI test automation replace manual testing?

AI can automate some repetitive manual testing activities and assist with exploration. Human judgment remains important for identifying business risks, interpreting ambiguous requirements, evaluating usability, and investigating unexpected behavior.

Can AI test automation tools convert Excel test cases into automated tests?

Some platforms, including Endtest, provide AI-assisted capabilities for converting human-readable manual test instructions into executable automation. The resulting tests should be reviewed for missing assumptions, incorrect actions, and incomplete assertions.

What is self-healing test automation?

Self-healing is the ability of an automation system to recover from certain changes that would otherwise break existing tests. A common application involves identifying an intended interface element after its locator changes. Effective self-healing must preserve the original testing objective.

Are AI-generated tests flaky?

They can be, just as manually generated tests can be. Flakiness depends on application synchronization, locator quality, test data, infrastructure, and execution architecture. AI-generated tests should undergo the same reliability checks as any other automated test.

Do AI testing agents produce deterministic results?

Not necessarily. Agents that select actions dynamically may produce different execution paths under equivalent conditions. Teams requiring predictable regression coverage should evaluate predefined execution flows or hybrid approaches.

What is the difference between visual AI and generative AI testing?

Visual AI primarily evaluates application appearance and visual changes. Generative AI can create test instructions, generate data, analyze failures, or participate in autonomous testing workflows. Some platforms combine these capabilities.

Can AI test automation tools test APIs?

Many comprehensive automation platforms include API testing capabilities or integrate with existing API testing frameworks. Evaluate whether the platform can combine API requests and browser interactions within a single end-to-end scenario.

Can AI test automation be used on-premises?

Some platforms offer on-premises deployment. Endtest is one example. Open-source frameworks can also be operated within an organization's infrastructure. Confirm whether external AI services are involved when individual AI features are enabled.

How should regulated industries use AI in automated testing?

Use synthetic or appropriately controlled test data, limit agent permissions, document data flows, establish audit trails, and validate applicable regulatory and contractual requirements. Prefer precise assertions for critical business outcomes.

What is MCP in AI test automation?

The Model Context Protocol provides a standardized way for compatible AI applications to interact with external tools and resources. In test automation, MCP can allow AI assistants to discover tests, initiate executions, inspect results, and participate in broader development workflows. Access should be controlled through appropriate permissions.

What is the difference between an AI testing agent and an AI testing workflow?

An AI testing workflow typically follows predefined orchestration logic with one or more AI-assisted operations. An autonomous agent can dynamically select actions based on observations and progress toward an objective. Many practical systems combine predefined workflows with agentic components.

Will AI replace Selenium?

AI may reduce the amount of Selenium code that engineers need to write manually. However, browser automation technologies remain useful for performing precise application interactions. AI can operate above those technologies rather than replacing them entirely.

How much do AI test automation tools cost?

Costs vary considerably. Open-source tools may have no software licensing fee but still require infrastructure and AI model expenses. Commercial platforms may charge based on subscription tiers, parallel execution capacity, users, devices, or AI usage. Endtest, for example, lists plans starting at $175 per month; confirm the current pricing before purchasing.

How do you choose an AI test automation tool?

Identify mandatory requirements, define representative testing scenarios, run comparable proofs of concept, measure maintenance and reliability, and calculate total operating costs. Avoid purchasing a platform solely on the quality of an AI demonstration.

For autonomous application exploration, QA.tech, Thunders.ai, and agentic capabilities within broader platforms offer different approaches.

The best choice is the one that performs reliably against the workflows your organization needs to verify. Rather than asking which platform has the most AI features, ask which platform provides the greatest sustainable confidence in your releases.

title: How Multi-Agent Bots Work Inside Facebook Messenger
description:
Most people think a Facebook Messenger chatbot is one script that receives a message and sends back a reply. That works for FAQs. It starts to break down when the same bot has to answer product questions, check order status, qualify leads, and hand off to a human, all in one thread.

This is where multiple AI agents working together help. In this post you'll learn how multi-agent chatbots work in Facebook Messenger: how a message travels from the user to your server, how a router agent picks the right specialist, how replies return through the Messenger Platform, and what the Messenger bot architecture looks like as a sequence diagram.

By the end you'll have a working skeleton of a multi-agent chatbot you can extend.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites
  • How chatbots work in Messenger (the basics)
  • Why a single bot isn't enough
  • The multi-agent AI system at a glance
  • Sequence diagram: one message, end to end
  • Step 1: Receive messages with a webhook
  • Step 2: Build the router agent
  • Step 3: Add specialist agents
  • Step 4: Send the reply to Messenger
  • Shared state and handoffs
  • Messenger rules that shape your design
  • Common pitfalls
  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

Before you start, you'll need:

  • A Facebook Page and a Meta developer app with the Messenger product added
  • A Page access token and an app secret (from your app settings)
  • Node.js 18+ and a public HTTPS URL for your webhook (a tunnel like ngrok works for development)
  • Basic familiarity with Express and async JavaScript
  • An LLM API key of your choice (the examples use a generic callLLM() helper)

Note: Meta updates Graph API versions regularly. The examples use v21.0 as a placeholder. Check the current version in Meta's docs before you ship.

How chatbots work in Messenger (the basics)

If you're asking how chatbots work on Messenger, the core loop is simple:

  1. A user sends a message to your Facebook Page.
  2. Meta sends an HTTPS POST request (a webhook event) to your server.
  3. Your server decides what to say.
  4. Your server calls the Send API to deliver the reply.

Every Facebook chatbot automation tool, from no-code builders to custom code, is some version of this loop. The interesting part is step 3: how does your server decide?

In a basic bot, step 3 is a rules engine or a single LLM prompt. In a multi-agent AI system, step 3 becomes a small team.

Why a single bot isn't enough

A single prompt that handles everything tends to hit the same walls:

  • Prompt bloat. Sales, support, and billing instructions compete for attention.
  • Tool confusion. One agent with 15 tools picks the wrong one more often.
  • Hard to test. You can't evaluate "support quality" separately from "sales quality."
  • Hard to change. Editing one behavior risks breaking another.

Splitting the work across AI agents in Messenger, each with a narrow job, fixes most of this. It's the same reason we split a monolith into services.

The multi-agent AI system at a glance

A typical multi-agent chatbot for Messenger has four parts:

Component Job
Webhook layer Verifies and receives Messenger events, returns 200 OK fast
Router agent Classifies intent and picks which specialist handles the turn
Specialist agents Narrow agents (FAQ, orders, lead capture, human handoff) with their own prompt and tools
Shared state Stores conversation history, user profile, and the current "owner" agent

The user only ever sees one bot. Behind the scenes, multiple AI agents work together on each turn.

Sequence diagram: one message, end to end

Here's what happens when a user asks, "Where is my order #1042?"

User        Messenger        Webhook        Router        Order Agent     State        Send API
 |              |               |              |               |            |              |
 |--message---->|               |              |               |            |              |
 |              |--POST event-->|              |               |            |              |
 |              |               |--200 OK----->| (ack fast)    |            |              |
 |              |               |--load ctx------------------------------>|              |
 |              |               |<-history/profile-------------------------|              |
 |              |               |--classify--->|               |            |              |
 |              |               |<-intent: order_status        |            |              |
 |              |               |--run agent-------------------->|           |              |
 |              |               |              |   call get_order(1042)      |              |
 |              |               |<-reply text-------------------|            |              |
 |              |               |--save turn--------------------------------->|              |
 |              |               |--typing_on + send message------------------------------>|
 |<--------------------------------------------reply----------------------------------------|

Three things to notice:

  1. The webhook acknowledges immediately. Meta expects a quick 200. Heavy agent work should happen after the ack.
  2. State is loaded before routing. The router needs context, not just the latest message.
  3. Only one agent speaks per turn. Others may work behind the scenes, but the user gets a single reply.

Step 1: Receive messages with a webhook

First, verify the webhook and receive events. Meta calls your GET endpoint once to verify, then sends events to your POST endpoint.

import express from "express";
import crypto from "crypto";

const app = express();

// Keep the raw body so we can verify Meta's signature
app.use(express.json({
  verify: (req, _res, buf) => { req.rawBody = buf; }
}));

const VERIFY_TOKEN = process.env.VERIFY_TOKEN;
const APP_SECRET = process.env.APP_SECRET;

// 1) Webhook verification
app.get("/webhook", (req, res) => {
  const mode = req.query["hub.mode"];
  const token = req.query["hub.verify_token"];
  const challenge = req.query["hub.challenge"];

  if (mode === "subscribe" && token === VERIFY_TOKEN) {
    return res.status(200).send(challenge);
  }
  res.sendStatus(403);
});

// 2) Receive events
app.post("/webhook", (req, res) => {
  if (!isValidSignature(req)) return res.sendStatus(401);

  // Acknowledge immediately, then process asynchronously
  res.sendStatus(200);

  if (req.body.object !== "page") return;

  for (const entry of req.body.entry) {
    for (const event of entry.messaging ?? []) {
      if (event.message && !event.message.is_echo) {
        handleMessage(event).catch(console.error);
      }
    }
  }
});

function isValidSignature(req) {
  const header = req.get("x-hub-signature-256");
  if (!header) return false;
  const expected =
    "sha256=" +
    crypto.createHmac("sha256", APP_SECRET).update(req.rawBody).digest("hex");
  const a = Buffer.from(header);
  const b = Buffer.from(expected);
  return a.length === b.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

Tip: Always verify X-Hub-Signature-256. Without it, anyone who finds your URL can send fake events to your agents.

Step 2: Build the router agent

The router's only job is to decide who should handle the turn. Keep it small, cheap, and strict about its output format.

const AGENTS = {
  faq: "Answers general questions about the business.",
  orders: "Checks order status and handles returns.",
  leads: "Qualifies new prospects and collects contact details.",
  human: "Hands the conversation to a human teammate.",
};

async function route({ message, history, currentAgent }) {
  const prompt = `
You are a routing agent for a Facebook Messenger chatbot.
Pick exactly one agent for the user's latest message.

Agents:
${Object.entries(AGENTS).map(([k, v]) => `- ${k}: ${v}`).join("\n")}

Current agent: ${currentAgent ?? "none"}
Rules:
- Stay with the current agent if the message is a follow-up.
- Choose "human" if the user is angry or asks for a person.
- Respond ONLY with JSON: {"agent": "<name>", "reason": "<short>"}

Recent history:
${history.slice(-6).map(m => `${m.role}: ${m.text}`).join("\n")}

Latest message: ${message}
`;

  const raw = await callLLM(prompt);
  try {
    const parsed = JSON.parse(raw);
    return AGENTS[parsed.agent] ? parsed.agent : "faq";
  } catch {
    return "faq"; // safe fallback
  }
}

Two design choices matter here:

  • Sticky routing. If the user is mid-way through an order lookup, a short reply like "yes" shouldn't bounce to a different agent.
  • A safe fallback. If the router returns garbage, default to the FAQ agent instead of failing silently.

Step 3: Add specialist agents

Each specialist agent has its own system prompt and its own small toolset. That's the main benefit of multi-agent chatbot design: narrow scope, fewer mistakes.

const specialists = {
  faq: {
    system: "You answer questions using the provided knowledge base. If unsure, say so.",
    tools: [searchKnowledgeBase],
  },
  orders: {
    system: "You help with order status. Never guess; always call get_order first.",
    tools: [getOrder, startReturn],
  },
  leads: {
    system: "You qualify leads politely. Collect name, need, and email. One question at a time.",
    tools: [saveLead],
  },
  human: {
    system: "Tell the user a teammate will follow up, then flag the thread.",
    tools: [flagForHuman],
  },
};

async function runAgent(name, { message, history, profile }) {
  const agent = specialists[name];
  return callLLM({
    system: agent.system,
    tools: agent.tools,
    messages: [...history, { role: "user", text: message }],
    context: { profile },
  });
}

Now wire it together:

async function handleMessage(event) {
  const userId = event.sender.id;
  const text = event.message.text;
  if (!text) return; // handle attachments separately

  const state = await loadState(userId); // history, profile, currentAgent

  await sendAction(userId, "typing_on");

  const agentName = await route({
    message: text,
    history: state.history,
    currentAgent: state.currentAgent,
  });

  const reply = await runAgent(agentName, {
    message: text,
    history: state.history,
    profile: state.profile,
  });

  await saveState(userId, {
    ...state,
    currentAgent: agentName,
    history: [
      ...state.history,
      { role: "user", text },
      { role: "assistant", text: reply, agent: agentName },
    ],
  });

  await sendText(userId, reply);
}

Step 4: Send the reply to Messenger

Replies go out through the Send API on the Graph API.

const GRAPH = "https://graph.facebook.com/v21.0/me/messages";
const PAGE_TOKEN = process.env.PAGE_ACCESS_TOKEN;

async function callSendAPI(body) {
  const res = await fetch(`${GRAPH}?access_token=${PAGE_TOKEN}`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });
  if (!res.ok) console.error("Send API error:", await res.text());
}

const sendText = (psid, text) =>
  callSendAPI({
    recipient: { id: psid },
    messaging_type: "RESPONSE",
    message: { text },
  });

const sendAction = (psid, action) =>
  callSendAPI({ recipient: { id: psid }, sender_action: action });

The typing_on action is a small touch, but it matters: LLM calls take a few seconds, and a typing indicator tells the user the bot is working.

Shared state and handoffs

When multiple AI agents work together, state is what keeps them from feeling like separate bots. A minimal state object looks like this:

{
  "userId": "PSID_12345",
  "currentAgent": "orders",
  "profile": { "name": "Sam", "email": "sam@example.com" },
  "openTask": { "type": "order_lookup", "orderId": "1042" },
  "history": [ ... ]
}

Good handoffs follow three rules:

  • Pass context, not just text. When the router moves a user from faq to leads, include what was already discussed.
  • Record who said what. Tag each assistant turn with its agent name so you can debug later.
  • Always keep an exit. Every agent should be able to escalate to human.

Messenger rules that shape your design

AI chatbot integration with Messenger isn't just code. Platform rules affect your architecture:

  • Respond quickly to webhooks. Ack first, process after.
  • Standard messaging window. In general, you can send promotional or follow-up content only within a limited window after the user's last message. Outside it, you need approved message tags or other supported formats. Check Meta's current policy before designing proactive flows.
  • Human handoff expectations. Meta's platform supports handover between apps (for example, bot to a human inbox). Plan for it from day one.
  • Rate limits and retries. Meta may retry failed webhook deliveries, so make your handler idempotent (dedupe by message ID). 
const seen = new Set(); // use Redis or a DB in production

function isDuplicate(event) {
  const id = event.message?.mid;
  if (!id) return false;
  if (seen.has(id)) return true;
  seen.add(id);
  return false;
}

Common pitfalls

  1. Routing on every turn without stickiness. Users get bounced between agents mid-task.
  2. Letting two agents reply. Pick one speaker per turn.
  3. No fallback. When the router or an agent fails, send a short, honest error message instead of silence.
  4. Skipping logs. Log the router's choice and reason on every turn. It's your best debugging tool.
  5. Testing only the happy path. Test angry users, off-topic messages, and attachments too.

Conclusion

Here's what to remember about how multi-agent chatbots work in Facebook Messenger:

  • A Messenger bot is a webhook loop: receive, decide, reply.
  • A multi-agent AI system upgrades the "decide" step into a router plus focused specialist agents.
  • Shared state and clean handoffs make several agents feel like one assistant.
  • Platform rules (fast acks, messaging windows, handover) should shape your Messenger bot architecture from the start.

If you'd rather not wire up webhooks, routing, and channel rules yourself, platforms like Botsailor handle Messenger automation alongside WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram, so you can focus on the agent logic instead of the plumbing.

Have you built a multi-agent bot for Messenger or another channel? What did your routing layer look like, and what broke first? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Accidental Deletion or Corrupted Hard Drive? 6 Crucial Steps to Protect Your Data Before Recovery
description:
Losing access to years of photos, financial records, or critical project files—whether due to a dead laptop, an accidentally formatted SSD, or a clicking hard drive—can feel overwhelming. However, the actions you take in the first few minutes after data loss often determine whether your files can be completely recovered or permanently overwritten.

  1. Stop Using the Device Immediately
    The moment you realize files are missing or a drive is malfunctioning, stop saving, downloading, or copying new files onto it. When data is deleted or a partition gets corrupted, the system marks that storage space as available. Continuing to use the laptop or external drive can overwrite the raw data sectors beyond recovery.

  2. Never Run "Format" When Prompted by Windows or macOS
    If you plug in a pen drive, memory card, or external hard disk and see a pop-up saying "You need to format the disk before you can use it," click Cancel. Formatting resets the file system structure and makes recovery significantly harder.

  3. Do Not Repeatedly Restart a Clicking or Beeping Hard Drive
    A faint clicking, grinding, or beeping sound from a 2.5-inch laptop hard disk or external HDD usually points to a mechanical read/write head failure. Powering the drive on and off repeatedly forces the damaged head to scratch the magnetic platters, destroying recoverable data permanently.

  4. Avoid Installing Recovery Software on the Same Drive
    If you attempt basic software recovery for minor accidental deletions, never download or install the recovery tool onto the same drive or partition where the lost data lived. Always install tools on a separate computer and save recovered files onto an external backup drive.

  5. Keep Water-Damaged Laptops Powered Off
    If a laptop or mobile device stops working after a liquid spill, do not try plugging in the charger to "check if the data is still there." Applying power to a wet motherboard or SSD can cause a short circuit across the storage controller chip.

  6. Choose a Specialized Lab Over Trial-and-Error Fixes
    For dead NVMe/M.2 SSDs, corrupted RAID/NAS arrays, or physically damaged drives, software tools will not work and can worsen media degradation.
