title: HTTP from scratch: a server without a framework
description:
The whole course you've been delegating the waiting. Now it's time to spend it on what Node was invented for: taking requests.

And before anyone sells you a framework, there's a question only the bare http module answers: what does Express do for you? This lesson shows it by doing the same thing without it, limitations included. The most useful one shows up on the first test: asking for /greeting with DELETE returns 404, not "method not allowed", because a three-line router can't tell the two apart.

The smallest server 

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" });
  res.end("hello\n");
});

server.listen(3133, () => console.log("listening on 3133"));

Two real lines: createServer takes a function, listen opens the port. And it answers:

curl -s -i http://localhost:3133/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Date: Sat, 14 Nov 2026 21:10:30 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

Look at what you didn't write: the status line, the date, Connection, and that Transfer-Encoding: chunked which appears because you gave no Content-Length. Node fills in what it can; what you decide is the code, the headers you care about, and the body.

That callback runs once per request, not once per connection. That's the difference from a socket server, and the reason the course's event loop matters here: a hundred requests are a hundred calls, not a hundred threads.

What the request brings

req is an IncomingMessage, and what you need lives in three places: method, URL and headers.

const url = new URL(req.url, `http://${req.headers.host}`);
const name = url.searchParams.get("name") ?? "world";

That new URL isn't ceremony: req.url is only the path and query part — /greeting?name=Ada — with no host or protocol. Building a URL needs a base, and req.headers.host provides it. With the object in hand you get searchParams, which decodes and encodes for you.

curl -s "http://localhost:3133/greeting?name=Ada"

{"greeting":"hello Ada"}

Headers arrive in req.headers, lowercased and as strings: host, user-agent, content-type, authorization. Everything a client wants to tell you is there, unvalidated.

You have to read the body yourself

Here's the first serious difference from a framework. req is a stream: the body isn't a property, it arrives in chunks.

routes.set("POST /echo", async (req, res) => {
  let body = "";
  for await (const chunk of req) body += chunk;

  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(body);
    res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ received: data }));
  } catch {
    res.writeHead(400, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: "invalid JSON" }));
  }
});

curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"book":"Emma"}' http://localhost:3133/echo

{"received":{"book":"Emma"}}

And with garbage:

curl -s -i -X POST -d 'not json' http://localhost:3133/echo

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

Three things you're doing by hand that a framework hands you done: accumulate the stream, parse it, and decide which code to return when the JSON is broken. Plus a fourth you can't see: there's no size limit. Someone can send you two gigabytes of body and your server piles it into a string until the process dies. A framework sets a default limit; with bare HTTP, you set it.

And a measured detail that corrects the intuition: if you don't read the body, the response still goes out fine (200 in 23 ms with two megabytes sent). Nothing breaks. You just lose the data, and Node has to drain the socket anyway. Not reading the body isn't a protocol error: it's a datum you throw away.

The response: codes and headers

res is a ServerResponse, and it has two ways to write: writeHead(code, headers) in one go, or setHeader first and writeHead after. The body goes in end().

The status code is information for the client, not for you. 200 is "here it is", 201 "I created it", 400 "your request is wrong", 404 "that route doesn't exist", 500 "I broke". Picking the wrong code turns a client bug into a server alert.

Then Content-Length, which is where you can tell whether someone thought about the client:

const body = "fixed response\n";
res.writeHead(200, {
  "Content-Type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8",
  "Content-Length": Buffer.byteLength(body),
});
res.end(body);

Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 15

Without Content-Length, Node uses Transfer-Encoding: chunked and the client receives pieces without knowing how much is left. With it, the client knows the exact size from the start. Buffer.byteLength and not .length: in UTF-8, "ñ" is two bytes and one letter.

A router in a Map

createServer knows nothing about routes: it hands you every request and you decide. With the Map from the modules lesson, a router fits in ten lines.

const routes = new Map();

routes.set("GET /", (req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" });
  res.end("hello\n");
});

routes.set("GET /greeting", (req, res) => {
  // …
});

const server = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const path = new URL(req.url, `http://${req.headers.host}`).pathname;
  const handler = routes.get(`${req.method} ${path}`);

  if (!handler) {
    res.writeHead(404, { "Content-Type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" });
    res.end("not found\n");
    return;
  }
  await handler(req, res);
});

It works, and that's where the trouble starts. The key is "METHOD path", so:

  • A DELETE /greeting finds nothing and returns 404, when the right answer would be 405 Method Not Allowed. Measured, and that's what this router does.

And here's a correction before you idealise the framework: Express doesn't tell those two cases apart either by default. In the next lesson, the same DELETE on a route that only accepts GET returns 404 as well. The 405 is written by whoever wants it: neither the three-line router nor the sixty-five-package framework hands it to you.

  • There are no route parameters: /books/42 isn't a concept. You'd have to split the string and compare prefixes.
  • There's no middleware: nothing that runs before or after every route.
  • There's no error handling: if a handler throws, the await propagates and the request sits unanswered until the client gives up.

That's exactly what Express solves, which is why the next lesson takes it apart instead of presenting it as magic. But now you know what's underneath, which is the difference between using a tool and believing in one.

Connections that get reused

An HTTP request doesn't have to open a new TCP connection. By default, HTTP/1.1 keeps the connection open and reuses it, and you can see it in the headers from the start: Connection: keep-alive and Keep-Alive: timeout=5.

It shows better with curl, asking for two URLs in one invocation.

curl -v http://localhost:3134/a http://localhost:3134/b

* Connection #0 to host localhost:3134 left intact
* Connection #0 to host localhost:3134 left intact

The same connection #0 for both requests: no new TCP or TLS handshake. Under load that's the difference between one connection per request and one per client, and it explains why killing servers abruptly leaves connections in a state nobody expects.

The client that never finishes talking

An HTTP server doesn't just wait for data: it waits for complete headers before it can answer you. A client can open a connection, send half a header and go quiet indefinitely. With enough clients like that, you run out of ports without having received a single valid request.

Node ships the limits, and here's the detail almost no tutorial mentions: they aren't per-connection timers, they're periodic checks.

const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  res.end("ok\n");
});

server.headersTimeout = 300;
server.connectionsCheckingInterval = 50;

With that, a client sending half a header and going quiet gets this:

closed after 318 ms · received: HTTP/1.1 408 Request Timeout

A 408, which is the right code and which almost nobody implements by hand. But try removing the second line: with headersTimeout = 300 and the default interval, the client was still connected at five seconds. The default checking interval is thirty seconds, so the limit is enforced when the check runs, not when it's reached.

The three values that matter: headersTimeout (60 s by default) for headers, requestTimeout (5 min) for the whole body, and keepAliveTimeout (5 s) for the idle connection left open between requests. In production there's almost always a proxy in front with its own timeouts, and it usually fires before yours.

CORS, the minimum

If a page on fjp.es calls an API on api.fjp.es, the browser blocks the response unless the server explicitly allows it. That's CORS, and with bare HTTP it's one header and one special case.

res.setHeader("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*");

if (req.method === "OPTIONS") {
  res.writeHead(204, {
    "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, POST, OPTIONS",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type",
  });
  res.end();
  return;
}

curl -s -i -X OPTIONS -H "Origin: https://fjp.es" http://localhost:3134/

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type

That OPTIONS is the preflight: the browser asks before sending the real request. 204 and no body, because there's nothing to return, only permissions. And * in Allow-Origin means "anyone", which is fine for a public API and wrong for one that carries cookies.

Common problems

res.end() returns nothing to the client

You forgot to call it, or you called writeHead after writing the body. A request without end() leaves the client waiting until timeout.

Cannot set headers after they are sent

You called writeHead twice, or wrote the body before the headers. Headers always come before the body.

The body arrives empty

You didn't read it. req is a stream: without for await or req.on("data"), there's no body.

JSON.parse explodes on real requests

You didn't check Content-Type or catch the error. An empty or malformed body isn't a server exception: it's a 400.

Many open connections and no completed requests

Slow clients that never finish sending headers. Without a tuned headersTimeout and a short checking interval, those connections hold ports until something outside cuts them.

Works with curl, fails from the browser

CORS. The browser demands the headers and, for non-simple requests, the OPTIONS first.

What you take from this lesson

  • createServer gives one function per request, with req and res, and knows nothing about routes.
  • req.url is path plus query; URL needs a base, and req.headers.host gives it.
  • The body is a stream: read it with for await, and the size limit is yours to set.
  • Not reading the body doesn't break the response: you lose the data.
  • Content-Length versus chunked, and why it's computed with Buffer.byteLength.
  • A router is a Map keyed by "METHOD path", which is why a wrong method returns 404 instead of 405. Express doesn't tell them apart either: the 405 is yours to write.
  • With no middleware and no error handling, that router falls short the moment it grows.
  • HTTP/1.1 reuses connections; curl -v shows the same connection twice.
  • CORS by hand is one header and an OPTIONS answering 204.
  • Server timeouts are enforced by a periodic check, not per connection: without tuning connectionsCheckingInterval, a short headersTimeout does nothing.

You have the floor now. The next lesson puts Express on top of it and takes it apart: what each piece actually does, what it saves you and what it hides. After writing the router by hand, the comparison reads differently.

Never stop coding!

title: How Pure Async HTTP/2 and Expat Byte-Offset Streaming Cut Apify Cloud Cost to $0.011 per 1,000 Rows
description:
Spinning up headless browsers over residential proxies ($7 to $8 per GB) typically burns $11 to $15 per 1,000 pages in raw infrastructure overhead. For solo builders and RevOps teams feeding Clay or n8n, browser-based scrapers break flat-rate unit economics before you even touch the dataset.

Over the past week, I moved a commercial B2B and regulatory telemetry fleet on Apify Cloud strictly onto pure async HTTP/2 (httpx[http2]), async DNS (dnspython), and streaming XML/JSON parsers in Python 3.12 with zero headless browsers and zero residential proxies.

Measured Apify Cloud Benchmarks (256 MB Container, Nov 25, 2026)

Every figure below comes directly from real Apify Cloud production runs under Limited permissions and Pay-Per-Event billing (zero +usage compute pass-through):

Engine Workload Cloud Runtime Compute Units (CU) Total Platform Cost / 1,000 Rows
WealthPulse V3.5 (SEC Form ADV) Stream 24,124 SEC RIAs, rank top 25 CA by AUM 3.943 s 0.000274 $0.0114
US Healthcare KOL & NPI Enricher 3-way CMS NPPES + Open Payments + Medicare join 6.496 s 0.000451 $0.0130
US SLED Gov Bids & RFP Monitor 30+ Bonfire portals + NYC Procurement Socrata 6.424 s 0.000446 $0.0132
SaaS Trust Center & SOC 2 Audit DNS CNAME/TXT + RFC 9116 security.txt + AI subprocessors 6.108 s 0.000424 $0.0455

Three Engineering Decisions That Made the Difference

1. Expat Byte-Offset Spooling Instead of Loading XML Trees into RAM

The official U.S. SEC Form ADV compilation (IA_FIRM_SEC_Feed_*.xml.gz) contains 24,124 <Firm> records. Loading the full DOM inflates memory and slows cold starts. Instead, we stream the gzipped file through a bounded decompression guard (BoundedGzipReader against zip bombs) into Python's C-backed expat parser, tracking only (rank_key, byte_start, byte_end) inside heapq.nsmallest(limit). Only the winning K firm byte slices are hydrated via lxml with resolve_entities=False and load_dtd=False.

Auditing the live Nov 24, 2026 SEC compilation also caught a silent data trap affecting 1,360 firms: they answered N on the Item 11 header attribute (Q11), yet answered Y on one or more of the 24 detailed affiliate disclosure questions (Item11A through Item11H). Keeping missing fields as explicit null or unknown_unreported prevents incomplete records from falsely passing clean-record compliance filters.

2. Strictly Flat snake_case Output Cuts Clay Actions by 91.7%

Nested JSON arrays force extra JavaScript parser nodes in n8n and burn extra paid Actions in Clay. A 12-step Clay enrichment table across 1,000 rows consumes 12,000 Actions. Collapsing tech-stack fingerprinting, DNS MX/SPF/DMARC checks, ad pixel extraction, or regulatory joins into a single flat-schema HTTP/2 call consumes 1,000 Actions per 1,000 rows and maps straight into CRM columns.

3. Streamable HTTP MCP Gateway on Cloudflare Workers

To let AI agents (Claude, Cursor, VS Code, ChatGPT) query the fleet directly without brittle scraping wrappers, we deployed a read-only Streamable HTTP MCP Gateway on Cloudflare Workers (protocol 2026-07-28, readOnlyHint: true, Authorization: Bearer). It is published on the Official MCP Registry (v1.2.0), approved on mcpservers.org, listed on Glama, merged into punkpeye/awesome-remote-mcp-servers (#5881), and live-monitored on mcptry.com.

  • Bulk Domain DMARC, SPF & MX Security Auditor (live DNS deliverability & email security for MSPs): https://apify.com/sayod111/dmarc-spf-mx-deliverability-auditor
  • B2B Revenue Intelligence (97 Flat ICP Fields) (110+ tech fingerprints, DNS, corporate contacts): https://apify.com/sayod111/b2b-revenue-lead-enricher-mcp

title: Generate a Printable Word Search in ~20 Lines of Python (With the Answer Key Free)
description:
I build kids' activity books. Word searches are the easy part to imagine and the slow part to make: place ten words on a grid without collisions, fill the empty cells, then — the part everyone forgets — write down exactly where every word landed so you can print an answer key. Do that by hand for one puzzle and you'll spend twenty minutes. Do it for a whole book and you'll spend your week.

So I automated it. This is the generator I use, exposed as an API called ActivityForge, and in this tutorial we'll call it from Python: send a theme, get back a finished, print-ready word search — grid, word list, answer key, and a PDF — in about twenty lines.

What we're building

A small Python script that:

  1. POSTs to the word-search endpoint with a theme (ocean), an age band (6-8), and a seed (42)
  2. Prints the letter grid and the words to find
  3. Saves the print-ready PDF that comes back in the same response

The API lives on RapidAPI. The free tier gives you 100 calls a day, and every plan — free included — reaches every endpoint and every format. The paid plans only change how many calls you get, starting at $19/month. Nothing in this tutorial needs a paid plan.

Setup

Subscribe on the ActivityForge listing (the free tier is fine), copy your key from the listing's Endpoints page, then:

pip install requests
export RAPIDAPI_KEY=your_key_here

Step 1: Make the call

The whole request is one POST. Two headers carry your key and the host; the JSON body carries the puzzle settings.

import os
import sys

import requests

HOST = "activityforge.p.rapidapi.com"


def generate_word_search() -> dict:
    response = requests.post(
        f"https://{HOST}/v1/word-search",
        headers={
            "X-RapidAPI-Key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"],
            "X-RapidAPI-Host": HOST,
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        json={
            "theme": "ocean",  # or send "words": [...] with your own list
            "age_band": "6-8",  # "3-5" | "6-8" | "9-12"
            "seed": 42,  # same seed = same puzzle, forever
            "format": "all",  # "json" | "svg" | "pdf" | "all"
        },
        timeout=30,
    )
    if not response.ok:
        try:
            message = response.json()["error"]["message"]
        except Exception:
            message = "request failed"
        sys.exit(f"ActivityForge {response.status_code}: {message}")
    return response.json()

A few things worth knowing about the parameters:

  • theme — there are 12 built-in word lists: animals, ocean, space, garden, food, weather, farm, jungle, arctic, school, sports, and music. If you'd rather use your own vocabulary, send words (a list of up to 50) instead of theme. Custom words pass through a kids-safety screen before they can reach a puzzle.
  • age_band — 3-5, 6-8, or 9-12. It tunes word length, grid size, and difficulty together, so a puzzle for a five-year-old is forwards-only on a small grid, and a puzzle for a ten-year-old runs in all directions.
  • format — json returns just the puzzle data, svg or pdf add a rendered page, and all returns everything in one response. Errors come back in a consistent shape — {"error": {"code", "message"}} — which is what the error handling above reads.

Step 2: Print the puzzle

The response carries the grid as a list of strings, one per row, plus the word list:

def main() -> None:
    if "RAPIDAPI_KEY" not in os.environ:
        sys.exit("Set RAPIDAPI_KEY first — see the docstring at the top of this file.")

    puzzle = generate_word_search()

    print(f"Word search — theme: {puzzle['theme']}, "
          f"ages {puzzle['age_band']}, seed {puzzle['seed']}\n")
    for row in puzzle["grid"]:
        print(" ".join(row))
    print("\nFind these words:", ", ".join(puzzle["words"]))

Run it and you get:

Word search — theme: ocean, ages 6-8, seed 42

A Y P P Y N S A I L
U L H K M C W T C P
C L E V A W V N S I
F L G S A A F I H H
I E E L M H D H I D
S H C O N E D P P N
H S C B R S I L I A
M P E A R L U O S S
P U B M M N Q D W M
T B E A C H S U E C

Find these words: DOLPHIN, SQUID, SHELL, BEACH, PEARL, FISH, WAVE, SAIL, SHIP, SAND

That's a real response, not a mockup — you can check BEACH across the bottom row yourself.

Step 3: The answer key is already in the response

Here's the part that saves the real time. The response includes a solution object with a placements list — every word's start and end coordinates (as [row, column]) and its direction:

{"word": "WAVE", "start": [2, 5], "end": [2, 2], "direction": "left"}
{"word": "BEACH", "start": [9, 1], "end": [9, 5], "direction": "right"}
{"word": "SHELL", "start": [6, 1], "end": [2, 1], "direction": "up"}

Check WAVE against the grid: row 2, column 5 is W, and reading left you cross A, V, E. The placements aren't decoration — the generator verifies each word at its stated coordinates before the puzzle is returned, so the key can't disagree with the grid. If you don't want the solution in the response, send "include_solution": false.

Step 4: Save the printable PDF

Because we asked for format: "all", the same response also carries svg (a print-ready page) and pdf_base64 (a vector PDF, base64-encoded). Saving the PDF is three lines:

import base64

with open("word-search.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(base64.b64decode(puzzle["pdf_base64"]))

That's the page you hand to a kid — no layout work, no drawing the grid yourself.

The seed trick

Look back at the request: "seed": 42. Run the script again tomorrow, next month, on a different machine — you get this exact puzzle, letter for letter. Leave the seed out and every call returns a fresh random puzzle.

This matters more than it sounds. If you're building a printable pack, you can generate a catalog once, record the seeds, and re-render the identical puzzles forever — your answer keys and page numbers never drift. And in tests, a seeded call is a fixed fixture: if the output ever changes, your test tells you.

What else it does

Word search is one of four generators, all with the same request shape and the same seed behavior:

  • POST /v1/maze — mazes sized by difficulty or by exact cols/rows (4–30), with the verified solution path as coordinates and directions.
  • POST /v1/dot-to-dot — 8 shapes (star, heart, flower, balloon, house, rocket, fish, tree), 10–60 dots, numbered in order.
  • POST /v1/activity-page — a themed, age-banded page set that bundles the activities together with answer-key pages, ready to print on US Letter.

Every generator proves its own output the same way the word search does — mazes are checked solvable, dot sequences are checked complete and ordered — because a broken puzzle in a printed book is a refund, not a bug report.

Try it

The free tier is 100 calls a day, which is plenty to build something real. The full script from this tutorial — plus a JavaScript version — is in the examples repo, and the API itself is on RapidAPI.

If you generate a puzzle pack with it, I'd like to see what you made.

Part of the ActivityForge series — the launch post covers how this generator came out of my activity-book pipeline and why every puzzle ships with a proof-checked answer key.

title: I Built a Pure-Rust Columnar OLAP Engine from Scratch: 701k Rows/Sec and 16.4x ZSTD Compression
description:
Legacy columnar databases like ClickHouse and Apache Druid are engineering marvels—but if you have ever operated them in cloud-native, multi-tenant environments, you know the operational tax they carry: massive C++ codebases, ZooKeeper/Keeper consensus clusters, stateful local NVMe disks, and complex S3 tiering configurations.

I wanted an analytical engine designed from first principles for the object-storage era: 100% pure safe Rust, zero C++ dependencies, single-binary deployment, crash-safe WAL durability, and open Apache Parquet storage on S3 or Cloudflare R2.

So I built Hercules OLAP—and open-sourced v0.1.0 under AGPLv3 (with a Commercial OEM option).

The Architecture: Decoupling Hot Ingestion from Cold Columnar Storage

Instead of mixing stateful disk trees with consensus daemons, Hercules splits the pipeline into four clean, lock-free Rust modules:

  1. Durable Append-Only WAL (src/wal.rs): Every incoming JSONEachRow HTTP batch is appended to a local Write-Ahead Log and flushed via sync_data() (fsync) before returning HTTP 200. On restart, uncompacted WAL segments replay automatically.
  2. Lock-Free Columnar MemTable (src/memtable.rs): Payloads are parsed into 64-byte aligned Apache Arrow RecordBatch arrays inside a concurrent DashMap.
  3. Async ZSTD Parquet Compactor (src/compactor.rs): A background Tokio worker drains active MemTable partitions, sorts and compresses them into immutable Apache Parquet segments using ZSTD, and truncates the corresponding WAL.
  4. Unified Hot + Cold SQL Federation (src/engine.rs): Powered by Apache DataFusion, every SQL query dynamically merges live uncompacted RAM batches with historical .parquet files on Local NVMe, AWS S3, or Cloudflare R2 via a zero-copy UNION ALL plan—guaranteeing real-time read-after-write visibility.

Verified Single-Node Benchmarks (10,000,000 Rows + WAL fsync)

All tests below were run on a single node with crash-safe fsync enabled on every batch (1,153.75 MB raw NDJSON across 6 columns):

  • Sustained Ingestion (16 concurrent workers): 701,931 rows/sec (10M rows ingested in 14.25 s)
  • Storage Compression (ZSTD Parquet): 16.40x (1,153.75 MB raw JSON → 70.33 MB on disk)
  • Filtered Predicate Pushdown (10M rows): 99.13 ms (WHERE status_code >= 500 GROUP BY service)
  • Full-Scan Group-By (10M rows): 135.55 ms (GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY reqs DESC LIMIT 10)

Every file written by Hercules is 100% open Apache Parquet—immediately readable by Polars, DuckDB, Spark, and PyTorch with zero ETL exports.

Try It in 30 Seconds 

git clone https://github.com/aetherial-online/hercules-olap.git
cd hercules-olap
cargo run --release

Full source code, modular Rust architecture, and reproducible 10M-row benchmark scripts are live on GitHub:
👉 ://github.com/aetherial-online/hercules-olap

(We are also building **Aetherial Omni, The Invisible Data Fabric, True physical per-tenant isolation and client-side Zero-Knowledge security—turning cold object storage (S3 / R2) into a sub-2ms, 6-in-1 multi-engine fabric.
Join the early access waitlist at aetherial.online).

title: Resumable Video Uploads Need a Server-Owned Offset
description:
A filmmaker uploads a 12 GB wedding film. At 83%, the Wi-Fi drops. The browser knows which chunk it was sending, but it has no idea whether the server saved it. Start the chunk again and you might write the same bytes twice. Skip it and you might leave a hole in the file. Either mistake can leave the editor staring at a completed progress bar while the video fails to process.

A client gallery FAQ covering video upload limits and delivery illustrates the size of the files this workflow can involve. The implementation below is an example of how to handle those uploads. It uses one number to settle every retry: the byte offset confirmed by the server.

Give the upload its own state

When an upload starts, the server creates a session tied to the account, the destination gallery, and the expected file size. The session has a committedBytes counter. If it says 16777216, the first 16 MiB are stored and accounted for. The next chunk starts at that offset.

A minimal API has three operations on an existing session:

  • GET /uploads/:id returns committedBytes.
  • PATCH /uploads/:id accepts a chunk and its starting offset. It returns the new committed offset or 409 Conflict if the starting offset is stale.
  • POST /uploads/:id/complete verifies the assembled file and schedules processing. Calling it again returns the same asset or job.

Keep the session ID with the upload job in the browser. After a failed request, read the session again. If the server saved the chunk but its response was lost, the offset has advanced. If the server never committed the chunk, the offset still points to its beginning. The browser can use the same resume path in both cases.

Slice the file at the confirmed offset

This client uses 8 MiB chunks. It pauses on a network or server error, so the UI can offer a retry that calls resumeUpload again with the same session and file.

const CHUNK_SIZE = 8 * 1024 * 1024

async function resumeUpload(file, uploadId, onProgress, signal) {
  const url = `/uploads/${encodeURIComponent(uploadId)}`

  async function readOffset() {
    const response = await fetch(url, { cache: "no-store", signal })
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Upload status: ${response.status}`)

    const { committedBytes } = await response.json()
    if (!Number.isSafeInteger(committedBytes) ||
        committedBytes < 0 || committedBytes > file.size) {
      throw new Error("Invalid upload offset")
    }
    return committedBytes
  }

  let offset = await readOffset()
  onProgress(offset, file.size)

  while (offset < file.size) {
    const end = Math.min(offset + CHUNK_SIZE, file.size)
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "PATCH",
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
        "Upload-Offset": String(offset)
      },
      body: file.slice(offset, end),
      signal
    })

    if (response.status === 409) {
      const latest = await readOffset()
      if (latest <= offset) throw new Error("Upload conflict. Retry later.")
      offset = latest
    } else {
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Chunk upload: ${response.status}`)

      const { committedBytes } = await response.json()
      if (committedBytes !== end) throw new Error("Unexpected upload offset")
      offset = committedBytes
    }

    onProgress(offset, file.size)
  }

  const done = await fetch(`${url}/complete`, { method: "POST", signal })
  if (!done.ok) throw new Error(`Upload completion: ${done.status}`)
  return done.json()
}

file.slice(offset, end) gives the request a Blob for that byte range. The end offset is exclusive, including on the final chunk. The progress bar uses the server’s acknowledgments. At 100%, switch the label to “Processing” until the video is playable.

Make each server commit safe to retry

Store a chunk under a unique staging key. Once the write succeeds, record its key and length and advance the offset in one database transaction. Use a conditional update that succeeds only if the current offset still matches the request. If two tabs send the same chunk, one transaction wins. The other gets a conflict, and its unreferenced staged object can be cleaned up. The committed chunk has its own key, so the losing request cannot overwrite it.

Authenticate each request and check that the caller can still upload to the destination gallery. Enforce chunk size and remaining upload length on the server. If a refresh makes the browser ask the user to select the file again, compare a content fingerprint before resuming. Filename and size alone can match a different export, and appending that export would create a file made from two versions.

Test the failure after the write

The most revealing test drops the connection after the server commits a chunk but before the browser receives the response. On retry, the client should skip that chunk. Repeat the test with a drop before commit. This time it should resend the same byte range.

The completion request deserves the same test. If its response disappears, retrying should return the existing processing job. At that point, losing a connection can delay delivery, but it can no longer silently corrupt the upload or schedule a second transcode.

title: How I Built a Deterministic Neural Compressor in Go to Archive Audit Logs for Years
description:
If you have ever been responsible for retaining years of audit logs, security events, or OpenTelemetry traces, you know the storage dilemma:

  1. Compliance says keep everything for 3, 5, or 7 years.
  2. Cloud storage bills grow linearly with your traffic.
  3. Standard compressors (gzip, zstd, xz) treat your logs like mystery bytes.

Every single time gzip or zstd compresses a batch of audit logs, it starts from scratch. It has no idea that "actor_type":"service_account" or "status":{"code":1} appears ten thousand times an hour in your system. It has to rediscover your schema on every single file.

On the flip side, modern neural compressors can learn your exact data schema and squeeze out dramatically better compression ratios. So why doesn't everyone use them for long-term archives?

Because in production, neural compression usually comes with three deal-breakers:

  • It's painfully slow and drags heavy Python/GPU runtimes into your backend.
  • It breaks when your schema evolves (if you retrain the model, old archives become unreadable).
  • It silently corrupts data across different CPUs because floating-point math isn't 100% identical between Intel/AMD (amd64) and Apple Silicon/Graviton (arm64).

To solve this, I built nzip—a zero-dependency Go compressor powered by a tiny, 100% integer-only neural network trained on your specific data format.

Here is how it works, what surprised me during benchmarking, and how you can use the same ideas for custom structured data.

The Core Idea: Split Training from Compression

Instead of shipping a heavy machine learning stack into production, nzip splits the problem into two clean planes:

  [ Control Plane: Python or Pure Go ]
  Sampled Audit Logs ──▶ Train tiny byte-level GRU ──▶ Verify on holdout ──▶ Export Model (.bin)
                                                                                    │
  [ Data Plane: Zero-Dependency Go ]                                                ▼
  Live Audit Stream  ──▶ Integer GRU + Match & Context Models ──▶ Arithmetic Coder ──▶ Archive (.nzip)
  1. Train once on your schema: You feed a 10–50 MB sample of your actual audit logs or telemetry JSON into the trainer. It learns the structure of your payloads—field names, punctuation patterns, enum values, and common prefixes—and exports a tiny model file (typically under a few hundred kilobytes).
  2. Compress everywhere with pure Go: Your production service loads that model into a dependency-free Go library (stream.Writer / stream.Reader). No Python, no CGO, no GPU required.

Think of it like generating a custom, learned compression dictionary on steroids.

Why "Integer-Only" Matters for 7-Year Archives

When you archive audit data, decodability years later is non-negotiable.

In neural compression, the encoder and decoder both run the exact same model step-by-step to predict the probability of the next byte. If the decoder's math differs from the encoder's by even 0.000001, their probability tables drift out of sync—and every byte after that turns into garbage.

During early testing, I ran into a classic systems trap: floating-point contraction. On arm64, compilers fuse a * b + c into a single hardware FMA (Fused Multiply-Add) instruction with one rounding step. On amd64, it executes as two separate instructions with two rounding steps.

The result? Encoding a file on an x86 machine and decoding it on an ARM machine corrupted 3,869 out of 4,096 bytes.

To make archives truly future-proof, nzip eliminates floating-point math from the compression hot path completely:

  • All model weights and activations are converted to fixed-point integers (int16 and int32).
  • Expensive math functions (sigmoid, tanh, exp) are replaced with precomputed integer lookup tables.
  • SIMD assembly (SSE2 on amd64) and the pure-Go scalar fallback execute the exact same integer arithmetic.

Whether you decompress an archive tomorrow on an Intel laptop or in 2033 on an ARM server, the output is guaranteed to be bit-for-bit identical.

How It Gets Fast: 8 Yes/No Questions Instead of 256

Early versions of neural compressors tried to predict all 256 possible values of the next byte at once using a softmax layer. That required 256 × H matrix multiplications plus 256 exp() calls for every single byte. Throughput crawled at 0.05 MB/s per core.

nzip flips this around by breaking every byte down into 8 binary decisions (one bit at a time, MSB to LSB):

  Previous Bytes ──▶ [ Integer GRU + Classic Context Models ]
                            │
                            ├──▶ Bit 7 (0 or 1?)
                            ├──▶ Bit 6 (0 or 1?)
                            │      ...
                            └──▶ Bit 0 (0 or 1?) ──▶ Binary Arithmetic Coder

Instead of asking "Which of these 256 characters comes next?", the engine asks "Is the next bit a 1 or a 0?" eight times in a row. That shrinks the neural network math from 256 × H down to 8 × H—a 25×–29× speedup, pushing throughput to ~1.2–1.7 MB/s per core (and 13.2 MB/s across 32 threads).

Benchmarks & An Honest Reality Check

To test nzip against real-world observability and audit workloads, I benchmarked it on 7.4 MB of OpenTelemetry JSON spans.

Crucially, these logs contained random hex traceId and spanId values. Roughly 25% of the raw file was pure cryptographic randomness—which is mathematically impossible to compress. All the real savings had to come from exploiting structure.

Compressor Compressed Size Ratio Bits / Byte
gzip -9 791,211 B 10.65% 0.85
xz -9e 670,440 B 9.02% 0.72
zstd -19 --long 667,324 B 8.98% 0.72
bzip2 -9 642,858 B 8.65% 0.69
nzip (H=32, blocks) 611,579 B 8.23% 0.66

nzip produced archives 20% smaller than gzip -9, 6% smaller than zstd -19 and xz -9e, and 2% smaller than bzip2 -9.

The Ablation Twist: Neural Nets Aren't Magic Alone

Here is the most interesting lesson from building this: if you run the neural network by itself, it actually loses to gzip.

When I isolated each component on a 1 MB test slice (gzip -9 = 97.6 KB), the numbers told a very clear story:

  • GRU neural network alone: 112.4 KB (worse than gzip!)
  • Byte-matching alone: 158.2 KB
  • Order-2 context table alone: 180.3 KB
  • All of them blended together: 84.8 KB (beats bzip2, xz, and zstd)

Why? Because a small neural network is great at learning global schema structure (like JSON syntax and field transitions), while classic statistical models are much better at memorizing exact repeated strings that just appeared 500 bytes ago (like a repeated service.name or user UUID).

By feeding the neural network's predictions alongside a multi-length match finder, an order-2 context table, and a run-length tracker into a lightweight mixer, each predictor covers the others' blind spots.

Built for Real Ingestion Pipelines

Compressing one giant static file is easy. Production audit pipelines rarely work like that—they push thousands of tiny batches over the network, schemas drift over time, and files get corrupted on disk.

nzip bakes operational safety directly into the wire format (NGR3) and Go API:

1. Three Ways to Move Bytes

  • Blocks Mode (Default): Splits large archives into independent blocks for multi-core parallel compression and fast random access.
  • Session Mode + Keyframes: Keeps the neural network's hidden state warm across small streaming batches (with periodic keyframes so you can still seek/resume). In tests with 64 × 2 KB batches, session mode shrank the total payload from 18.2 KB down to 7.2 KB.
  • Dictionary Priming: Just like zstd, you can prime both encoder and decoder with a shared dictionary to eliminate cold-start overhead on tiny payloads—cutting a 50 KB stream from 14.2% down to 4.0%.

2. Schema-Safe Retraining

Every compressed stream header records the Model ID and the CRC32C content hash of the exact model artifact used to write it. When you retrain a model next month, the pipeline publishes a new content-addressed artifact without deleting old ones—so archives written last year never break.

3. Built-In Drift Detection

Audit schemas evolve when developers add new fields. nzip includes a rolling EWMA drift monitor (drift.Monitor) that watches your live compression ratio in bits-per-byte and triggers an alert (or automated retrain) if compression degrades past your threshold.

Quickstart: Using nzip in CLI or Go

You can train a model on your own log format and benchmark it against gzip -9 in four commands:

# 1. Build the zero-dependency Go binary
go build -o nzip ./cmd/nzip

# 2. Train a schema-specific model on a sample of your logs
./nzip train -data audit-sample.ndjson -out models/audit-v1.bin -model-id 1 -hidden 32 -epochs 6

# 3. Benchmark against gzip -9 on a holdout file it has never seen
./nzip bench -model models/audit-v1.bin -in holdout.ndjson

# 4. Compress and verify with full CRC32C integrity checks
./nzip compress -model models/audit-v1.bin -in audit.ndjson -out audit.nzip
./nzip verify -models ./models -in audit.nzip

And if you want to embed it directly inside a Go ingestion service, it implements standard io.Writer and io.Reader interfaces:

// Streaming compressor: keeps model state warm across small batches
w, err := stream.NewWriter(dst, registry, "audit-logs",
    stream.WithMode(stream.ModeSession),
    stream.WithDictionary(dict),
)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
w.Write(batch)
w.Flush()

// Streaming decompressor: looks up the exact model hash from the stream header
r, err := stream.NewReader(src, registry)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
io.Copy(out, r)

Wrapping Up

If you are archiving homogeneous, high-volume structured records—audit trails, telemetry spans, financial event logs—general-purpose compression algorithms leave real storage savings on the table.

You don't need a massive LLM or a GPU cluster to take advantage of learned compression. A tiny, integer-only neural network combined with classic context modeling gives you better-than-bzip2 ratios, multi-core Go performance, and deterministic cross-CPU safety you can trust years down the road.

Check out the full source code, wire format docs, and benchmarks on GitHub: github.com/radryc/compressor

title: Looking for Android testers: Moim, a free app for meetups, RSVPs and entry QR
description:
I'm building Moim on my own: a free app for small groups and clubs to plan meetups. You create an event, share one link, and people RSVP. The app handles the guest list, an entry QR code for check-in, event chat, and reminders.

The Android app is in Google Play's closed test. I need testers who will keep it installed for 14 days, and I'd love to hear from people who actually try it.

  1. Join the tester group: https://groups.google.com/g/moim-android-testers
  2. Opt in and install from Google Play: https://play.google.com/apps/testing/com.mymoim.www

Use the same Google account as your phone's Play Store.

What to try

  • RSVP to an event and open your entry QR

Also in a closed test? Leave your app's link in the comments and I'll install it and keep it for the 14 days too.

Thanks for helping a solo developer out!

title: Model Routing: Stop Wasting Budget on Frontier AI Models for Easy Tasks
description:
When building AI agents or integrating LLMs into backend services, a common mistake is sending every incoming request to the strongest model available.

Need to extract a date from a paragraph? Call GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Need to classify a incoming support ticket into one of three categories? Call the frontier model again.

Running basic classification, extraction, or formatting tasks through an expensive reasoning model is the equivalent of hiring a principal architect just to reply to routine emails. It inflates your API bills, introduces unnecessary latency, and wastes compute budget that should be reserved for actual, complex logic.

The solution to this problem is model routing.

What is Model Routing?

Model routing is an architectural pattern where an application evaluates incoming requests and dynamically directs them to the most cost-effective model capable of handling the task.

Instead of treating your LLM provider as a single endpoint, you break your application tasks down into difficulty tiers:

  1. Tier 1 (Deterministic / Simple): JSON extraction, sentiment analysis, text classification, simple reformatting. Handled by fast, lightweight models like gpt-4o-mini, claude-3-haiku, or small open-source models.
  2. Tier 2 (Reasoning / High Stakes): Architecture design, complex code synthesis, multi-step planning, nuanced legal or financial analysis. Handled by frontier models.
  3. Dynamic / Escalation Tier: Tasks with uncertain difficulty. You run the query through a cheap model first, validate the response against predefined criteria, and escalate to a higher-tier model only if the initial output fails validation.

By routing traffic based on task complexity, teams routinely reduce token spend by 50% to 70% without sacrificing output quality.

Step 1: Static Task-Based Routing

The simplest way to implement model routing is at the workflow level. If your backend architecture relies on chain-of-thought workflows or discrete agent steps, assign specific models to specific functions.

Here is a practical Python example demonstrating task-based routing:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))

def classify_ticket(user_message: str) -> str:
    """Uses a cheap model for deterministic text classification."""
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": "Classify the message into one category: BUG, BILLING, FEATURE, OTHER."
            },
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message}
        ],
        temperature=0.0
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

def generate_resolution_plan(user_message: str, category: str) -> str:
    """Uses a frontier model for complex problem solving."""
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o",
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "system",content": "You are a senior technical support specialist. Draft a detailed resolution plan."
            },
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Category: {category}\nIssue: {user_message}"}
        ],
        temperature=0.2
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Step 2: Dynamic Escalation Logic

Sometimes you cannot determine the difficulty of a user's prompt in advance. In these scenarios, implement an escalation pattern.

Run the request through your fast model first. Parse and validate the output programmatically (e.g., verifying structured JSON outputs, checking confidence scores, or running a secondary validation check). If validation fails, catch the error and route the prompt to the frontier model.

import json
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

class ExtractedPayload(BaseModel):
    user_id: int
    action: str
    urgency: int

def extract_structured_data(raw_text: str) -> dict:
    """Tries a fast model first; falls back to a strong model if validation fails."""
    prompt = f"Extract payload from text as JSON: {raw_text}"

    # Attempt with cheap tier
    try:
        res = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o-mini",
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            timeout=4.0
        )
        parsed = json.loads(res.choices[0].message.content)
        validated = ExtractedPayload(**parsed)
        return {"tier": "cheap", "data": validated.model_dump()}
    except (ValidationError, Exception):
        # Fallback to high-tier model upon failure or bad schema
        pass

    # Escalation to frontier tier
    res = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o",
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )
    parsed = json.loads(res.choices[0].message.content)
    validated = ExtractedPayload(**parsed)
    return {"tier": "frontier", "data": validated.model_dump()}

Best Practices for Routing Architecture

  • Set Strict Timeouts: When running dynamic escalation, configure low timeout thresholds for the fast model so a failure doesn't add high latency to the end user's experience.
  • Log Routing Decisions: Track how often your fallback logic triggers. If 95% of cheap-model attempts succeed, your threshold is well-tuned. If cheap models fail consistently on a specific prompt type, update your routing logic to bypass the cheap tier for that route.
  • Decouple Provider Code: Wrap model calls inside an abstraction layer or API gateway (like LiteLLM or custom backend services) so you can swap models without changing your application business logic.

Optimizing AI systems is rarely about waiting for cheaper foundation models to launch—it is about designing backend systems that use the right tool for each step of the pipeline.

About me: Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn.

title: Is Aurelia Actually Dead? Looking at the Framework Beyond Its Reputation
description:
If you spend enough time in JavaScript communities, you may eventually come across a familiar opinion about Aurelia:

It's dead.

Sometimes the statement comes with an explanation. The original creator moved on. Aurelia 2 has been taking too long. Nobody seems to be using it. There is little discussion about it compared with React, Vue, Angular, or even newer frameworks.

Sometimes there is no explanation at all. Just two words: Aurelia is dead.

I wanted to understand how much truth there is behind that impression.

Not because I want to convince anyone to use Aurelia. A framework does not become relevant just because its existing users like it, and an active GitHub repository does not automatically make a project a good choice for a new application.

But I was curious about the distance between what people say about Aurelia and what is actually happening with it.

The reputation is understandable

Aurelia has a visibility problem.

It rarely appears in the same conversations as the frameworks that dominate the JavaScript ecosystem. It does not have the same hiring market, volume of tutorials, conference presence, or ecosystem attention as React or Angular.

That matters more than framework maintainers sometimes acknowledge.

When a team chooses a framework, it is not evaluating the rendering engine alone. It is also thinking about whether developers can be hired, whether problems have already been discussed somewhere, whether libraries will still be maintained, and whether the framework will be around in several years.

A framework with a small community has to answer those questions differently.

The concern is visible in community discussions. In a 2025 Reddit thread asking how common Aurelia is, some responses described it as effectively dead or recommended Angular as the safer choice. Other participants reported using it successfully in real projects.

Those comments are not adoption statistics. They are individual experiences and opinions. Still, they tell us something about Aurelia's public image: developers who are not already inside its community may see very little reason to investigate it.

Discussion:
https://www.reddit.com/r/webdev/comments/1lw88we/how_common_is_the_usage_of_aurelia_framework/

There is another issue: time.

Aurelia 2 has had a long development journey. The official release-candidate announcement itself acknowledges years of alpha releases, 27 beta releases, a pandemic, and changes within the team.

That is a substantial amount of time for a framework to remain in a pre-final release state.

The concern is not irrational. Long release cycles create uncertainty, especially for companies that need predictable maintenance and support. Even when the software is technically usable, the release label influences how people evaluate risk.

The official announcement:
https://aurelia.io/blog/2026/1/14/aurelia-2-release-candidate/

There is still development happening

The other side of the story is easier to verify.

Aurelia 2 reached release-candidate status in January 2026. The project continued publishing release candidates afterward, with RC.2 appearing in August 2026.

The Aurelia team described the release-candidate milestone as an API-stability milestone. That is an important distinction: the project was not announcing a completely new framework or asking users to wait for the first usable version. It was communicating that the API had reached a level of stability intended for production work.

That does not settle every concern about the project. API stability is not the same as a large support ecosystem, a predictable release schedule, or a strong hiring market.

But it does make the simple claim that nobody is developing Aurelia difficult to defend.

There is also activity beyond the core framework repository: documentation, tooling, community discussions, and related ecosystem projects.

The Aurelia Discourse forum remains accessible and contains ongoing discussions. Its existence does not prove a large community, but it does show that there are still people using the framework, asking questions, and working through problems.

https://discourse.aurelia.io/

An independent article by Dwayne Charrington also discusses Aurelia's ongoing development and direction:

https://ilikekillnerds.com/2026/01/04/aurelia-2-in-2026-the-framework-that-refused-to-die-is-thriving/

There is a distinction worth keeping here.

Aurelia is not a mainstream framework. That is a reasonable description of its position in the ecosystem.

Aurelia is abandoned. That is a different claim, and the available development activity does not support it.

Being technically interesting does not make a framework popular

Aurelia has always had an approach that I find interesting.

Its programming model allows developers to work with ordinary JavaScript or TypeScript classes and connect them to views through its binding system. Dependency injection is integrated into the framework. Templates support binding expressions, value converters, binding behaviors, custom attributes, and template controllers.

The result is a framework that gives developers a fairly direct way to describe application behavior.

Some of these ideas are no longer unusual in modern frontend development. Fine-grained reactivity, TypeScript, dependency injection, and avoiding a virtual DOM are not exclusive to Aurelia. Other frameworks have their own approaches to these problems, and several have evolved considerably.

So I would not argue that Aurelia is automatically more modern, faster, or more productive than the frameworks with larger communities.

That would require specific comparisons and evidence.

What I find more interesting is the combination of its design decisions.

Aurelia has a strong convention-based approach. It tries to reduce the amount of configuration developers need to write while keeping the application code relatively close to ordinary JavaScript and HTML.

That can be appealing to developers who prefer working with the platform rather than constantly adapting their code to a framework-specific abstraction.

It can also be unfamiliar to developers whose experience is shaped by React's component model or Angular's more explicit application structure.

Whether that is an advantage depends on the application and the team.

The difficult part is the ecosystem around the framework

When developers ask whether a framework is suitable for production, they are rarely asking only whether its core runtime can render a page.

They are asking about the surrounding infrastructure.

How does routing work? What about server-side rendering? How are deployments handled? Can the application run on the infrastructure the team already uses? What happens when something fails? Are there examples that resemble the system they are building?

This is where a smaller framework can become difficult to evaluate.

Aurelia has a router, a dependency-injection system, a binding engine, and a broader collection of tools. But the existence of those pieces does not mean every modern application architecture is equally well supported or documented.

Server-side rendering is a good example.

Aurelia provides client-side hydration APIs, including Aurelia.hydrate(). However, that should not be casually interpreted as meaning that Aurelia provides a complete, first-party SSR solution comparable to the integrated server-rendering systems available in some other ecosystems.

The server-side rendering pipeline involves additional tooling and integration work. The documentation and surrounding ecosystem deserve careful examination before making claims about how complete that experience is.

This distinction matters.

A framework can have a capable client runtime and still leave developers with significant work when they want to build a full-stack application around it.

For teams evaluating Aurelia, this is a more useful question than whether the framework is alive or dead.

What can I build with it today, what do I have to integrate myself, and how much maintenance responsibility am I taking on?

Popularity and technical quality are different measurements

There is a temptation to use popularity as a shortcut for technical evaluation.

It is understandable. Popular frameworks usually have more tutorials, more answers on Stack Overflow, more third-party packages, and more developers who already know how to use them.

Those are real advantages.

But popularity does not tell us everything about the quality of a framework's programming model. Likewise, a technically elegant framework does not automatically become a safe organizational choice.

Aurelia currently sits in an uncomfortable position between those two measurements.

It has continued development and a set of design decisions that some developers genuinely appreciate. At the same time, it has much less visibility and ecosystem momentum than the mainstream alternatives.

The long transition to Aurelia 2 has also given people a reason to question the project's direction. That reputation will not disappear simply because a release candidate has been published.

Trust takes longer to rebuild than software takes to release.

So, should someone choose Aurelia in 2026?

I would not recommend Aurelia to every team.

If a company needs a large hiring pool, extensive third-party integrations, and a broad community that can help solve almost any problem, Angular or React may be easier choices.

If a project depends heavily on a mature, integrated SSR ecosystem, the team should compare the available solutions carefully rather than assuming Aurelia provides the same experience out of the box.

Those are practical considerations, not insults.

Aurelia may make more sense for teams that already understand its programming model, value its conventions, or have existing applications built around it. It may also be worth evaluating for developers who want a different way to structure frontend applications and are comfortable assessing the ecosystem themselves.

The important thing is to evaluate the actual requirements rather than make the decision based on a short comment saying that the framework is dead.

What I take away from this

I think Aurelia has a visibility problem, a long release history that has affected confidence, and an ecosystem that is much smaller than those of the mainstream frameworks.

Those are real weaknesses. They should not be hidden behind enthusiastic descriptions of its features.

At the same time, the project has continued to move forward. Its development history and release activity do not fit neatly into the idea of an abandoned framework.

I don't think Aurelia needs another article declaring that it is secretly better than React or Angular. That would not help anyone make a sound technical decision.

What would be more useful is a closer look at what Aurelia can actually do today, where its architecture works well, and where developers still have to fill in the gaps themselves.

That is the part I want to explore further.

For now, I would describe Aurelia as a framework that is still being developed, still has users who value it, and still has to overcome a very real gap in visibility and ecosystem reach.

Whether that is enough for a particular project is a separate question.

And it deserves a more technical answer than simply calling the framework dead.

title: CSS round(), mod(), rem(): snap anything to a grid
description:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

CSS can round now, and on 17 November it became safe to use everywhere: round(), mod() and rem() reached Baseline Widely available, two and a half years after the last major engine shipped them. They're small functions, but they move a whole category of "snap this to a step" logic out of JavaScript.

The demo above is a snapping lab. The teal point moves freely, and JavaScript only writes its position into two custom properties. The orange node is placed by CSS alone, with round(). Change the rounding strategy or the step and watch where the node lands. Move the point to the left of the centre and the mod() and rem() bars stop agreeing.

What they do

The specification calls them stepped-value functions: each one transforms a value according to a step.

  • round(<strategy>?, A, B) returns A rounded to a multiple of B.
  • mod(A, B) and rem(A, B) return what's left of A after you remove whole multiples of B.

They work with numbers, lengths, angles, times and percentages. The one rule is that both arguments must have a consistent type: round(10px, 2) is invalid, and so is round(10px). For a plain number you can leave out B and it defaults to 1. For anything with a unit, B is required. I checked both invalid cases: all three engines drop the declaration.

round() and its four strategies

This is the CSS the demo uses for the node:

.stage { --x: 0px; --y: 0px; --step: 40px; --mode: nearest; }

.node {
  translate:
    round(var(--mode), var(--x), var(--step))
    round(var(--mode), var(--y), var(--step));
}

The strategy is the optional first argument, and as the demo shows, it can come from a custom property too. The spec defines four of them:

  • nearest (the default): the closest multiple. If A is exactly halfway, it picks the upper one.
  • up: always the multiple towards +∞, like Math.ceil().
  • down: always towards −∞, like Math.floor().
  • to-zero: the multiple closer to zero, like Math.trunc().

On screen, "up" means right and down, because the y axis grows downwards. That's why up and down look odd above the centre line in the demo. And because nearest breaks ties towards +∞, round(-105px, 10px) gives -100px, not -110px.

The demo is a toy, but the same idea works in layouts. Rounding against a percentage resolves it first, so this keeps a container at an exact multiple of a column width:

.gallery {
  width: round(down, 100%, 180px); /* 1000px of space → 900px */
  margin-inline: auto;
}

MDN makes a useful point: rounding only makes sense when at least one of the values isn't known in advance. That means a custom property, a percentage or a viewport unit. round(117px, 25px) is valid, but you could just write 125px.

mod() vs rem(): it's all about the sign

When A and B have the same sign, both functions give the same result. The spec's examples show where they differ:

translate: mod(-18px, 5px);  /* 2px:  takes the sign of the step */
translate: rem(-18px, 5px);  /* -3px: takes the sign of A, like JS's % */
rotate: mod(140deg, -90deg); /* -40deg */
rotate: rem(140deg, -90deg); /* 50deg */

I ran all four in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and the computed values match the spec. In JavaScript, -18 % 5 is -3 too, and the spec gives exactly that as a reason to use rem(): when CSS has to match JS code.

Most of the time you want mod(). You control the step and the input is unknown, so you want a result that always stays between 0 and the step. mod(-450deg, 360deg) gives 270deg, a clean normalised angle. The demo makes this easy to see: drag the point left of the vertical axis and the rem() dot jumps to the negative side, while the mod() dot stays on the positive side.

Browser support and gotchas

According to webstatus.dev, Firefox 118 shipped all three functions first (September 2023), then Safari 17.2 (December 2023), and Chrome and Edge 125 (May 2024). That made them Baseline Newly available on 17 May 2024 and Widely available on 17 November 2026. The demo still checks CSS.supports('translate', 'round(down, 7px, 3px)') and computes the values in JavaScript if that fails, but under Baseline Widely available that path should almost never run.

  • You can't divide units away yet. round() gives you 120px, not "column 3". Turning a length into a plain number needs typed arithmetic, which I covered in another note. It's much newer and still needs a fallback. The demo calculates the column in JavaScript for its screen reader message.
  • Watch the types. Mixing a length with a bare number makes the whole declaration invalid, and the browser ignores it without any warning. If something doesn't snap, check this first.
  • The computed value is already rounded. getComputedStyle() returns the final value (120px), which is how the demo fills its readouts. If the property has a transition, as the node does, read from an element without one, or you'll get the in-between value.
  • Floating point still applies. opacity: round(0.37, 0.1) gives 0.4 in all three engines, but don't build equality checks on top of non-integer steps.

What to keep an eye on

  • Typed arithmetic reaching Widely available. Combined with round() and mod(), it would let CSS calculate "which cell" and "odd or even" on its own. Patterns like striping by position wouldn't need JavaScript any more.
  • Design tokens on a step. A spacing or type scale snapped with round() to a 4px or 8px grid, even when the base value is fluid, is now a one-liner instead of a build step.

Sources

  • round() - CSS | MDN
  • mod() - CSS | MDN
  • rem() - CSS | MDN
  • CSS Values and Units Level 4: stepped value functions
  • round(), mod(), and rem() on webstatus.dev
