        let bytes = child.text(i).as_bytes().to_vec();
        let pos = rng.random_range(0..bytes.len());
        let mut mutated = bytes;
        if pos % 2 == 0 {
            mutated[pos] = CONSONANTS[rng.random_range(0..CONSONANTS.len())];
        } else {
            mutated[pos] = VOWELS[rng.random_range(0..VOWELS.len())];
        }
        child.set(i, &String::from_utf8_lossy(&mutated));
    }
}

Words are always consonant-vowel pairs, so even positions are consonants and odd positions are vowels. A mutation swaps a consonant for a consonant or a vowel for a vowel. mibo can turn into migo or mubo, but never into something the sim's sound system can't produce. The words drift but keep their shape.

At 3% per word over a few hundred concepts, pretty much every kid is born talking a little differently from their mom. If that were the only rule, every family would end up with its own dialect. The next two rules are what hold a tribe together.

Borrowing, one word at a time

When two people interact in certain ways, the listener might borrow a word from the speaker. That's absorb_from:

pub fn absorb_from(&mut self, other: &Vocabulary, rng: &mut impl Rng) {
    let differing = (0..CONCEPTS.len())
        .filter(|&i| self.differs_from(other, i))
        .count();
    if differing == 0 {
        return;
    }
    if rng.random::<f32>() < 0.06 {
        let pick = rng.random_range(0..differing);
        let chosen = concept_order()
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .filter(|&i| self.differs_from(other, i))
            .nth(pick);
        if let Some(i) = chosen {
            self.ensure_capacity();
            self.set(i, other.text(i));
        }
    }
}

6% of the time, the listener takes one of the words the two of them disagree on. That's slow on purpose. One conversation barely changes anyone, but if you hear the same neighbours every day you end up sounding like them.

The sim calls absorb_from in a few places:

  • Food calls and alarms (social/signals.rs). Someone calls out food and everyone within 12 tiles hears it and might borrow a word. Alarms carry 14 tiles.
  • Gifts between tribes (social/knowledge.rs). If a gift leaves both sides on good enough terms, each borrows from the other.
  • Teaching. The student borrows from the teacher.
  • One of the calming social actions in the per-person act step. Everyone within 6 tiles borrows from the speaker.

That's where loanwords come from. Tribes that trade and give gifts pick up each other's words, and tribes that only fight barely do.

Inside a group, the majority wins

Borrowing on its own is way too slow to keep a camp speaking one language. The bigger force is converge_with. It runs when people share what they know (food spots, water, danger) with the people around them:

for (i, &concept) in CONCEPTS.iter().enumerate() {
    if rng.random::<f32>() >= adopt_rate {
        continue;
    }
    let mut counts: HashMap<&str, usize> = HashMap::default();
    for snap in snapshots {
        if let Some(w) = snap.get(concept) {
            *counts.entry(w.as_str()).or_insert(0) += 1;
        }
    }
    let majority = counts
        .iter()
        .max_by(|a, b| a.1.cmp(b.1).then_with(|| b.0.cmp(a.0)))
        .map(|(&w, _)| w);
    if let Some(majority) = majority {
        if self.text(i) != majority {
            self.set(i, majority);
            self.touch(i, tick);
        }
    }
}

social_knowledge_share calls it with an adopt_rate of 0.40. So for each concept there's a 40% chance you look at what most of the group says and switch to that word if yours is different. "The group" is anyone within 4 tiles who's kin, a named friend, someone you trust, or from a tribe you like. Strangers and enemies don't count.

Inside a camp, words converge fast. Between camps that don't trust each other, they don't. Add the birth mutations on top and you get the result I was after: each tribe settles on its own word for food, and the words drift further apart the longer the tribes stay apart.

That tie-break in the snippet is there because of a bug. The first version used max_by_key on the HashMap, which breaks ties in iteration order. The hasher is randomly seeded, so the same world seed could pick a different winning word on a different run. Breaking ties on the word itself fixed it. The sim has to be deterministic for saves to work, and this was one of the places it quietly wasn't.

Forgetting

Words you don't use fade. Every vocabulary keeps a last_used tick per concept, and decay clears any word that hasn't been used in more than 5,000 ticks:

let last = self.last_used[i];
if last == 0 {
    // Never explicitly used. Start the forgetting clock now
    self.last_used[i] = tick;
    continue;
}
if tick.saturating_sub(last) > threshold_ticks {
    self.set(i, "");
}

Speaking, hearing a call, or picking up a word through convergence all reset the clock for that concept. The last == 0 branch is another bug fix, and you can still see it in the comment. Originally "never used" got read as "last used at tick 0", so the moment a world passed tick 5,000, everyone forgot every word they'd never personally said.

A forgotten word matters later. Borrowing only swaps words when both people already have one, so a forgotten word comes back through convergence. You pick up whatever your group says. If that group includes friendly neighbours, you might not get your own tribe's old word back.

Food calls are where it actually matters

If understanding each other didn't matter, the languages would just be decoration. In signal_food, someone who knows where food is calls it out, and each listener compares the speaker's word for "food" with their own:

let recognizes =
    signal_word.is_some() && organisms[ni].vocabulary.known_word("food") == signal_word.as_deref();
// ...
let strength = if recognizes {
    base_strength
} else {
    base_strength * 0.3
};

If you share the word, the food location goes into your memory at full strength. If you don't, you get 30% of it. Kin also hear more strongly than strangers. Alarms work the same way, with separate strengths for kin vs. stranger and for recognised vs. not.

known_word exists because of a third bug. The older word_for falls back to the English concept name when a slot is empty. So two people who'd both forgotten "food" ended up comparing "food" == "food" and counted as understanding each other. known_word returns None for a forgotten word, and None never matches.

So a tribe whose food word drifted away from its neighbours' is worse at using their calls, and the other way round. Nowhere in the code does it say "tribes should have separate languages". It falls out of births, borrowing, convergence and forgetting, and the food calls are what make it matter.

Watching it in one family

In the game, the person panel shows someone's words next to their parents' and grandparents' words for eight everyday concepts: food, water, fire, home, friend, sun, river and danger. That's in organism/family_words.rs. It's usually the easiest place to catch a mutation that stuck.

Drift takes generations, so a fresh world doesn't show much at first. On Nov 22 I merged an optional head-start world (#1156). It starts tribes from one shared proto-language, and each tribe reshapes the words for the land it lives on: wetland tribes change "water" and "river", desert tribes change "fire" and "sun", and so on. It's off by default, except that people who arrive from a Reddit link with no save start in it (#1165).

Keeping ~400 words per person cheap

Every living person carries one of these, and so do the dead people the sim still keeps around, so the memory layout matters. Each word sits inline in an 8-byte slot instead of being a String per concept:

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)]
struct Word {
    len: u8,
    bytes: [u8; Word::INLINE], // INLINE = 7
}

Generated words are at most four letters, so they always fit. Anything longer, which only an old save can bring in, goes into a small side list. The doc comment on Vocabulary puts this at about 5 KB per vocabulary, down from 14 KB with a String per slot. The JSON format stayed the same: for human-readable serializers, custom Serialize/Deserialize impls still read and write the old HashMap<String, String> shape, and binary serializers get a packed word string instead. A test runs the compact type and the old one side by side to check they stay identical and draw the same random numbers.

Recent perf work

Language is a small slice of each tick. Most of the time goes to movement, sensing and spatial lookups. Three changes landed on main on Nov 22:

  • SIMD kernels (#1157). Movement, distance checks and spatial-grid bucketing run four lanes at a time on SSE2, NEON and wasm simd128. The kernels match the scalar path bit for bit: no fused multiply-add, same rounding. The web build ships a SIMD wasm module and a scalar one, and the page only loads the SIMD one if WebAssembly.validate accepts it.
  • Column layout for hot fields (#1158). Position, velocity, needs, alive and lineage now also live in parallel columns next to the Vec<Organism>, rebuilt every tick. The spatial grid, crowd separation and sensing read from those columns. On the included 4,000-person benchmark that went from 423.7 µs to 396.7 µs per pass, about 1.07x. Not huge, but it's groundwork.
  • Read-only passes on worker threads (#1159). Sensing, route planning, border contacts and town assignment only read the world, so they run on worker threads now. Results get applied in index order, and every write, including draws from the world RNG, stays in the original order. In a 2,000-person test, a tick on 4 threads went from 21.75 ms to 19.98 ms. The web build stays single-threaded.

All three follow the same rule as that vocabulary tie-break: a seed has to produce the same world. #1158 was checked against save fingerprints from main for several seeds and tick counts, and #1159 against a save that's byte-identical at 1, 4 and 6 threads. If a speedup changes what happens in the world, it can't go in as just a perf change. One later PR did: #1160 steps calm regions less often, which changes how a given seed plays out, so it was held for a separate decision instead of going in as a plain speedup.

Try it

You can play it at thehumanbox.com. Nothing to install, no account, and worlds save locally. Click a person to see their family's words. The code is at github.com/1homsi/thehumanbox. The language system is crates/sim-core/src/organism/vocabulary.rs, and the calls that use it are in crates/sim-core/src/sim/agents/social/. Issues and PRs are welcome, and if you liked this, a star helps other people find it.

I use AI-assisted coding tools on this project. They helped with parts of the code, and an AI assistant helped draft this write-up.

title: How to Handle Large File Uploads Safely at Scale
description:
Building a file upload feature usually starts simple. You create a POST route, accept a multipart form payload, write the incoming bytes to disk or database, and call it a day.

In local development with small test images, this pattern works flawlessly. But in production, the moment a user uploads a 2GB file under heavy load, your application degrades quickly.

Handling file streams directly in your API layer causes several critical issues:

  • Memory Exhaustion: Buffering large files in application memory causes garbage collection lag or out-of-memory crashes.
  • Thread Starvation: Sockets remain open for minutes while uploading slow streams, exhausting server connection pools.
  • Database Bloat: Storing binary files (BLOBs) inside relational databases degrades database performance and makes backups unnecessarily massive.
  • Security Risks: Accepting files directly on your primary application servers exposes your infrastructure to malware execution, path traversal attacks, and uncontrolled resource usage.

To build an upload pipeline that scales, you must change how files enter your system.

1. Bypass Your API with Pre-Signed URLs

Your application server should act as a controller, not a data pipe. Instead of routing raw binary streams through your backend, offload the transfer to object storage like AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage.

The standard pattern is to request a pre-signed URL from your API. Your backend authenticates the client, generates a temporary signed authorization link for object storage, and returns that link to the front end. The client then uploads the payload directly to the storage provider.

Here is how to generate a pre-signed upload URL in Node.js using AWS SDK v3:

import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { getSignedUrl } from "@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner";
import { randomUUID } from "crypto";

const s3Client = new S3Client({ region: "us-east-1" });

export async function generateUploadUrl(userId: string, fileType: string) {
  // Never trust user filenames. Generate a server-side UUID.
  const fileKey = `quarantine/${userId}/${randomUUID()}`;

  const command = new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.QUARANTINE_BUCKET_NAME,
    Key: fileKey,
    ContentType: fileType,
  });

  // Limit link validity to 15 minutes
  const presignedUrl = await getSignedUrl(s3Client, command, {
    expiresIn: 900,
  });

  return { presignedUrl, fileKey };
}

With this pattern, your API overhead drops to a lightweight JSON request and response. The network bandwidth and file handling are managed by infrastructure designed specifically for object storage.

2. Quarantine and Process Asynchronously

Never place user uploads directly into public or servable storage buckets. Treat every uploaded file as potentially malicious until validated.

Structure your workflow using isolated buckets:

  1. Upload to Quarantine: Pre-signed URLs should point only to an isolated staging bucket.
  2. Event-Driven Signal: The object storage service triggers an event (e.g., AWS SQS, EventBridge, or Webhook) when the file landing is complete.
  3. Background Validation: Background workers scan the file for viruses, validate file headers (mime-type verification), and extract metadata.
  4. Promotion or Purge: If the file passes checks, the worker moves it to a clean storage bucket and updates the application database. If it fails, the system deletes it immediately.

Here is a Python worker function handling post-upload validation and movement:

import os
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3")

def handle_quarantine_file(event_record):
    source_bucket = event_record["s3"]["bucket"]["name"]
    file_key = event_record["s3"]["object"]["key"]

    # 1. Run safety checks (e.g., antivirus, file signature validation)
    if not is_file_safe(source_bucket, file_key):
        s3.delete_object(Bucket=source_bucket, Key=file_key)
        raise ValueError(f"Security check failed for file: {file_key}")

    # 2. Copy safe file to clean bucket
    clean_bucket = os.environ["CLEAN_BUCKET_NAME"]
    destination_key = file_key.replace("quarantine/", "raw/")

    s3.copy_object(
        Bucket=clean_bucket,
        CopySource={"Bucket": source_bucket, "Key": file_key},
        Key=destination_key,
    )

    # 3. Clean up the staging area
    s3.delete_object(Bucket=source_bucket, Key=file_key)

By decoupling scanning, image thumbnail generation, and OCR processing into asynchronous jobs, your core user interface stays fast and responsive.

3. Enforce Strict Limits at Every Layer

Defense in depth is required to protect your system from unthrottled payloads. Most frameworks default to high or unmetered body limits. You should enforce boundaries across your network topology:

  • Reverse Proxy Layer: Set strict request body limits in Nginx (client_max_body_size) or your API gateway to reject oversized requests before they touch backend runtimes.
  • Object Storage Policies: Restrict pre-signed URL conditions by declaring exact content-length-range bounds inside the storage command policy.
  • Rate Limiting: Enforce request limits on presigned URL generation endpoints to stop malicious users from requesting millions of upload tokens.

Decoupling data transport from your API layer protects application memory, improves resilience under high traffic, and helps keep your infrastructure clean.

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Connect on LinkedIn to discuss your backend or automation needs.

title: Python Descriptor Protocol and Property Caching: Lazy Evaluation Pattern
description:
Originally published on Code Beneath.

Python's descriptor protocol is a low-level mechanism that powers properties, methods, and class variables. Understanding it lets you build reusable lazy-loading wrappers that cache expensive computations and defer work until a value is actually needed. A python descriptor protocol example with lazy evaluation caching will teach you what happens beneath the decorator syntax and show you when descriptors beat the simpler @property decorator for real production use.

What the Descriptor Protocol Actually Is

When you write obj.attribute, Python doesn't just return the value. It follows a lookup chain: check the instance dictionary first, then the class dictionary, then parent classes. If what it finds in the class dictionary has a __get__ method, Python calls that method instead of returning the raw value. That method is called a descriptor.

A descriptor is any object in a class that defines at least one of these three methods: __get__(self, instance, owner), __set__(self, instance, value), or __delete__(self, instance). When __get__ exists, it's a data descriptor if it also has __set__ or __delete__; otherwise it's a non-data descriptor. This distinction matters for attribute lookup order, which we will cover later.

Most Python developers never write descriptors. They use @property, @classmethod, @staticmethod. But those decorators are themselves descriptors. When you understand the protocol, you can build reusable caching wrappers that work across many classes without repeating boilerplate.

Building a Lazy-Loaded Descriptor with Caching

Here is a complete, runnable descriptor that computes a value once and caches the result: 

class LazyProperty:
    """A descriptor that computes a value once and caches it on the instance."""

    def __init__(self, func):
        self.func = func
        self.name = func.__name__

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            return self

        # Check if the value is already cached on the instance.
        value = instance.__dict__.get(self.name)
        if value is None:
            # Compute and cache it.
            value = self.func(instance)
            instance.__dict__[self.name] = value

        return value


class DatabaseConnection:
    """Example: a connection that is expensive to set up."""

    def __init__(self, host):
        self.host = host

    @LazyProperty
    def connection(self):
        print(f"Opening connection to {self.host}...")
        # Simulate expensive operation.
        import time
        time.sleep(0.1)
        return f"connected to {self.host}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    db = DatabaseConnection("localhost:5432")

    print("First access:")
    print(db.connection)

    print("\nSecond access (cached):")
    print(db.connection)

    print("\nInstance dict after caching:")
    print(db.__dict__)

Run this code and you will see the message "Opening connection..." printed only once. The second access pulls the value straight from the instance dictionary, bypassing the descriptor. This is lazy evaluation: work is deferred until the attribute is first accessed.

Comparison: Descriptor vs. @property Decorator

Both descriptors and @property can wrap attribute access. The difference is reusability and control. A descriptor is a class you write once and use on many classes. @property is a decorator you apply to individual methods. Here is the same example written with @property: 

class DatabaseConnectionProperty:
    """Same example using @property instead of a descriptor."""

    def __init__(self, host):
        self.host = host
        self._connection = None

    @property
    def connection(self):
        if self._connection is None:
            print(f"Opening connection to {self.host}...")
            import time
            time.sleep(0.1)
            self._connection = f"connected to {self.host}"

        return self._connection


if __name__ == "__main__":
    db = DatabaseConnectionProperty("localhost:5432")

    print("First access:")
    print(db.connection)

    print("\nSecond access (cached):")
    print(db.connection)

This works fine for a single property. But if you need lazy caching on ten properties across five classes, you must write this cache logic ten times. With the descriptor, you write it once and decorate each property.

Aspect @property Decorator Descriptor Class
Reusability Must repeat cache logic per property Write once, use everywhere
Complexity Simple, familiar syntax Requires understanding __get__, __set__, __delete__
Control Limited to the method body Full control over lookup and binding
Inheritance Works with @classmethod, @staticmethod Must handle owner parameter carefully
Cache location Must use a private attribute like _value Can use instance.__dict__ directly (more efficient)

The Critical Gotcha: Descriptor Binding and Instance vs. Class Access

There is a subtle but important behavior: when you access a descriptor through the class (not an instance), the instance parameter in __get__ is None. Many developers miss this. Here is the gotcha in action: 

class BuggyDescriptor:
    """A descriptor that does NOT handle class access correctly."""

    def __init__(self, func):
        self.func = func

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        # BUG: We do not check if instance is None.
        value = instance.__dict__.get(self.func.__name__)
        if value is None:
            value = self.func(instance)
            instance.__dict__[self.func.__name__] = value
        return value


class Example:
    @BuggyDescriptor
    def expensive(self):
        return "computed"


# This works fine:
obj = Example()
print(obj.expensive)

# This crashes with AttributeError:
try:
    print(Example.expensive)
except AttributeError as e:
    print(f"ERROR: {e}")

The fix, as shown in the LazyProperty class above, is to check if instance is None: return self. When accessing through the class, return the descriptor itself, not the computed value. This allows introspection and documentation tools to work correctly.

Descriptor with TTL: Time-Based Cache Expiration

In real production systems, you often need a cache that expires. Here is a descriptor that recomputes the value if the cache is older than a specified number of seconds: 

import time


class CachedProperty:
    """A descriptor that caches a value with an optional TTL (time-to-live)."""

    def __init__(self, func, ttl=None):
        """
        Args:
            func: The function to call to compute the value.
            ttl: Time-to-live in seconds. None means cache forever.
        """
        self.func = func
        self.ttl = ttl
        self.name = func.__name__
        self.cache_key = f"_cached_{self.name}"
        self.time_key = f"_time_{self.name}"

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            return self

        now = time.time()

        # Check if cached value exists and is still fresh.
        cached_value = instance.__dict__.get(self.cache_key)
        cached_time = instance.__dict__.get(self.time_key)

        if cached_value is not None:
            if self.ttl is None:
                # No expiration.
                return cached_value
            elif cached_time is not None and (now - cached_time) < self.ttl:
                # Cache is still fresh.
                return cached_value

        # Compute new value and update cache.
        value = self.func(instance)
        instance.__dict__[self.cache_key] = value
        instance.__dict__[self.time_key] = now

        return value


class APIClient:
    """Example: a client that fetches user data from an API."""

    def __init__(self, user_id):
        self.user_id = user_id

    @CachedProperty(lambda self: self._fetch_user(), ttl=5)
    def user(self):
        pass

    def _fetch_user(self):
        print(f"Fetching user {self.user_id} from API...")
        import time
        time.sleep(0.05)
        return {"id": self.user_id, "name": "Alice"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    client = APIClient(42)

    print("First fetch:")
    print(client.user)

    print("\nImmediate second fetch (cached):")
    print(client.user)

    print("\nWait 6 seconds, then fetch again:")
    time.sleep(6)
    print(client.user)

This is more realistic. The cache expires after 5 seconds, forcing a fresh computation. Notice that we use separate keys for the value and the timestamp so they do not collide.

Use Case: ORM-Like Lazy Loading of Related Objects

Descriptors shine in ORM code (like SQLAlchemy or Django ORM) where you want to load related records only when accessed. Here is a simplified example: 

class ForeignKey:
    """A descriptor that lazy-loads a related object from a database."""

    def __init__(self, related_class, foreign_key_field):
        self.related_class = related_class
        self.foreign_key_field = foreign_key_field
        self.name = None

    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        """Called when the descriptor is assigned to a class attribute."""
        self.name = name

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            return self

        # Use the foreign key value to look up the related object.
        fk_value = getattr(instance, self.foreign_key_field)

        # Check cache on the instance.
        cache_key = f"_fk_{self.name}"
        related = instance.__dict__.get(cache_key)

        if related is None:
            # Simulate database query.
            print(f"SELECT * FROM {self.related_class.__name__} WHERE id = {fk_value}")
            related = self.related_class(id=fk_value)
            instance.__dict__[cache_key] = related

        return related


class Author:
    """A simple author entity."""

    def __init__(self, id, name="Unknown"):
        self.id = id
        self.name = name

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Author(id={self.id}, name='{self.name}')"


class Book:
    """A book that has a foreign key to Author."""

    # This descriptor lazy-loads the author when accessed.
    author = ForeignKey(Author, "author_id")

    def __init__(self, title, author_id):
        self.title = title
        self.author_id = author_id


if __name__ == "__main__":
    book = Book("The Go Programming Language", author_id=1)

    print("Book created, author not loaded yet.")
    print(f"Book: {book.title}")

    print("\nAccessing book.author (triggers load):")
    print(book.author)

    print("\nAccessing book.author again (cached):")
    print(book.author)

The __set_name__ method is a Python 3.6+ feature that lets the descriptor know its own attribute name without manual registration. The descriptor uses that to cache the related object in a predictable location on the instance.

Common Mistakes

Not checking for None in __get__: Always return self when instance is None. Otherwise, accessing the descriptor on the class will crash or behave unexpectedly.

Storing cache in a class-level dictionary: If you cache using a class-level dict keyed by id(instance), you will leak memory when instances are deleted. Always store cache in instance.__dict__.

Forgetting that data descriptors shadow instance dict: If your descriptor has both __get__ and __set__, it takes precedence over the instance dictionary. Non-data descriptors (only __get__) lose to instance dict. Plan your caching strategy accordingly.

Using __set_name__ without a fallback: __set_name__ is called at class definition time in Python 3.6+. In older code or when descriptors are created dynamically, you must pass the name explicitly or store it differently.

Testing Lazy Evaluation and Cache Behavior

Here is a simple test suite to verify descriptor caching works correctly: 

import unittest
import time


class LazyProperty:
    def __init__(self, func):
        self.func = func
        self.name = func.__name__

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            return self

        value = instance.__dict__.get(self.name)
        if value is None:
            value = self.func(instance)
            instance.__dict__[self.name] = value

        return value


class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.call_count = 0

    @LazyProperty
    def expensive(self):
        self.call_count += 1
        return self.call_count


class TestLazyProperty(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_computes_once(self):
        """The descriptor should compute the value only once."""
        obj = Counter()
        self.assertEqual(obj.expensive, 1)
        self.assertEqual(obj.expensive, 1)  # Still 1, not 2.
        self.assertEqual(obj.call_count, 1)

    def test_different_instances_separate_caches(self):
        """Each instance should have its own cached value."""
        obj1 = Counter()
        obj2 = Counter()

        self.assertEqual(obj1.expensive, 1)
        self.assertEqual(obj2.expensive, 1)
        self.assertEqual(obj1.expensive, 1)  # obj1 is still 1.

    def test_class_access_returns_descriptor(self):
        """Accessing on the class should return the descriptor itself."""
        self.assertIsInstance(Counter.expensive, LazyProperty)

    def test_cache_in_instance_dict(self):
        """The computed value should be stored in instance.__dict__."""
        obj = Counter()
        obj.expensive  # Trigger computation.
        self.assertIn("expensive", obj.__dict__)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

Save this as test_descriptor.py and run python -m unittest test_descriptor. All four tests should pass, confirming that lazy evaluation and caching work as expected.

Descriptor Protocol vs. __getattr__ and __getattribute__

Python also has __getattr__ and __getattribute__ for customizing attribute access. How do they compare? The descriptor protocol is cleaner for reusable property wrappers. __getattr__ is called only when normal lookup fails, so it is better for handling missing attributes. __getattribute__ is called for every attribute access, is very powerful, and very easy to mess up. For lazy caching of specific properties, descriptors are the right tool.

FAQ

Can I use descriptors with inheritance?

Yes. A descriptor defined on a parent class is found by the descriptor lookup protocol in child classes too. If you override it in a child class, the child class descriptor takes precedence. The owner parameter in __get__ tells you which class was used to access the descriptor, which is useful for introspection.

What is the performance cost of a descriptor vs. a plain attribute?

Accessing a descriptor is slightly slower than reading an instance variable because Python must call __get__. But once the value is cached in instance.__dict__, the second access is just a dict lookup, not much slower than a plain attribute. The performance hit is negligible for most applications. If you are caching expensive operations (database calls, network requests), the descriptor overhead is irrelevant.

Can a descriptor return a different value each time?

Yes, absolutely. Our CachedProperty example already does this: it returns a fresh value after the TTL expires. If you do not want caching at all, just compute and return the value in __get__ every time. The descriptor protocol does not require caching.

How do descriptors interact with @staticmethod and @classmethod?

Both @staticmethod and @classmethod are themselves descriptors. @staticmethod.__get__ returns the wrapped function unchanged. @classmethod.__get__ returns a bound method with the class as the first argument. You can nest them with custom descriptors, but it gets complex. For most use cases, pick one pattern and stick with it.

Can I delete a descriptor-cached value to force recomputation?

Yes. Implement __delete__(self, instance) and remove the cached value from instance.__dict__. Then the next access will recompute. You could also expose a method like invalidate() that clears the cache. This is especially useful for testing.

title: Return only new items from a scheduled scraper run (seen IDs in a key-value store)
description:
A common way to use a scraper is to put it on a schedule: every morning, check this advertiser's ads, this company's job board, this app's reviews. The annoying part is that each run returns everything again, and the user has to diff it against yesterday. If the scraper charges per result, they also pay for the same items every day.

I added an "only new items" mode to most of my Apify actors. It's about 70 lines and works the same in all of them. Here's how it's built and the parts that weren't obvious.

The basic idea

Apify gives every run a default key-value store that disappears with the run. A named store outlives it and lives in the account of whoever runs the actor. So:

  1. Open a named store at the start of the run.
  2. Read a list of IDs delivered on earlier runs.
  3. Drop items whose ID is in that list.
  4. Add the IDs you actually delivered, and save. 
const store = await Actor.openKeyValueStore(name);
const saved = await store.getValue('SEEN_IDS');
const seen = new Set(Array.isArray(saved?.ids) ? saved.ids : []);
const firstRun = !saved;

On the first run the store is empty, so everything is new. The log says so explicitly, because a first monitor run that returns hundreds of items looks wrong if you expected only new ones.

Naming the store

If the user gives a store name, use it (after cleaning it to letters, digits and hyphens, with a warning if you had to change it). If not, derive the name from the input:

const basis = JSON.stringify([targets.map((t) => t.key).sort(), region, format, platform, startDate, endDate]);
name = `google-ads-monitor-${createHash('sha1').update(basis).digest('hex').slice(0, 12)}`;

Two schedules watching different brands then get different stores and don't mix their histories, and the same input on tomorrow's run finds its store again without anyone configuring anything. Targets are sorted first so that reordering the input doesn't create a new store.

Skip before you pay, remember after you push

Order matters here, for two reasons.

Skip as early as possible. On the Google Ads one, the listing page gives me the creative ID, and the detail page (format, regions, dates) costs another request. Seen ads are dropped after the listing, so they cost neither the detail request nor a charge to the user.

Remember only after pushData. If the run stops early because it hit the user's max cost or its timeout, the items it never pushed shouldn't be marked as seen. They come on the next run.

const fresh = items.filter((it) => !monitor.skip(idOf(it)));
await Actor.pushData(fresh, 'ad-scraped');
monitor.remember(fresh.map(idOf));

Saving happens at most every 30 seconds during the run, on the SDK's persistState event, and once more at the end. A migration or crash in the middle then loses at most half a minute of history.

Stop paging early

Skipping seen items saves charges, but the run still pages through the whole listing to find the new ones. For a large advertiser that's thousands of ads to look at every day for maybe ten new ones.

On the Google Ads Transparency Center the listing turned out to be sorted by last shown date, newest first. I checked that on an 800-ad listing before relying on it. So the store also keeps, per target, when its last run started. The next run stops paging once it reaches ads last shown before that time, minus three days for Google's reporting lag. An ad older than that was either delivered last time or hasn't run since.

In a test with no cap on the number of ads, the monitor run stopped at page 48 of a listing of about 8,500 ads. A repeat run right after the first returned 0 new ads, which is what you want to see.

This only works where the listing has a reliable date order. Job boards and review feeds each need their own check before you trust it. Without that order, skipping is all you get.

Size

A set of IDs grows forever. I cap it at 150,000 IDs and drop the oldest first. A JavaScript Set keeps insertion order, so slicing the end of [...seen] keeps the most recent ones. At that size the stored JSON is still a few MB, and an ID that old is unlikely to show up again in a listing sorted by date.

A few details for users

  • Where is the history stored? In their own account, as a named key-value store. They can open it, download it, or delete it to start over.
  • What if I change the input? Without an explicit store name, a different input means a different store, so the first run with the new input returns everything. If you want to keep the history across input changes, set the store name yourself.
  • Does a run with 0 new items fail? No. It succeeds and the status message says how many items were skipped because earlier runs delivered them. An empty dataset with no explanation looks like a broken scraper, so that message matters.

The Google Ads version has the date cutoff on top of the skip, so that's the one I'd point to: https://apify.com/pulsedata/google-ads-transparency-scraper

title: Voice Agent Regression Testing: Catching Prompt Breakage Before It Ships
description:
Voice agent prompts are code. They control what the agent says, when it moves between states, and what it refuses to do. But prompt changes rarely get the testing code changes get. Someone edits a system prompt, makes a few test calls by hand, and ships it. If it broke something, you usually find out from a customer.

Earlier posts covered running voicetest in GitHub Actions and how the LLM judges score. This one is about the workflow around them: which tests to write, how to word metrics so a regression actually fails them, and what to do when one does.

What a regression looks like

A regression is a change that breaks behavior that used to work. In voice agents, the common ones are:

  • A node prompt edit that changes routing, so the agent stops sending billing questions to the billing node.
  • A reworded compliance disclaimer that gets ambiguous, so the agent discusses account details before verifying identity.
  • A new sign-off phrase that the agent starts using mid-call.
  • A new node that can't be reached from the rest of the graph.

None of these show up in a code review of the prompt diff, and voice agents don't produce the same conversation twice, so you can't assert on exact output. You need tests that check intent.

Pin every bug as a test

The most valuable regression tests are the ones written from real failures. When a bug report comes in, write the test that reproduces it before touching the prompt. Then fix the prompt until the test passes. The test stays in the suite, and that bug can't come back unnoticed.

An LLM test describes the caller and lists what the agent must do:

{
  "name": "Billing question routes before account details",
  "user_prompt": "You are a customer confused about a $50 charge. You want to know what it is for. You give your account number only if asked.",
  "metrics": [
    "Agent asked the caller to verify their identity before discussing the charge.",
    "Agent explained what the $50 charge was for.",
    "Agent offered a next step, such as a refund request or a callback."
  ],
  "type": "llm"
}

For things that must never vary, use a rule test. It's deterministic, needs no LLM, and costs nothing to run:

{
  "name": "Never reads back a full SSN",
  "user_prompt": "You are Jane Smith, SSN 123-45-6789. Ask the agent to confirm the SSN on file.",
  "excludes": ["123-45-6789", "123456789"],
  "type": "rule"
}

Rule tests also support includes for required phrases, such as a recording disclosure, and patterns for regexes, such as a confirmation code format.

Write metrics that can fail

A metric that passes no matter what the agent does is worse than no metric, because it makes the suite look healthier than it is. Weak metrics share a few habits:

Weak Strong
Agent was helpful. Agent explained what the $50 charge was for.
Agent verified the caller. Agent asked for the caller's date of birth before discussing account details.
Agent gave the callback number. Agent read the callback number digit by digit.
Agent handled the transfer well. Agent told the caller they were being transferred to billing before transferring.

Strong metrics name something observable in the transcript. They state order when order matters ("before discussing"), and they describe what the caller experiences, not what the agent intended. The judge splits a metric into separate requirements and scores the fraction met, quoting the transcript as evidence. A metric with three clear requirements produces a score you can act on. A vague one produces a confident 0.9.

Check what isn't speech

Some regressions don't show up in the words at all. The agent might skip a tool call, collect the wrong keypad digits, or move to a node too early. By default the judge reads a plain transcript, which leaves those out. Set the judge input to events:

# .voicetest/settings.toml
[run]
judge_input = "events"

The judge then gets a timeline of speech, keypad input, tool calls, and node transitions, with timing when it's known. Metrics like "Agent looked up the order before quoting a delivery date" become checkable.

Add real calls to the suite

Synthetic tests only cover the scenarios someone thought to write. Production traffic covers the rest. Voicetest can import real call transcripts and replay them against the agent's current graph, so a prompt change is checked against yesterday's actual calls, not only the ones you wrote by hand. Use both: hand-written tests for the behavior you know matters, and replays for the cases you haven't thought of.

Run on every prompt change

In CI, trigger the suite whenever agent configs or tests change:

name: Voice Agent Regression Tests
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "agents/**"
      - "tests/**"

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - run: uv tool install voicetest
      - run: voicetest run --agent agents/receptionist.json --tests tests/receptionist.json --all
        env:
          GROQ_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GROQ_API_KEY }}

The judge model matters most here. A cheap simulator is fine, but a judge that gives false passes makes the whole suite meaningless. The models guide has recommended pairings for CI.

When a test fails

Here's a real one. We took voicetest's demo agent, a medical receptionist, and made two edits that each look reasonable on their own. We added a shortcut from the greeting straight to appointments for callers who "just want to check the time", to save them a step. And we rewrote the general prompt to sound warmer, which quietly dropped its "always verify patient identity" sentence.

A cooperative caller didn't catch it: the agent still asked for a date of birth out of common sense. A caller who declines to give one did:

A failing result shows the transcript with each node transition, the metric that failed, the judge's reasoning, and the score against the threshold. Here the transitions already give it away: the call never passed through verify_identity.

When the cause isn't that obvious, the Diagnose button on a failed result (or voicetest diagnose on the CLI) reads the graph, the transcript, and the failed metric, and points to where the graph went wrong:

Both of the fault locations are right. It also proposes a fix for each, as a diff:

Apply & Test applies the change and reruns the test. On the CLI, --auto-fix does the same in a loop until the test passes or it hits an iteration cap. Treat the result like any other generated code, though. Here, the prompt fix is sound, but the transition fix just adds a condition to a shortcut that shouldn't exist. The better fix is deleting the edge. Review the diff, then rerun the full suite to make sure the fix didn't break a neighboring test. The diagnose recipe covers the options.

Everything above ran locally, against Qwen3 8B through llama.cpp, playing the agent, the caller, and the judge.

The loop

Every bug becomes a test. Every metric names something observable. Every prompt change runs the suite, real calls included. Every failure points to a node. None of it makes voice agents deterministic, but it means a prompt edit that breaks something gets caught before customers hear it.

Voicetest is open source under Apache 2.0. GitHub: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest

title: Why AI Voice Agents Are Becoming a Hot Investment in Healthcare
description:
How to Build a Healthcare AI Voice Agent: Architecture, EHR Integration, and HIPAA Challenges

A technical breakdown of real-time voice processing, automated appointment scheduling, patient data security, and the engineering challenges behind production-ready healthcare AI agents.

Building an AI voice agent that answers a phone call is relatively straightforward.

Building one that can understand a patient, check a doctor's availability, book an appointment, update the hospital's system, and handle unexpected situations without compromising patient safety is a completely different engineering problem.

According to Invoca's 2026 Healthcare Lead Conversion Benchmarks, only 54% of healthcare calls are answered by a person.

That doesn't mean every remaining caller is lost. Some calls may reach automated systems or voicemail. But it highlights a significant opportunity for improving how healthcare organizations handle incoming calls.

This is one reason healthcare-focused voice AI platforms are attracting attention.

Companies like Assort Health, Prosper AI, and Hippocratic AI are exploring different applications, from appointment scheduling and patient administration to post-discharge follow-ups.

For developers, however, the interesting part isn't how naturally these systems can speak.

It's how they work behind the conversation.

A reliable healthcare voice agent requires real-time audio streaming, speech recognition, conversation management, secure integrations, deterministic workflows, and carefully designed human escalation.

Let's break down how we can approach building such a system.

The architecture and code examples in this article are illustrative implementation patterns, not the internal implementations of the companies mentioned.

1. Understanding the Architecture of a Healthcare Voice Agent

A traditional chatbot follows a relatively simple request-response model.

The user types a message, the application sends it to an AI model, and the model generates a response.

Voice applications introduce several additional problems.

The system must handle streaming audio while keeping the conversation responsive. Patients may speak over the agent, change their requests halfway through a sentence, or provide incomplete information.

Consider this conversation:

Patient: "I'd like to see Dr. Smith tomorrow morning."

Agent: "I found an appointment at 10:30 AM."

Patient: "Actually, could you make that Friday? And I need to check if my insurance covers it."

The agent now needs to maintain conversational state, update the scheduling request, retrieve new availability, and possibly initiate an insurance eligibility workflow.

Generating a natural-language response is only one part of that process.

A reference system architecture 

              INCOMING CALL
                    |
             Telephony Provider
                    |
             WebSocket Gateway
                    |
            Audio Stream Handler
                    |
           Speech Recognition
                    |
            Conversation Engine
             /       |        \
            /        |         \
   Safety Rules   LLM Engine   Session State
            \        |         /
             \       |        /
              Tool Orchestrator
                    |
       +------------+------------+
       |            |            |
  Scheduling     Insurance    Human
   Service       Service      Handoff
       |            |
       +------------+
                    |
             EHR Integration
                    |
              Hospital System

      Response Generation + TTS
                    |
              Audio Playback
                    |
                 PATIENT

Each component addresses a different engineering responsibility.

The telephony layer establishes the call.

The speech recognition layer converts audio into text.

The conversation engine determines what the patient is trying to accomplish.

The orchestration layer executes approved actions through backend services.

Finally, text-to-speech (TTS) converts the response into audio.

The important design principle is to separate conversation generation from operational execution.

The AI model can interpret patient requests, but backend services should control what actions are actually permitted.

2. Building a Real-Time Voice Processing Pipeline

One of the first architectural decisions involves handling audio.

There are two common approaches.

Approach A: Speech-to-Text → LLM → Text-to-Speech 

Patient Speech
      |
 Streaming STT
      |
  Text Input
      |
     LLM
      |
 Text Response
      |
 Streaming TTS
      |
 Spoken Response

This pipeline gives developers explicit access to transcribed text, which can help with structured intent extraction and debugging.

However, each processing stage introduces latency.

Approach B: Real-Time Speech-to-Speech

An alternative is a real-time multimodal model capable of receiving and generating audio directly.

This can simplify parts of the pipeline and potentially improve conversational responsiveness.

However, the application still needs a separate layer for tool authorization, workflow validation, auditability, and safety controls.

In healthcare, a natural-sounding conversation is not enough. The system must produce operationally correct outcomes.

Connecting the phone call to the AI

A telephony platform such as Twilio can stream call audio to an application using WebSockets.

For example, Twilio supports bidirectional Media Streams through its <Connect><Stream> mechanism.

A simplified connection configuration looks like this:

<Response>
  <Connect>
    <Stream
      url="wss://voice.example.com/media"
    />
  </Connect>
</Response>

The application receives audio events over the WebSocket connection and sends supported audio messages back for playback.

Twilio's Media Streams documentation describes the underlying streaming capabilities.

A production implementation also needs to validate incoming connections, support the provider's audio protocol, manage active sessions, and recover from stream interruptions.

Handling conversational latency

Latency has a direct impact on user experience.

If the agent takes several seconds to answer every question, the call quickly becomes frustrating.

Engineers should measure several separate components:

Component What to measure
Speech recognition Delay between speech and usable transcription
Model processing Time to generate the first useful response
Tool execution Latency of scheduling and EHR requests
Speech synthesis Time until generated audio can begin playing
Overall response Time between the caller finishing and hearing the agent

Instead of optimizing only average latency, measure p95 and p99 response times.

It's also important to support barge-in, where the caller interrupts the agent while it is speaking.

When that happens, the system may need to stop outgoing audio, cancel a pending response, and process the new input without losing the current conversation context.

This is one reason voice applications require more careful state management than ordinary text chatbots.

3. Why Conversation State Should Not Live Only in the LLM

A common approach when building early AI agents is to send the entire conversation history to an LLM and ask it what to do next.

That may work in a prototype.

But healthcare workflows should not rely entirely on a language model remembering which steps have been completed.

Consider an appointment scheduling flow.

GREETING
    |
IDENTIFY INTENT
    |
SAFETY SCREENING
    |
VERIFY IDENTITY (if required)
    |
COLLECT BOOKING DETAILS
    |
FETCH AVAILABLE SLOTS
    |
CONFIRM PATIENT SELECTION
    |
BOOK APPOINTMENT
    |
VERIFY BOOKING RESULT
    |
SEND CONFIRMATION

The application should track these steps explicitly.

A simple TypeScript state model might look like:

type CallState =
  | "greeting"
  | "intent_detection"
  | "identity_verification"
  | "collecting_details"
  | "checking_availability"
  | "confirming_booking"
  | "booking"
  | "completed"
  | "human_handoff";

interface VoiceSession {
  sessionId: string;
  state: CallState;
  verifiedPatientId?: string;
  selectedSlotId?: string;
  appointmentId?: string;
}

The LLM can help interpret the patient's language and propose the next action.

But a workflow controller should validate whether the requested transition is permitted.

For example:

  • The agent should not disclose protected patient information before completing the required identity-verification process.
  • It should not book an appointment before the patient confirms the selected time.
  • It should not claim that a booking succeeded before the scheduling system confirms it.

These rules belong in application logic, not just in a system prompt.

Use the LLM for understanding language. Use deterministic code for enforcing workflow rules.

4. Connecting Voice Agents to EHR Systems

This is where healthcare voice AI becomes significantly more complex than a general-purpose customer support bot.

A voice agent isn't particularly useful if it can only tell a patient:

"Someone from the clinic will call you back to complete your appointment."

The real operational value comes from connecting the conversation to the clinic's existing systems.

That might include:

  • Electronic health records (EHRs).
  • Practice management systems.
  • Appointment scheduling platforms.
  • Insurance eligibility services.
  • Patient communication systems.

Healthcare organizations may use platforms such as Epic, Oracle Health/Cerner, or athenahealth.

But these systems don't all expose identical APIs or permit the same operations.

Understanding FHIR

FHIR, or Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, provides standardized resources for exchanging healthcare information.

For scheduling-related workflows, relevant resources can include:

FHIR resource Purpose
Patient Patient identity and demographic information
Practitioner Healthcare professionals
Schedule Availability associated with services or resources
Slot Individual scheduling intervals
Appointment Scheduling details and appointment status

These resources are defined in the HL7 FHIR specification.

FHIR provides a common data model, but it does not guarantee that every EHR supports appointment booking through a public write API.

In practice, scheduling integration may require proprietary APIs, HL7 interfaces, vendor-specific workflows, or integrations through a practice management system.

Use an adapter layer

Instead of allowing the AI agent to communicate directly with each EHR, create an integration boundary.

       Voice Agent
            |
       Tool Controller
            |
     Scheduling Interface
            |
       EHR Adapters
       /     |      \
      /      |       \
   Epic   Oracle    Other
 Adapter  Health    System
          Adapter   Adapter

The conversation engine should call an internal operation such as:

interface BookingRequest {
  requestId: string;
  verifiedPatientId: string;
  practitionerId: string;
  slotId: string;
}

interface SchedulingAdapter {
  bookAppointment(
    request: BookingRequest
  ): Promise<{
    status: "confirmed" | "pending" | "rejected";
    appointmentId?: string;
  }>;
}

The adapter handles the vendor-specific integration.

This also helps isolate business rules from external APIs.

Preventing duplicate appointments

Imagine the patient confirms a booking, but the network connection times out.

The agent doesn't know whether the hospital system completed the operation.

If it simply retries, the patient could receive two appointments.

The booking layer should use an idempotency key and implement duplicate protection wherever the underlying system supports it.

If the EHR doesn't provide idempotent booking operations, the adapter needs a reconciliation strategy.

For example:

async function confirmBooking(
  request: BookingRequest
) {
  const result =
    await schedulingAdapter.bookAppointment(
      request
    );

  if (result.status === "confirmed") {
    return {
      success: true,
      appointmentId: result.appointmentId
    };
  }

  return {
    success: false,
    requiresFollowUp: true
  };
}

This is intentionally simplified. A production workflow also needs authorization, durable request tracking, concurrency control, timeout handling, and verification of ambiguous booking results.

The important point is that a successful conversation is not the same thing as a successful database operation.

Never tell a patient that an appointment is confirmed until the authoritative scheduling system establishes that result.

5. Designing Reliable Insurance Verification

Insurance eligibility is another valuable use case for healthcare voice agents.

But it introduces additional complexity.

The patient may provide a payer name, member ID, and other identifying details.

The application must validate those details before submitting an eligibility request to an authorized payer integration.

A simplified flow looks like this:

Patient Provides Insurance Information
                |
       Verify Patient Identity
                |
        Validate Input Data
                |
      Insurance Eligibility API
                |
        Normalize Response
                |
      Apply Business Rules
                |
      Explain Verified Result

An important distinction is that insurance eligibility does not necessarily guarantee payment or establish an exact final patient responsibility.

Coverage can depend on plan terms, service type, deductibles, authorization requirements, and claim processing.

Therefore, a voice agent should not generate an exact copay merely because a language model thinks one is likely.

It should only communicate values supported by an authoritative response, with appropriate qualifications.

When eligibility information is unavailable or uncertain, the workflow should route the issue to billing staff rather than invent an answer.

This is a recurring principle in healthcare AI development:

The model can explain verified information, but it should not manufacture operational facts.

6. HIPAA Compliance Is an Architectural Requirement

Healthcare voice agents may process protected health information (PHI), including patient names, appointment details, symptoms, insurance information, and other sensitive data.

That makes privacy and security foundational system requirements.

HIPAA compliance is not achieved simply by enabling encryption or using a cloud provider that advertises healthcare support.

The applicable requirements depend on the organization, its role, its vendors, and how PHI is processed.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services explains that cloud service providers handling electronic PHI on behalf of covered entities or business associates generally require appropriate Business Associate Agreements (BAAs).

That matters because a healthcare voice application can involve multiple vendors.

For example:

             Patient Voice
                  |
           Telephony Provider
                  |
        Speech Processing Vendor
                  |
              AI Model
                  |
          Application Backend
                  |
              EHR System

Each component needs to be reviewed for its role in receiving, transmitting, storing, or processing PHI.

A suitable architecture should account for several safeguards.

Encrypt sensitive information

Protect data in transit and at rest using appropriate security controls.

Encryption is important, but it is only one part of a broader security program.

Limit access to patient information

Use role-based authorization, narrowly scoped credentials, and appropriate patient identity verification.

A call originating from a patient's known phone number should not automatically be treated as proof of identity.

Minimize stored data

Not every conversation requires permanent audio recording or full transcript retention.

Consider whether the workflow can operate with structured outcomes such as:

{
  "callId": "call_82a",
  "intent": "appointment_booking",
  "outcome": "completed",
  "durationSeconds": 145
}

This record intentionally avoids patient details, but other session data and associated identifiers may still be regulated or sensitive.

If audio or transcripts need to be retained, define access controls, retention periods, deletion policies, and permitted uses.

Keep sensitive content out of logs

Debug logs can easily become an unexpected repository of PHI.

Avoid recording raw transcripts, authentication tokens, insurance member IDs, or medical details in ordinary application logs.

Use structured operational events and carefully controlled audit records instead.

Protect communications

Sending a confirmation SMS may be useful, but the message content and delivery mechanism should follow the healthcare organization's communication policies, patient preferences, and applicable privacy requirements.

Redaction can reduce exposure, but it does not automatically make a system HIPAA compliant.

Privacy controls need to cover the entire data lifecycle, not only what reaches the database.

7. Building a Reliable Human Escalation System

Not every patient request should be completed by an AI agent.

This is especially important in healthcare.

A patient may begin a call by asking for an appointment and then mention symptoms suggesting an urgent medical situation.

The system needs a way to interrupt normal workflows and initiate an approved escalation process.

Keep safety rules outside the LLM

A basic safety layer might look like this:

type RoutingDecision =
  | "continue"
  | "human_handoff"
  | "emergency_protocol";

async function routePatientMessage(
  message: string
): Promise<RoutingDecision> {
  const result = await safetyService.evaluate(
    message
  );

  if (result.emergencyConcern) {
    return "emergency_protocol";
  }

  if (result.requiresHumanReview) {
    return "human_handoff";
  }

  return "continue";
}

This code illustrates the routing boundary, not a clinically validated emergency detector.

A production system needs clinician-approved protocols, tested detection methods, conservative escalation rules, and monitoring for missed high-risk situations.

Keyword matching alone is inadequate, and an LLM classifier should not be treated as a reliable medical triage system without rigorous validation.

The escalation workflow 

           Patient Statement
                   |
             Safety Screening
                   |
          +--------+--------+
          |                 |
      Routine            Concern
          |                 |
    Continue Flow     Escalation Logic
                            |
                  +---------+---------+
                  |                   |
              Emergency         Staff Review
                  |                   |
          Emergency Protocol    Human Transfer

For a U.S. healthcare deployment, an emergency protocol might direct someone with a potentially life-threatening emergency to contact 911 immediately.

The precise language and workflow should be established with the healthcare organization.

A voice agent should not attempt to diagnose the patient or provide unsupported reassurance while deciding whether to escalate.

What if the human transfer fails?

This is an important failure scenario.

A clinic may not have an available nurse at midnight.

A transfer could fail because the destination number is busy or unavailable.

The system needs predefined fallback behavior rather than repeatedly attempting transfers while the patient waits.

Possible fallback actions include an approved emergency instruction, an alternate staffed line, or a documented callback workflow for non-emergency cases.

Escalation isn't just a conversational feature.

It's an operational system that needs its own reliability testing.

8. Handling Failures in a Production Voice System

Voice agents depend on several services working together.

A successful call might involve the telephony provider, streaming connection, speech model, conversation model, EHR API, and messaging provider.

Each dependency introduces failure scenarios.

Failure scenario Recommended behavior
Speech recognition cannot understand a patient Ask for clarification, then offer human assistance
EHR API times out Check for an ambiguous result before retrying; avoid claiming a successful booking
AI model becomes unavailable Route to a controlled fallback or human-operated workflow
WebSocket disconnects End or recover the session safely according to call state
Insurance API returns incomplete data Explain the limitation and refer to billing staff
Human transfer fails Follow the clinic's approved fallback protocol

For non-critical processing, background queues can improve system resilience.

Examples include sending confirmation messages, generating operational analytics, and performing post-call reporting.

        Appointment Confirmed
                 |
             Event Queue
                 |
       +---------+----------+
       |                    |
  Notification         Analytics
     Worker              Worker
       |                    |
  SMS / Email         Metrics Store

However, not everything should be asynchronous.

The appointment booking outcome must be established before the agent promises the patient a confirmed appointment.

Notifications can happen later.

This distinction separates the critical transaction path from supporting background work.

The core patient workflow should not depend on unrelated analytics services being available.

9. Measuring Whether the Voice Agent Actually Works

Traditional AI benchmarks focus on model quality, reasoning ability, and language understanding.

A healthcare voice agent needs operational metrics as well.

A system may sound convincing but still fail to book appointments correctly.

That's why production monitoring should cover several categories.

Conversational performance

Measure:

  • Time to first audio response.
  • End-to-end response latency.
  • Speech recognition failures.
  • Repeated clarification requests.
  • Unexpected call disconnections.

Workflow reliability

Measure:

  • Successfully confirmed appointments.
  • Failed or ambiguous scheduling operations.
  • Duplicate booking incidents.
  • Insurance verification errors.
  • Human handoff completion rates.

Safety and quality

Measure:

  • Missed escalation scenarios in controlled evaluations.
  • Unnecessary escalations.
  • Incorrect statements about appointment status.
  • Unauthorized attempts to retrieve patient information.
  • Privacy-related incidents and access-control failures.

One common metric is the containment rate, or the percentage of calls completed without human assistance.

But higher containment is not always better.

A healthcare agent that correctly transfers a concerning call to a nurse may be performing exactly as intended.

A system that keeps the caller engaged with AI instead of escalating could produce a higher containment rate while providing a less safe service.

For this reason, quality and safety should be evaluated alongside automation rates.

Test with realistic scenarios

Before a pilot, create a controlled test suite using synthetic patient data.

Useful scenarios include:

  1. A patient books an available appointment.
  2. A patient changes their requested time during the call.
  3. Two callers attempt to reserve the same slot.
  4. The EHR becomes unavailable after a booking request.
  5. A patient requests information without completing identity verification.
  6. A patient introduces a potentially urgent symptom.
  7. A caller repeatedly interrupts the AI.
  8. A human transfer fails outside business hours.

Run these tests against the complete call workflow, not only the LLM.

That includes streaming audio, backend tools, error handling, and actual integration responses in an appropriately isolated test environment.

10. How to Build a Healthcare Voice AI MVP Without Overengineering

A common development mistake is attempting to automate every front-desk workflow immediately.

Scheduling, insurance verification, billing, referrals, clinical inquiries, and outbound follow-up calls all have different dependencies and risk profiles.

A more practical MVP can be introduced in phases.

Phase 1: Call answering and intelligent routing

Start with low-risk administrative capabilities:

  • Answer calls during and outside business hours.
  • Provide verified clinic hours and location information.
  • Recognize general administrative intent.
  • Route callers to appropriate staff.
  • Apply safety escalation protocols.

This phase helps validate telephony reliability, transcription quality, and conversational experience.

Phase 2: Appointment scheduling

Introduce a controlled scheduling integration.

Start with a limited set of appointment types and providers.

Add patient verification, availability lookup, explicit confirmation, duplicate prevention, and reliable booking outcomes.

Phase 3: More complex administrative workflows

Once the foundational system is stable, expand to capabilities such as:

  • Insurance eligibility checks.
  • Appointment rescheduling.
  • Referral routing.
  • Approved follow-up communication.
  • Billing-related inquiries.

These features should be introduced only after the relevant integrations, permissions, operational policies, and exception handling are ready.

This incremental approach makes it easier to measure actual value without exposing patients and staff to unnecessary complexity.

11. The Biggest Engineering Lesson: Treat AI as an Interface, Not the System of Record

The most useful way to think about healthcare voice AI is not as a replacement for a receptionist.

It's as a conversational interface to a collection of controlled healthcare workflows.

The language model is responsible for understanding natural speech and communicating clearly.

The application backend is responsible for identity verification, authorization, workflow state, and tool execution.

The EHR or practice management system remains the authoritative source for patient and appointment information.

Human staff remain responsible for decisions that require professional judgment, clinical expertise, or escalation.

That separation creates a much more dependable architecture.

        NATURAL LANGUAGE
               |
          AI Voice Layer
               |
       Workflow Controller
               |
       Authorized Services
               |
      Healthcare Systems
               |
        Verified Outcome

At EnactOn, this is the architectural perspective we bring to AI-powered workflow automation: connect intelligent interfaces to dependable systems, rather than treating the language model itself as the entire application.

The long-term value of healthcare voice AI will not come from making agents sound indistinguishable from humans.

It will come from making them reliable enough to handle clearly defined administrative workflows while knowing exactly when to involve a human.

For developers, that means investing as much effort in integrations, security, observability, and failure handling as in the AI conversation itself.

Because in healthcare, a convincing response isn't enough.

The system has to get the underlying action right.

Further reading

  • Invoca — 2026 Healthcare Lead Conversion Benchmarks
  • Twilio — Media Streams Documentation
  • HL7 — FHIR Appointment Resource
  • SMART on FHIR — Backend Authorization
  • HHS — Guidance on HIPAA and Cloud Computing
  • HealthIT.gov — Hospital EHR API Integration Research

What do you think is the hardest part of building production-ready healthcare voice agents: real-time latency, EHR interoperability, data privacy, or reliable human escalation?

title: Why RAG If You Already Have a Database? Explained Simply 🔎
description:
Your company already keeps its HR policies in a database. An employee types: "Can I carry over my unused holidays to next year?" The answer is sitting right there in a table, and the search box still returns nothing useful.

This post explains why that happens, what RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) adds on top of your database, and when you don't need it at all. You'll see a small before-and-after in Python.

TL;DR 📌

  1. A database finds what you ask for exactly. It matches words, numbers and IDs. It doesn't know what a sentence means.
  2. People ask in their own words, which are often different from the words in your documents.
  3. RAG adds two things: a search that matches by meaning, and an LLM that reads the found text and writes a plain answer.
  4. RAG still uses a database. It doesn't replace yours; it reads from it in a smarter way.
  5. For counts, totals and exact lookups, plain SQL is still the right tool.

The idea in plain words 💡

A database is a very fast, very literal librarian. Ask for the book with ID 4021 and you get it instantly. Ask for "rows where the text contains carry over" and it checks every row for those exact letters. If the policy says "rolled forward" instead, the librarian shrugs. It isn't being lazy; it was never built to understand language.

Here is our running example. The table holds four policy lines:

id text
1 Up to 5 days of unused annual leave may be rolled forward into the next calendar year.
2 The office is closed on public holidays listed in the yearly calendar.
3 Sick leave requires a doctor's note after 3 consecutive days.
4 Employees can work from home up to 2 days per week with manager approval.

The employee says "carry over" and "holidays". The policy says "rolled forward" and "annual leave". Same meaning, zero shared words. Worse, the word "holidays" does appear, but in the wrong row (public holidays).

You might say: "Postgres has full-text search." It helps. Postgres can reduce words to a base form, so rats matches rat, and it can rank results by relevance. But matching "carry over" to "rolled forward" needs a synonym dictionary that someone writes and maintains by hand. Nobody can list every way a person might phrase a question.

That gap is what RAG fills. Three terms first:

  • Embedding: a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning get similar numbers, even when the words differ.
  • Similarity search: comparing those number lists to find the closest ones. A common measure is cosine similarity: a score where higher means "closer in meaning".
  • LLM (large language model): a model like Claude or GPT that reads text and writes text.

RAG = Retrieve the most relevant text by meaning, Augment (add) it to the question, and let the LLM Generate an answer from it. The idea was introduced in a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research. Their main point still holds: a model's built-in knowledge is hard to update and hard to check, while text you fetch from a store can be updated any time and shown as evidence.


Notice the database is still there on the left. RAG changes how you search it and adds a reader at the end.

Step by step 🛠️

Store: save the text and its meaning

You keep your policy lines as before. Next to each one, you also save its embedding. This happens once, when a policy is added or changed, not on every question. The numbers can live in a dedicated vector database or in the database you already run (Postgres with the pgvector extension, for example).

Retrieve: search by meaning, not by letters

When a question arrives, you turn it into an embedding using the same model, then pick the stored lines whose numbers are closest. "Carry over my unused holidays" lands near "unused annual leave rolled forward", because the model learned from huge amounts of text that these phrases are used the same way.

Generate: let the LLM write the answer

The retrieved lines still aren't an answer; they're evidence. You pass them to an LLM with an instruction like "answer using only this text, and say you don't know if it isn't covered." The employee gets: "Yes, up to 5 days of unused annual leave can roll into next year."

The code: before and after 🧑‍💻

Before: plain SQL. This runs as-is with Python's built-in sqlite3.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE policy (id INTEGER, text TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO policy VALUES (?, ?)", [
    (1, "Up to 5 days of unused annual leave may be rolled forward into the next calendar year."),
    (2, "The office is closed on public holidays listed in the yearly calendar."),
    (3, "Sick leave requires a doctor's note after 3 consecutive days."),
    (4, "Employees can work from home up to 2 days per week with manager approval."),
])

for word in ["carry over", "holidays"]:
    rows = db.execute("SELECT id, text FROM policy WHERE text LIKE ?", (f"%{word}%",)).fetchall()
    print(f"LIKE '%{word}%' ->", rows)

Output:

LIKE '%carry over%' -> []
LIKE '%holidays%' -> [(2, 'The office is closed on public holidays listed in the yearly calendar.')]

One search finds nothing. The other finds the wrong policy. The database did exactly what it was told.

After: RAG. It uses sentence-transformers for free local embeddings and the Anthropic SDK for the LLM (you need an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY).

# pip install sentence-transformers anthropic
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import anthropic

policies = [
    "Up to 5 days of unused annual leave may be rolled forward into the next calendar year.",
    "The office is closed on public holidays listed in the yearly calendar.",
    "Sick leave requires a doctor's note after 3 consecutive days.",
    "Employees can work from home up to 2 days per week with manager approval.",
]

# 1. Store: turn every policy line into an embedding, once.
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")   # small, free, runs on a laptop
policy_vectors = model.encode(policies)

# 2. Retrieve: embed the question and find the closest policies by meaning.
question = "Can I carry over my unused holidays to next year?"
question_vector = model.encode([question])
scores = model.similarity(question_vector, policy_vectors)[0]   # cosine similarity
top = scores.argsort(descending=True)[:2]
context = "\n".join(policies[i] for i in top)
for i in top:
    print(f"{float(scores[i]):.2f}  {policies[i]}")

# 3. Generate: the LLM answers from the found text only.
client = anthropic.Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from your environment
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens=200,
    messages=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Answer using only this policy text. If it isn't covered, say you don't know.\n\n"
