title: Build a Spice Label Checker in Vanilla JavaScript
description:
Small utility projects are a great way to practise JavaScript, especially when they check real-world data. In this tutorial we will build a spice label checker: you type in the details printed on a pack, and the tool tells you what looks incomplete or suspicious.

Why spices? Because people who search for the best spices online often have no way to compare packs except by reading the label. A few simple rules, such as a full ingredient list and sensible dates, catch many problems before you order. The same idea works for any packaged food, so you can reuse the code.

No framework, no build step. Just HTML and plain JavaScript.

What We Are Building

A small page with a form. The user enters:

Ingredients
Packed-on date
Best-before date
Licence number (the 14-digit FSSAI number printed on Indian food packs)
Seller contact details

When they click Check label, the page lists every issue it found, or shows a clean pass.

Where the Rules Come From

Rules should come from something real, not guesswork. The checks below follow the label checklist in this guide to the best spices online, which covers ingredients, dates, licence number, net weight, seller details and policies. We will code the ones that can be validated from text and dates alone.

A note on scope: this tool only checks the format and logic of what you type. It cannot confirm that a licence number is real or that a pack is genuine. For that, you still need to check the seller and the product yourself.

Step 1: The HTML
html
<!DOCTYPE html>




Spice Label Checker



Spice Label Checker

<form id="label-form">
  <label>Ingredients
    <textarea name="ingredients" rows="2"></textarea>
  </label>
  <label>Packed on
    <input type="date" name="packedOn" />
  </label>
  <label>Best before
    <input type="date" name="bestBefore" />
  </label>
  <label>Licence number (14 digits)
    <input type="text" name="fssai" inputmode="numeric" />
  </label>
  <label>Seller contact
    <input type="text" name="sellerContact" />
  </label>
  <button type="submit">Check label</button>
</form>

<section aria-live="polite">
  <h2 id="status"></h2>
  <ul id="issues"></ul>
</section>




Step 2: The Validation Function

Create app.js. The core is one pure function that takes the label data and returns a list of issues. Keeping it separate from the DOM makes it easy to test.

js
function parseDate(value) {
const date = new Date(value);
return Number.isNaN(date.getTime()) ? null : date;
}

function checkLabel(label, today = new Date()) {
const issues = [];

const ingredients = (label.ingredients || "").trim();
if (!ingredients) {
issues.push("Ingredients are missing.");
} else if (ingredients.toLowerCase() === "spices") {
issues.push("Ingredients are too vague. Each spice should be named.");
}

const packed = parseDate(label.packedOn);
const best = parseDate(label.bestBefore);

if (!packed) issues.push("Packed-on date is missing or invalid.");
if (!best) issues.push("Best-before date is missing or invalid.");

if (packed && best && best <= packed) {
issues.push("Best-before date must be after the packed-on date.");
}
if (best && best < today) {
issues.push("This pack is past its best-before date.");
}

const licence = (label.fssai || "").replace(/\s+/g, "");
if (!/^\d{14}$/.test(licence)) {
issues.push("Licence number should be exactly 14 digits.");
}

if (!(label.sellerContact || "").trim()) {
issues.push("Seller contact details are missing.");
}

return { ok: issues.length === 0, issues };
}
Step 3: Connect It to the Form
js
const form = document.getElementById("label-form");
const statusEl = document.getElementById("status");
const issuesEl = document.getElementById("issues");

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
event.preventDefault();

const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
const result = checkLabel(data);

issuesEl.innerHTML = "";

if (result.ok) {
statusEl.textContent = "No label issues found.";
return;
}

statusEl.textContent = ${result.issues.length} issue(s) found;
result.issues.forEach((text) => {
const li = document.createElement("li");
li.textContent = text; // textContent avoids injecting raw HTML
issuesEl.appendChild(li);
});
});

Open index.html, leave the ingredients as just spices, and submit. You should see the vague-ingredients message along with any other missing fields.

Step 4: Test the Logic

Because checkLabel takes today as a parameter, you can test it with a fixed date instead of waiting for real time to pass.

js
const today = new Date("2026-11-25");

const good = {
ingredients: "Coriander, red chilli, cumin, turmeric",
packedOn: "2026-10-01",
bestBefore: "2027-04-01",
fssai: "12345678901234",
sellerContact: "support@example.com",
};

console.log(checkLabel(good, today).ok); // true

const bad = { ...good, ingredients: "spices", bestBefore: "2026-09-01" };
console.log(checkLabel(bad, today).issues);
// ["Ingredients are too vague...", "Best-before date must be after...", "This pack is past..."]

The licence number above is a made-up example, used only to test the format.

Step 5: Make It Better

Some easy upgrades to practise with:

Live feedback. Run the check on the input event and show issues as the user types.
Severity levels. Mark some issues as warnings and others as errors.
More fields. Add net weight and price per 100 g, then calculate and show it.
Save drafts. Use localStorage to keep the last entry.
Reuse the function. Because it is pure, you can drop it into a React or Vue component or a Node script.
Common Mistakes
Comparing date strings instead of Date objects.
Forgetting that new Date("invalid") returns an “Invalid Date” object, not null.
Using innerHTML with user input.
Putting validation logic inside the click handler, which makes it hard to test.
Treating a format check as proof that a product is genuine.
Where This Idea Is Useful

If you are building a food or ecommerce site, a label checklist like this can help buyers compare products, whether they want to buy Indian spices, snacks or anything else sold with a printed label. A seller-side version also helps catch missing fields before a product page goes live. For a list of what to look for in authentic Indian spices, and which basics most kitchens stock first, see this guide to the best Indian spices.

FAQ

Does this tell me if a spice is authentic?
No. It only checks whether the label information looks complete and consistent. Smell, texture and seller reputation still matter.

Why does checkLabel take today as an argument?
It makes the function predictable and easy to test, because the result no longer depends on the real clock.

Can I use it for other products?
Yes. Change the ingredient rule and the licence format, and it works for most packaged foods.

Why not use a library?
For a small tool like this, plain JavaScript is simpler and teaches you the DOM and Date basics.

Should I validate on the server too?
Yes, if you store or act on the data. Client-side checks are a convenience, not a security measure.

Wrapping Up

In under 100 lines, we built a label checker that validates text, dates and a number format, with a pure function that is easy to test. It is a small project, but it covers forms, FormData, dates, regular expressions and safe DOM updates.

If you try it, tell me which field you would add next.

title: AWS dobra para 30 minutos o timeout do Lambda sob demanda
description:
A AWS dobrou de 15 para 30 minutos o tempo máximo de execução das funções de evento sob demanda do Lambda. A mudança vale em todas as regiões comerciais, sem adesão prévia e com os preços padrão. O novo limite pode ser configurado por função e se aplica a invocações síncronas, assíncronas e a mapeamentos de fontes de eventos.

Configuração e cenários de uso

O teto de 15 minutos estava em vigor desde 2018. Para ampliar o prazo, administradores precisam alterar a configuração de cada função; valores acima de 1.800 segundos são rejeitados com erro de validação. A AWS cita como casos de uso agentes de IA que encadeiam chamadas a modelos e ferramentas, transcodificação de mídia, simulações de Monte Carlo e geração de relatórios.

aws lambda update-function-configuration \
--function-name my-demo-function \
--timeout 1800

A atualização não uniformiza os limites de todos os formatos do serviço. Web Functions continuam com o máximo de 15 minutos, enquanto Lambda MicroVMs podem executar por até oito horas. Nas Lambda Managed Instances, invocações síncronas chegam a 30 minutos, mas as assíncronas mantêm o limite de 90 minutos introduzido em setembro.

Capacidade, filas e streams

Antes de aumentar o timeout, equipes devem recalcular a concorrência necessária. A AWS apresenta a relação entre concorrência, requisições por segundo e duração média em segundos: à mesma taxa de requisições, uma execução de 30 minutos exige o dobro da concorrência de uma execução de 15 minutos. Um fluxo de uma requisição por segundo durante 30 minutos requer 1.800 execuções simultâneas.

Para processamento com SQS, o timeout de visibilidade da fila deve ser pelo menos seis vezes o prazo da função, chegando a três horas quando ela pode executar por 30 minutos. Em Kinesis e DynamoDB Streams, cada shard entrega um lote por vez; por isso, uma função mais lenta também retarda o processamento daquele shard.

Há ainda diferenças nos mapeamentos de outras fontes. Mapeamentos de Amazon MQ, DocumentDB e Kafka criados antes de 19 de novembro permanecem limitados a 14 minutos. O gateway NAT encerra conexões ociosas após 350 segundos, e a fase Init da função continua sujeita ao limite de dez segundos.

Validações e efeitos operacionais

O profissional de AWS Wibo van der Sluis testou a regra de visibilidade com uma função configurada para 1.800 segundos. No teste, uma fila com visibilidade de 90 minutos e depois de 60 segundos foi aceita enquanto o mapeamento já existia; um novo mapeamento para a mesma fila foi recusado. A validação ocorreu na criação, não em alterações posteriores.

Van der Sluis também observou que, na criação, a checagem comparou a fila ao timeout da função, e não ao múltiplo de seis recomendado. Equipes devem tratar essa relação como uma configuração operacional a garantir, em vez de depender exclusivamente da validação do serviço.

Em funções assíncronas que expiram três vezes, o evento pode acumular até 90 minutos de execução antes de chegar a uma fila de mensagens não entregues. Para tarefas longas, vale manter os handlers idempotentes e planejar retentativas e tratamento de trabalho parcial, pois uma falha no meio da execução pode deixar efeitos incompletos.

Quando considerar outras arquiteturas

Um timeout maior não resolve necessariamente código lento atrás de uma API, e execuções longas precisam ser avaliadas pelo custo por invocação, que acompanha a memória configurada e o tempo usado. Para fluxos com várias etapas, estado explícito e retentativas, Step Functions com Fargate ou ECS pode oferecer uma estrutura mais adequada.

A mudança amplia o espaço de uso do Lambda para tarefas que ultrapassavam o limite anterior, mas não elimina diferenças de preço, concorrência e comportamento entre serviços. A escolha deve considerar duração, volume de chamadas, integração com filas ou streams e o modo como a aplicação recupera trabalho após falhas.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/aws-lambda-amplia-limite-timeout-30-minutos/

title: What is Props Children in React?
description:
In React, props.children is a special prop used to access the content placed between the opening and closing tags of a component.

In simple words, it allows us to pass content inside a reusable component.

function Welcome(props) {
return (


{props.children}



);
}

function App() {
return (

Hello React!

);
}

export default App;

output;
Hello React!

Example with multiple children:

function Card(props) {
return (


{props.children}

);
}

function App() {
return (

My Profile


I am learning React.


View Profile

);
}

export default App;

Here, props.children receives all three elements:

Props vs Props.children:

 Props                                 Props.children

Used to pass data to components. Used to pass nested content.
Can pass name, age, etc. Can pass text, JSX, or components.
Access using props.name. Access using props.children.

title: Migrating from mypy & pyright to Astral's ty in One Command
description:
Python tooling has consolidated fast around Astral's stack: uv for packages, ruff for linting and formatting, and ty for Rust-speed static type checking.

While migrate-to-uv handles moving away from Poetry/Pipenv, moving an existing codebase from mypy, pyright, or basedpyright to ty still had a tedious manual step:

  1. Translating mypy.ini, setup.cfg, pyrightconfig.json, or [tool.mypy] / [tool.pyright] into [tool.ty.*].
  2. Converting per-module overrides ([mypy-tests.*], executionEnvironments) into [[tool.ty.overrides]] or allowed-unresolved-imports.
  3. Rewriting dozens or hundreds of # type: ignore[arg-type] and # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue] comments to # ty: ignore[...] without breaking strings or docstrings.

So I built ty-migrate — a zero-dependency Python 3.11+ CLI published on PyPI.

Try It Without Installing

Preview what would change on your project without modifying any files:

uvx ty-migrate --rewrite-ignores --dry-run --diff --report

Apply the migration and immediately verify with ty check:

uvx ty-migrate --rewrite-ignores --report --verify

What It Automates

1. Multi-Format Config Discovery & Parsing

ty-migrate discovers and normalizes:

  • Mypy: mypy.ini, .mypy.ini, setup.cfg ([mypy] + [mypy-*]), and pyproject.toml ([tool.mypy] + [[tool.mypy.overrides]]).
  • Pyright / Basedpyright: pyrightconfig.json (JSONC-safe — strips //, /* */, and trailing commas without breaking URLs in strings) and pyproject.toml ([tool.pyright], [tool.basedpyright], and executionEnvironments).

2. Idiomatic [tool.ty.*] Generation

Instead of naive key renaming, it maps settings into ty's actual structure:

  • python_version / pythonVersion → [tool.ty.environment].python-version
  • mypy_path / extraPaths → [tool.ty.environment].extra-paths
  • Pure ignore_missing_imports = True module sections (like [mypy-vendor_missing.*]) → [tool.ty.analysis].allowed-unresolved-imports
  • disable_error_code / report* → [tool.ty.rules] validated against ty's official 163-rule catalog (ignore / warn / error).
  • Safely updates existing pyproject.toml files without touching [project] or [tool.ruff], or writes a standalone ty.toml.

3. Tokenizer-Safe Inline Ignore Rewriting

Regex find-and-replace over Python source files inevitably corrupts docstrings, test fixtures, or string literals mentioning # type: ignore.

ty-migrate uses Python's standard-library tokenize module so only real COMMENT tokens are rewritten:

"""Docstring mentioning # type: ignore[arg-type] stays untouched."""

# Before:
x: int = "bad"  # type: ignore[assignment]  # legacy fixture
y = obj.x       # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue]

# After:
x: int = "bad"  # ty: ignore[invalid-assignment]  # legacy fixture
y = obj.x       # ty: ignore[missing-attribute, invalid-attribute-access]

By default, bare # type: ignore and unmapped plugin error codes are left untouched (--unmapped-strategy keep) rather than silently widening ignores.

4. Honest Audit Reporting (--report & --check)

ty has real behavioral differences from mypy and pyright — for instance, ty checks unannotated function bodies unconditionally (check_untyped_defs is always on), has no single strict = True flag, and does not run mypy plugins.

Rather than silently ignoring those keys, --report breaks every option down into Translated, Guidance / Implicit in ty, and Unmapped, and --check returns exit code 3 in CI if anything needs manual review.

Links

  • GitHub: https://github.com/Prateek-squadron/ty-migrate
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/ty-migrate/

If you try it on a real codebase and hit an unmapped error code or edge case, open an issue or PR!

title: Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts
description:
Rust 1.100.0, released 12 November 2026, stabilises the never type (!) after ten years of work and makes Infallible an alias for it. The release also stabilises the core of the allocator API, adds DropGuard, and gives Cargo an opt-in dependency cooldown setting. Some critics note the allocator design still lacks inline storage support.

By Daniel Curtis

title: Three Ministers, One Meeting: Morocco Just Put Data Centers at the Center of Its Digital Strategy
description:
On November 23, 2026, three Moroccan ministers, Industry, Energy, and Digital Transition, sat at one table with a single agenda: how to build data centers in Morocco at scale. No budget figures were announced, no megawatts promised. But the composition of the meeting is the story: Morocco now treats data-center capacity as an industrial policy issue, an energy policy issue, and a sovereignty issue at once. If your business stores or processes data in North Africa, here is why this matters to you.

What happened

Les Inspirations ECO reported on November 23, 2026 that Ryad Mezzour (Minister of Industry, Trade, Investment and Economic Inclusion), Charafat Afailal (Minister of Energy, Mines and Sustainable Development) and Ahmed Rahhou (Minister of AI, Digital Transition and Administrative Reform) met to examine the conditions for developing data centers in Morocco. The aim, per the ministry's own communication to the outlet: establish a common operating model across the three departments and launch the workstream, rather than set quantified targets. Mezzour framed the infrastructure on LinkedIn as a lever of digital sovereignty, with attracting investment among the stated ambitions.

Why data centers are suddenly a three-ministry file

Data centers look like real estate with servers. They are actually an energy business and an industrial business wearing a digital costume:

  • Energy: data centers are among the most power-hungry facilities an economy can host. Their viability depends on electricity pricing, grid capacity and increasingly on renewables, which is why the energy minister is in the room.
  • Industry: building and operating them at scale requires land, permits, construction capacity, fiber routes and a supply chain, which is industry ministry territory.
  • Digital: they underpin cloud services, AI workloads, government digitization and data-residency rules, which is the digital ministry's file.

The three-ministry format is Morocco acknowledging that a data-center strategy fails if any one of these legs moves alone.

The buildout already underway

This coordination meeting lands on top of concrete projects already announced:

  • Nexus AI Factory Platform (launched April 2026 at GITEX Africa): an initial investment of about 12 billion MAD across two phases, a Nouaceur hub at 16 MW, then a 20 MW northern expansion, targeting 36 MW total capacity, with a stated goal of 125 direct jobs by end of 2027.
  • Oracle's Morocco West cloud region in Casablanca, made available in February 2026, Oracle's first public cloud region in North Africa, plus Oracle R&D centers in Casablanca (June 2025) and Agadir (June 2026).
  • "Jazari" and "Igoudar Digital" (Dakhla) national data-center projects referenced in the AI ministry's 2027 roadmap, with Oracle's cloud regions representing an investment of about 1.4 billion MAD.

The November meeting is the state organising itself to multiply, not just host, this kind of infrastructure.

What it means for businesses choosing hosting

  1. Local hosting is becoming a serious default. For Moroccan businesses, keeping data in-country will soon be a competitive option on price and latency, not a patriotic sacrifice.
  2. Compliance gets easier. Morocco's Law 09-08 restricts transferring personal data abroad, and its revision now working through the legislative process keeps data protection central. Local regions simplify the answer to "where is our data?"
  3. AI workloads follow the compute. Companies planning AI features should track where Moroccan GPU and cloud capacity actually lands; procurement advantage goes to those who plan early.
  4. Energy is the constraint to watch. The pace of this buildout will be set by power availability as much as by capital.

What to watch next

  • The common operating model the three ministries are setting up: incentives, land, energy tariffs for data-center investors.
  • Whether quantified targets follow in the 2027 budget cycle.
  • The promised Cloud First circular (Q1 2027 per the digital ministry's 2027 program), which would open public-sector cloud procurement.

Bottom line

Morocco is moving data centers from a real-estate topic to a sovereignty topic, and aligning industry, energy and digital policy to do it. For businesses, the direction is clear: local, compliant, well-connected infrastructure is coming, and architecture decisions made today should anticipate it. At Manadger Tech, hosting and cloud architecture for Moroccan businesses is core to what we do, including planning for data residency under Law 09-08. Talk to us.

Sources

  • Les Inspirations ECO, Nov 23, 2026: Infrastructures numeriques: Data centers, trois ministeres pour lancer le chantier — https://leseco.ma/business/infrastructures-numeriques-data-centers-trois-ministeres-pour-lancer-le-chantier.html
  • Ministry of Digital Transition, Apr 8, 2026: Launch of the Nexus AI Factory Platform — https://www.mmsp.gov.ma/ar/مستجدات/إطلاق-منصة-«nexus-ai-factory-platform»-بالمغرب
  • Morocco World News, Nov 20, 2026 (Oracle cloud region and R&D centers) — https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2026/11/347472/morocco-oracle-discuss-ai-and-cloud-cooperation-in-rabat-meeting/

title: What is CSS Modules in React? Difference between Normal CSS and CSS Modules in React?
description:
CSS Modules is a CSS styling technique in React that allows us to write CSS for individual components.

It automatically creates unique class names to avoid CSS conflicts between components.

In simple words, CSS Modules prevent one component's CSS from affecting another component.

import React from 'react';
import styles from './Home.module.css';

function Home() {
return (



Welcome to React

  <button className={styles.button}>
    Click Me
  </button>
</div>

);
}

export default Home;

Main Advantages:

  1. Avoids CSS conflicts.
  2. Provides component-level styling.
  3. Makes code easier to maintain.
  4. Keeps styles separate for each component.
  5. Automatically generates unique class names.

Both are used to style React components, but the main difference is how CSS class names are managed.

  1. Comparison:

Normal CSS CSS Modules
Uses global class names. Uses locally scoped class names.
Styles can conflict. Prevents class name conflicts.
Uses className="title". Uses className={styles.title}.
Imported as a normal CSS file. Imported as a CSS Module file.
File extension: .css File extension: .module.css

Normal CSS:
App.css

import './App.css';

function App() {
return

Hello React

;
}

export default App;

CSS Modules:
App.module.css

import styles from './App.module.css';

function App() {
return

Hello React

;
}

export default App;

title: PostgreSQL 19: ON CONFLICT DO SELECT
description:
When inserting data into PostgreSQL, you may encounter a situation where the row already exists. Traditionally, you could use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and execute another SELECT to retrieve the existing row. Alternatively, you could use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE with an update that does not actually change any data.
PostgreSQL 19 introduces ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, providing a simpler way to handle this scenario. It allows an INSERT statement to return either the newly inserted row or the existing conflicting row, without performing an unnecessary UPDATE.
In this article, we will explore these approaches using a practical user registration scenario.

Creating the users table

Let's start by creating a table to store user account information.

vahiddb=# CREATE TABLE tbl_users (
    user_id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    email            VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    full_name        VARCHAR(100),
    registered_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE

The email column has a UNIQUE constraint to prevent multiple accounts from being registered with the same email address.
Now, let's register our first user:

vahiddb=# insert into tbl_users (email,full_name) 
 values('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com','Vahid Yousefzadeh');
INSERT 0 1
vahiddb=# select * from tbl_users;
 user_id |          email           |     full_name     |         registered_at
---------+--------------------------+-------------------+-------------------------------
       1 | vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com | Vahid Yousefzadeh | 2026-11-24 11:09:01.753137+03
(1 row)

Inserting an Existing Email

Imagine that the application receives another registration request with the same email address. PostgreSQL raises an error:

vahiddb=# INSERT INTO tbl_users (email, full_name)
 VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid Yousefzadeh');

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "tbl_users_email_key"
DETAIL:  Key (email)=(vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com) already exists.

However, our application does not necessarily want an error. It may simply need the existing user's user_id.
Let's explore the available solutions.

Using ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING with a CTE

One traditional approach is to use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and then retrieve the existing user's ID with a SELECT statement.

vahiddb=# WITH tbl_users_new AS (
    INSERT INTO tbl_users (email, full_name)
    VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid Yousefzadeh')
    ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING
    RETURNING User_id
)
SELECT User_id
FROM tbl_users_new
UNION ALL
SELECT User_id
FROM tbl_users
WHERE email = 'vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com'
LIMIT 1;

 user_id
---------
       1
(1 row)

This query handles both situations:
If the user does not exist, the INSERT succeeds and the CTE returns the newly generated ID.
If the user already exists, the INSERT does nothing, and the second SELECT retrieves the existing ID.

Using ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE to retrieve the existing ID

Another common workaround is to use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and return the ID.
For example:

vahiddb=# INSERT INTO tbl_users (email, full_name)
VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid Yousefzadeh')
ON CONFLICT (email)
DO UPDATE
SET email = EXCLUDED.email
RETURNING User_id;

 user_id
---------
       1
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1

This works, but notice the UPDATE operation:

SET email = EXCLUDED.email

We are assigning the existing email its current value just to retrieve the user's ID.
Even though the value does not change, PostgreSQL still performs an UPDATE. This can create a new row version, generate WAL, and fire UPDATE triggers. It can also affect audit columns or other application logic.
In other words, we are modifying a record when our actual requirement is only to retrieve it.
This is where PostgreSQL 19 provides a better alternative.

ON CONFLICT DO SELECT

PostgreSQL 19 introduces a new conflict action:
ON CONFLICT (…) DO SELECT
Unlike DO NOTHING, this action returns the existing row when a uniqueness conflict occurs.
Unlike DO UPDATE, it does not modify the existing row.
The general syntax is:

INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, ...)
VALUES (value1, value2, ...)
ON CONFLICT (unique_column)
DO SELECT [ FOR { UPDATE | NO KEY UPDATE | SHARE | KEY SHARE } ] [ WHERE condition ]
RETURNING column1, column2, ...;

Let's apply it to our user registration example:

vahiddb=# INSERT INTO tbl_users (email, full_name)
 VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid Yousefzadeh')
ON CONFLICT (email)
DO SELECT
RETURNING user_id, email, registered_at;
 user_id |          email           |         registered_at
---------+--------------------------+-------------------------------
       1 | vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com | 2026-11-24 11:09:01.753137+03
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1

PostgreSQL detects the conflict on the email column and returns the existing user's information.
The same statement handles both cases:
If the email does not exist, PostgreSQL inserts a new user and returns the inserted row.
If the email already exists, PostgreSQL returns the conflicting row.

We no longer need a separate SELECT or an unnecessary UPDATE.
This is particularly useful for application-level get-or-create operations.

WHERE condition with DO SELECT

PostgreSQL 19 also allows us to specify a condition in the DO SELECT action. This lets us control whether the conflicting row should be returned.
For example, suppose we want to return the existing user only when the proposed full name differs from the stored full name.
We can use the EXCLUDED table to reference the values proposed for insertion and a target-table alias to reference the existing row.

vahiddb=# INSERT INTO tbl_users AS u (email, full_name)
VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid')
ON CONFLICT (email)
DO SELECT
WHERE u.full_name != EXCLUDED.full_name
RETURNING user_id, email, full_name, registered_at;
 user_id |          email           |     full_name     |         registered_at
---------+--------------------------+-------------------+-------------------------------
       1 | vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com | Vahid Yousefzadeh | 2026-11-24 11:09:01.753137+03
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1

Because the existing name is Vahid Yousefzadeh and the proposed name is Vahid, the condition is true.
Notice that PostgreSQL returns the existing full name, not the proposed value. Now let's execute the statement with the same name as the existing record:

vahiddb=# INSERT INTO tbl_users AS u (email, full_name)
VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid')
ON CONFLICT (email)
DO SELECT
WHERE u.full_name = EXCLUDED.full_name
RETURNING user_id, email, full_name, registered_at;
 user_id | email | full_name | registered_at
---------+-------+-----------+---------------
(0 rows)

INSERT 0 0

The condition evaluates to false, so PostgreSQL does not return the conflicting row.
An important distinction: the WHERE condition filters the row returned by DO SELECT. It does not update the existing user's information.
Using IS DISTINCT FROM instead of != also handles NULL values correctly.
Locking the conflicting row
Sometimes retrieving an existing row is not sufficient. An application may need to ensure that the row cannot be modified by another transaction while it performs additional operations.
PostgreSQL 19 allows us to request a row-level lock directly in the DO SELECT action.
For example:

INSERT INTO tbl_users (email, full_name)
VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid Yousefzadeh')
ON CONFLICT (email)
DO SELECT FOR UPDATE
RETURNING user_id, email, full_name;

When a conflict occurs, PostgreSQL retrieves the existing row and locks it for update.
The lock is held until the transaction ends.
This is useful when an application needs to retrieve an existing record and then perform additional operations that depend on that record remaining protected from concurrent updates.
Other supported locking options are:

  1. - FOR UPDATE
  2. - FOR NO KEY UPDATE
  3. - FOR SHARE
  4. - FOR KEY SHARE

Without a locking clause, DO SELECT does not request a row-level lock on the conflicting row.
Using the returned user_id to create or update a profile
Now let's extend our example to a more realistic application scenario.
A user account contains basic registration information, while additional professional information is stored in a separate table.
Create a User Profile Table and Insert a Record:

vahiddb=# CREATE TABLE tbl_user_profiles (
    profile_id       BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id          BIGINT NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES tbl_users(user_id),
    city             VARCHAR(50),
    job_title        VARCHAR(100)
);
CREATE TABLE

vahiddb=# insert into tbl_user_profiles(user_id,city,job_title)
 values(1,'Babol','Database Administrator');
INSERT 0 1

vahiddb=# select * from tbl_user_profiles;
 profile_id | user_id | city  |       job_title
------------+---------+-------+------------------------
          5 |       1 | Babol | Database Administrator
(1 row)

Now suppose the user submits another registration or profile request. We want to:
Insert the user if the email does not exist.
Retrieve the existing user's ID if the email already exists.
Create the profile if it does not exist.
Update the profile if it already exists.

We can implement this workflow using PostgreSQL 19's DO SELECT inside a PL/pgSQL block.

vahiddb=# BEGIN;
DO $$
DECLARE
    v_user_id BIGINT;
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO tbl_users (email, full_name)
    VALUES ('vahidusefzadeh@gmail.com', 'Vahid Yousefzadeh')
    ON CONFLICT (email)
    DO SELECT
    RETURNING user_id INTO v_user_id;

    INSERT INTO tbl_user_profiles (user_id, city, job_title)
    VALUES (
        v_user_id,
        'Sari',
        'PostgreSQL Administrator'
    )
    ON CONFLICT (user_id)
    DO UPDATE
    SET city = EXCLUDED.city,
        job_title = EXCLUDED.job_title;
END $$;

COMMIT;
BEGIN
DO
COMMIT

Let's verify the profile:

vahiddb=# select * from tbl_user_profiles;
 profile_id | user_id | city |        job_title
------------+---------+------+--------------------------
          5 |       1 | Sari | PostgreSQL Administrator
(1 row)

The workflow successfully retrieved the existing user's ID and used it to update the corresponding profile.

Conclusion

PostgreSQL 19's ON CONFLICT DO SELECT provides a simple and efficient way to insert a new row or retrieve an existing one without unnecessary updates. It makes common get-or-create operations easier to implement and maintain.

title: Advantages of cloud computing
description:
Small businesses need to utilise their resources efficiently and continue to provide a good service to their customers. Companies can however find ongoing IT provision costly and time consuming.

Cloud computing solves this issue by providing companies with the ability to access technology via the internet and charge accordingly for what is used.

Whilst previously associated mainly with larger businesses, small and medium sized businesses (SMBs) can also successfully implement cloud solutions and enjoy the associated benefits, including adaptable provision, enhanced team working and better data handling.

Whilst cloud computing can be a good option for some organisations, it is essential to consider both its benefits and drawbacks so that business owners can decide whether it is the ideal solution for their business.

1. Cost effective

IT provision can often incur substantial costs. Businesses must invest in servers, networking, storage and other hardware and also pay for appropriate software.

With cloud computing, much of this initial expenditure can be converted into more regular and controllable costs.

Businesses can tailor the level of provision they receive and then adapt this as their business develops. Keeping funds in this way can allow a business to reinvest in areas such as marketing, recruitment and new products and customers.

Whilst cloud computing can provide cost effective solutions, businesses still need to manage and control costs. This can be ensured by analysing cloud use and deactivating any under-utilised components. Subscription levels should also be periodically assessed.

2. Adaptable provision

Generally, a company’s needs vary over time. Businesses may face peak trading periods, greater web traffic or higher data handling demands.

Conventional IT provision can then necessitate further investment in hardware to accommodate these developments.

Cloud provision can be adapted to meet fluctuating needs. Extra data, computer and/or application provision can therefore be added without the requirement to procure extra hardware.

For instance, during a key sales promotion an online store could boost its cloud provision. Following the promotion, provision can again be adjusted to align with usual web traffic levels.

Thus, companies can easily modify provision to meet their needs – without having to pre-emptively make large infrastructure investments.

3. Remote working and team working

Many businesses now operate in a dispersed manner where team members are not all based in one place.

Cloud based solutions let people access company data and applications from a range of devices in differing locations, provided they have the correct authorisation.

Further, cloud based tools including data storage, project and team working applications, enable staff to share and manage information effectively.

Advantages of this include:

  • Increased accessibility to company data.
  • Enhanced cross department communication.
  • Less reliance on in-office provision.
  • Greater ease in working with remote and external personnel.
  • Streamlined induction procedures.

For SMBs in dispersed working environments, cloud provision can therefore contribute to more adaptable and effective business functioning.

4. Enhanced data security and business resilience

Irrespective of business size, data security is an important area. Significant implications for business resilience can arise from unauthorised access to or loss of data including that relating to customers, finances and general business use.

Typically, cloud providers incorporate data security measures such as encryption, authorisation and oversight and automatic updating.

Furthermore, cloud provision can facilitate data back-up and disaster recovery by enabling duplicate data to be held in different locations.

Nonetheless, just by utilising a cloud host, there is no automatic assurance of total data security.

Whilst cloud providers can provide infrastructure, it is up to the business to appropriately set authorisations, implement multi-factor authorisation and protect personnel accounts. Suitable data security procedures should also be in place.

Equally, periodic assessment is needed to ensure that data back-up procedures are effective. Only when data can successfully be retrieved will a back-up process be of real benefit to a business.

5. Reduced IT management effort

There is usually an ongoing requirement to manage on-site IT provision.

Such management can involve updating software, rectifying hardware issues and applying security updates. It can also encompass replacing hardware and carrying out general oversight.

Cloud provision largely relieves companies of these tasks and so enables staff to refocus on other areas of business function.

Despite this, businesses still need to manage cloud provision, oversee personnel authorisation, analyse billing information and continue to apply suitable data security procedures.

6. Access to innovative technology

Cloud computing facilitates access to more advanced technology for even smaller businesses.

Rather than having to establish and manage all associated technology provision, companies can use cloud based database, analysis, artificial intelligence, automation and application provision.

For example, a small online retail outlet can analyse customer data via the cloud in order to recognise buying behaviour and highlight best selling goods. These insights in turn can inform marketing strategy.

Moreover, cloud hosted applications can automate business processes and thus boost efficiency.

It is important though that technology is selected for and applied within a business in a manner that effectively addresses particular business issues.

7. Facilitated business growth

As a business grows and enters new geographical or market areas, further IT needs can emerge.

Staff might need access to applications; there may be a requirement for a central database and staff within different business divisions may need to communicate more effectively.

Cloud provision can facilitate centralised access to business applications and data in multiple locations.

This can in turn ease the challenge of managing diverse on-site IT provision for each business location.

In addition, new digital offerings and procedures can be implemented without necessarily having to fully redevelop a business’s IT provision.

Key points to note prior to cloud migration

Alongside the numerous benefits that cloud provision can offer, business owners should consider various factors before embarking on their cloud transition.

- Cost of cloud provision

If cloud provision is not analysed effectively, costs can unexpectedly rise. Decide on a cloud related expenditure budget and set up warning notifications to help manage costs. This should be undertaken prior to initiating your cloud transition.

- Internet connection

Cloud provision relies upon a good quality internet connection. Businesses should also consider having an alternative internet connection for key business functions.

- Data regulation

Depending on sector and/or contractual arrangements, there may be particular rules governing where data can be held, how it can be processed and who can access it.

- Supplier lock-in

Transferring data and applications between cloud providers can be difficult if a business is highly reliant on a particular provider’s technology.

- Cloud transition

Poorly planned transitions to cloud provision can lead to business interruptions together with incompatibility and other issues.

Typically it is more feasible for a business to transition its provision incrementally, as opposed to simultaneously re-directing all business functions to the cloud.

How to begin a cloud transition

An understanding of current business needs is fundamental to an effective cloud transition.

Below are 5 key areas to consider:

- Analyse present IT provision

Consider which applications, servers and storage are currently in place together with key business IT provision.

- Analyse business needs

Decide which applications would gain most from being cloud hosted and which systems are best suited to continued on-site provision.

- Research cloud providers

Compare the charges, data security provision, availability, regulatory compliance and support offered by different cloud providers.

- Begin with a limited scope

Initially, consider transitioning elements such as email provision, data storage and/or a secondary application to the cloud. More highly involved systems can then subsequently be migrated.

- Review performance and costs

Following transition, analyse application performance, data security, usage and associated costs.

Furthermore, a hybrid cloud solution may represent a good option for those businesses wishing to continue to host some functions onsite, alongside utilising cloud provision.

Conclusion

Cloud computing presents small and medium sized businesses with a route to update their IT provision. Crucially, this does not require businesses to personally manage all physical IT provision.

Advantages of cloud provision such as adaptability, remote working facilities, improved data back-up and access to innovation can in these ways aid business progression.

Yet beyond selecting and transitioning to a cloud provider, businesses also need to devise a suitable transition plan, assess costs and apply suitable data security procedures and continue to review developments.

Effectively, individual areas of business function should be analysed to determine where cloud provision can offer tangible business value. Transition can then optimally occur progressively.

Those seeking further information regarding the benefits and possible issues presented by cloud provision, as well as details about costs and transition approaches, may wish to refer to this useful guide to cloud transition for SMBs.

title: Prototyping a Property App: Keep Spatial Concepts Separate From Application Data
description:
A property application can have polished listing cards, responsive filters, and a smooth booking flow while leaving an important question unanswered: can users understand the space?

A bedroom count tells someone how many rooms exist. A floor plan helps explain how those rooms connect. A rendered interior suggests how the space might feel.

These assets serve different purposes, and treating them as interchangeable can create problems during development. An attractive image may contain assumptions that never appear in the property data. A generated layout may look convincing while representing an unverified arrangement.

For an early prototype, a useful approach is to manage spatial concepts as reviewable assets with explicit assumptions. Here is a workflow for doing that without building a custom floor-planning system.

1. Define the User Decision Before Generating Assets

Start with the question the interface needs to help someone answer.

For a rental application, that could be whether a room can accommodate a desk. For a renovation inquiry form, it might be whether a customer prefers an open or separated kitchen. For a property comparison tool, circulation between rooms may matter more than interior styling.

Write this decision into the prototype brief.

For example:

A remote worker needs to compare two possible desk positions in a one-bedroom apartment while preserving access to the balcony.

This gives the design exercise a clear scope. It also helps distinguish relevant visual information from decorative detail.

A rendering of an attractive living room would not, by itself, answer that question.

2. Separate Known Facts From Design Assumptions

Create a small source-of-truth document before producing concepts.

Known facts might include measured wall lengths, existing door positions, and supplied property drawings. Assumptions might include furniture dimensions, preferred desk placement, or an imagined storage unit.

Keep those categories visibly separate.

A simple project note could contain:

Known:
- Balcony door location supplied in source drawing
- Existing bedroom and bathroom boundaries

Assumed:
- Desk size used for concept comparison
- Furniture style
- Proposed storage arrangement

Unverified:
- Exact clearance behind the office chair

This is a record for your team, rather than an input format required by a generation tool.

The distinction becomes especially useful when someone later asks whether an image depicts the actual property.

3. Generate a Small Set of Spatial Concepts

An AI floor plan generator, such as Floor Plan AI’s tool, can help turn a written brief into an initial layout concept.

Describe the purpose of the space, required rooms or furniture, and constraints that matter to the user decision. If you have a relevant reference image, use it within the appropriate supported workflow.

Generate a limited number of alternatives. Two layouts with a meaningful difference are often easier to evaluate than a large collection of loosely related images.

For the remote-work example, compare a window-facing desk with a wall-facing desk. Keep other requirements as consistent as possible.

Inspect each result against the source information. Generation is a proposal stage; it does not establish that the geometry or dimensions are correct.

4. Change One Requirement at a Time

Visual iteration becomes difficult to evaluate when every revision changes several things.

If you move the desk, change the bedroom size, add storage, and alter the kitchen simultaneously, you lose a clear explanation for the result.

Instead, record one intended change per revision:

layout-01: initial concept
layout-02: move desk away from balcony route
layout-03: retain desk position, revise storage placement

Keep the earlier versions. A later revision may improve one requirement while introducing another problem.

This resembles ordinary interface iteration: define the change, inspect its effect, and decide whether to keep it. The useful artifact is the comparison and its reasoning, rather than the number of images generated.

5. Use Rendered Images for a Different Review

Once a layout concept is worth exploring, floor plan to 3D rendering can provide a visual interpretation.

Floor Plan AI supports generating rendered images from floor plans. These can help stakeholders discuss furniture presence, visual balance, and style.

Be precise about the output. A rendered image is different from an interactive 3D model, a navigable scene, or structured geometry that your frontend can manipulate.

That distinction affects implementation scope. If your prototype only needs an image comparison, static assets may be sufficient. If users must move walls or inspect a model from arbitrary angles, that is a separate product requirement requiring its own evaluation.

Avoid letting an appealing render silently expand the technical promise of the application.

6. Give Every Asset a Review Status

Store lightweight metadata alongside the exported assets.

Useful fields include the source drawing, concept identifier, intended use, assumptions, and review status. A local record might look like this:

{
  "asset": "desk-layout-02.png",
  "purpose": "prototype comparison",
  "status": "concept",
  "source": "supplied-apartment-drawing",
  "verifiedDimensions": false,
  "reviewNote": "Check balcony access against measurements"
}

This is application-side metadata you maintain yourself. It does not imply that the generation service exports this structure.

Keep large binary assets wherever your project normally manages media. Preserve enough metadata in the project to explain which version the interface uses and why.

7. Make the Interface Explain the Asset

The prototype should communicate the status of its visuals.

Use captions such as “proposed furniture arrangement” or “concept rendering” where appropriate. Keep verified property information separate from design suggestions.

Provide descriptive alternative text that explains the asset’s purpose. For a comparison image, mention the meaningful difference, such as the desk position, rather than writing only “floor plan.”

Check the image at mobile sizes. Labels that are readable on a desktop can become unusable inside a small listing card. A dedicated detail view may be necessary.

These presentation decisions should be reviewed with the same care as the image itself.

8. Test Understanding Before Expanding the Feature

Give someone the prototype and ask them to explain what they believe the image represents.

Do they understand that it is a proposed arrangement? Can they identify the difference between the two options? Are they assuming that furniture dimensions have been verified?

Their answers expose communication problems that visual polish can hide.

Before using an asset in a real property workflow, verify measurements and obtain appropriate professional review for construction-related decisions.

For an early application prototype, the practical goal is a clear chain from user question to source information, concept, review, and presentation. Keeping that chain visible makes spatial assets easier to evaluate and easier to replace when better information arrives.

title: MoTekLab MetaForge: Why Your Linux Media Library Needs a Privacy-First Automated Metadata Tagger
description:
Every digital archivist, home theater enthusiast, and Linux desktop user eventually hits the same wall: a hard drive filled with hundreds of video files—independent films, recorded university lectures, documentaries, television series, and personal family archives—that look like an unreadable spreadsheet of raw filenames.

When you open those folders in VLC, MPV, or a local media server such as Jellyfin, Kodi, or Emby, missing container metadata means blank thumbnails, ungrouped episodes, missing synopses, and mismatched years. Fixing that manually with command-line flags is tedious, while legacy desktop taggers often force you into paid subscriptions, cloud accounts, or painfully slow file-copying remux operations.

MoTekLab MetaForge was engineered to solve all of these problems in a single, fast, completely private Linux-first desktop application. Built on Tauri v2 (Rust core) and Svelte 5, MetaForge brings automated multi-source metadata discovery, instant container tagging, chapter authoring, artwork embedding, and media-server .nfo generation together—with zero cloud telemetry and zero hardcoded developer keys.

Why People Need MoTekLab MetaForge

Embedded metadata is the backbone of a clean, self-hosted media library. Without structured tags inside your .mp4, .m4v, and .mkv containers, your files depend entirely on fragile folder conventions and external scraper caches that vanish whenever you move drives or rebuild a media server.

MetaForge matters because it addresses the five biggest pain points of modern media organization:

  1. Instant Performance Without Disk Wear: Traditional tagging utilities rewrite an entire 8 GB video file to a temporary copy just to change a title or embed a poster. MetaForge uses native in-place atomic atom writing for MP4 containers and native MKVToolNix property editing for Matroska files, completing tag writes in milliseconds rather than minutes.
  2. True Privacy and Local-First Ownership: Every inspection, file rename, artwork embed, and .nfo export executes locally on your machine. MetaForge has no user accounts, no usage analytics, and no remote tracking.
  3. Zero API Key Paywalls Out of the Box: Most competing taggers stop working until you register developer accounts across multiple third-party portals. MetaForge works immediately after installation using keyless public catalogs including Wikidata, Wikipedia, TVmaze, Apple TV, and Elcinema—while still supporting optional personal keys for TMDB, TVDB, and OMDb stored securely in your local system keychain.
  4. Media Server Compatibility Everywhere: By writing both embedded container tags and standards-compliant Kodi NFO XML files, your library is recognized accurately across Kodi, Jellyfin, Emby, Plex, and standalone players on the first scan.
  5. First-Class Multilingual and Arabic Support: Mixed-direction titles (such as Arabic film or series titles paired with Latin numbers, season codes, or file extensions) frequently break standard desktop UIs. MetaForge isolates every mixed-direction string using <bdi> bidirectional isolation rules and pairs an English interface with a dual-language (English and Arabic) built-in help guide. 
BEFORE MetaForge:
  Blender_Tears_Of_Steel_Master_4K.mp4
  (Blank cover art, no synopsis, no cast/director tags, no chapter index)

AFTER MetaForge:
  Tears of Steel (2012).mp4
  |-- High-resolution poster embedded atomically inside the container
  |-- Complete synopsis, director, writers, studio, genres, and cast metadata
  |-- Clean chapter markers imported or auto-generated
  |-- Companion Tears of Steel (2012).nfo generated for Kodi / Jellyfin / Emby

Latest Updates and Upgrades

Over the recent development cycle (through v0.10.2), MetaForge has received major architectural upgrades focused on real-world search resilience, speed, and effortless maintenance:

1. In-App Release Update Center and Quiet Startup Notifications (v0.10.2)

Keeping Linux desktop software current should not require manually polling release pages. MetaForge now includes a lightweight Rust backend update checker that quietly queries the official public release feed on startup without slowing down launch time.

  • Subtle Notification Indicator: When a newer release is published, a clean indicator dot appears on the About button in the top bar.
  • Manual Check and One-Click Upgrade Command: Opening the About dialog provides a dedicated Check for Updates button with live status feedback, a direct link to the GitHub release notes, and a one-click Copy button for sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade.

2. Fuzzy Typo Tolerance and Punctuation Invariance (v0.10.1)

Real-world media filenames and quick manual searches rarely match catalog punctuation character for character. Previously, typing Greys Anatomy instead of Grey's Anatomy, or Spiderman instead of Spider-Man, could cause strict local filters to discard valid results.

  • Bounded Damerau-Levenshtein Matching: MetaForge now tolerates single-character typos (transpositions, insertions, deletions, and substitutions) on words of five or more letters, and up to two edits on words of seven or more letters.
  • Alphanumeric Punctuation Normalization: Apostrophes, hyphens, and dotted acronyms are normalized automatically so queries like Agents of SHIELD cleanly match Marvel's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D..
  • Strict Short-Word Safeguards: Words of four characters or fewer remain strictly matched so unrelated short titles (such as Thor versus Tron, or Lost versus Last) never cross-match.
  • OMDb Possessive Fallback and Wikipedia Optimization: Queries missing an apostrophe on words ending in s automatically retry with possessive formatting on OMDb, while non-Arabic searches skip Arabic Wikipedia to cut latency in half and avoid rate limits.

3. Two-Tier TV Series Year Matching (v0.10.1)

TV databases catalog shows by their original premiere year, which creates a classic conflict between two common scenarios:

  • Reboots Sharing a Name: When tagging an episode of Dark Matter (2024), the file's year metadata must strictly filter out the unrelated Dark Matter (2015) series.
  • Long-Running Ongoing Series: When tagging a 2026 episode of Grey's Anatomy (which premiered in 2005), a rigid year filter should never erase the 2005 series just because a season catalog entry carries a 2026 date.

MetaForge resolves both cases cleanly with a two-tier filter: if any primary TV series matches target ± 1, conflicting older series are strictly removed; if no series premiered in that window, earlier ongoing series are preserved and ranked by proximity.

4. Instant In-Place Atomic MP4 Tagging and .nfo XML Export (v0.10.0)

  • Native mp4ameta Tagging: Replaced full-file ffmpeg remuxing with atomic in-place MP4 atom writing for standard metadata, custom freeform tags, and embedded cover art.
  • Kodi / Jellyfin / Emby .nfo Exporter: Generates clean <movie> and <episodedetails> XML sidecars complete with XML-escaped descriptions, cast, directors, writers, studios, and external ID cross-references (imdb, tmdb, tvdb), either automatically on every write or on demand.
  • Parallel Multi-Source Dispatch: Concurrent Rust async queries cut multi-provider search latency by roughly 85 percent.

Complete Feature Overview

Everything included in MoTekLab MetaForge today:

Metadata Discovery and Inspection

  • Eight Integrated Metadata Sources: Keyless out-of-the-box access to Wikidata, Wikipedia, TVmaze, Apple TV / iTunes, and Elcinema (Arabic cinema and TV), plus optional user-provisioned TMDB, TVDB v4, and OMDb / IMDb integration.
  • Hot-Reload API Keys: Add or rotate optional API keys in Preferences and apply them immediately without restarting the application.
  • Field Explorer and Conflict Resolution: Compare metadata side by side across multiple providers and cherry-pick the best poster, synopsis, cast list, or release date field by field.
  • Smart Filename and Ancestor Folder Parser: Automatically detects SxxExx season/episode numbers, show names, and release years from both filenames and parent directories (such as Arcane (2021)/).
  • Strict Movie vs. TV Isolation: Prevents television series from polluting movie searches and movies from polluting TV searches across encyclopedic and catalog providers.
  • Title Localization Toggle: Pulls both the English localized title and the Original Title, allowing a single click to choose which one writes as the primary title tag.

Tagging, Artwork, and Chapter Authoring

  • Native Container Writers: In-place atomic MP4/M4V tagging (mp4ameta) and Matroska MKV/MKA property and attachment writing (mkvpropedit).
  • High-Resolution Artwork Pipeline: Fetches remote posters (JPEG, PNG, WebP), supports browsing custom local cover images with strict magic-byte validation, and includes automatic local video frame extraction strictly as an emergency fallback when online artwork is unavailable.
  • Full Chapter Studio: Read existing chapters from media files, edit timestamps and titles, import XML or sidecar chapter lists, search Apple Chapters and ChapterDB, run scene-change detection, or generate evenly spaced chapters automatically with the Every X min interval generator.
  • Media Server .nfo Generation: One-click or automatic XML .nfo sidecar export tailored for Kodi, Jellyfin, and Emby libraries.

Workflow, Batch Automation, and Design

  • Native Drag-and-Drop Queue: Intercepts local file and folder drops natively through Tauri's backend window stream.
  • Multi-Select Batch Controls: Select multiple queue items to toggle file rename overrides (AUTO, ON, OFF), switch Movie/TV badges per file, or apply a single show lookup across an entire season while automatically pulling individual episode titles and synopses.
  • Customizable File Renaming Templates: Live-preview naming templates (for example, {show} - S{season:02}E{episode:02} - {title} {year}) with clean state hygiene across resets.
  • MoTekLab Brand Theme and Accessibility: Polished light (Warm Rose) and dark (Deep Ember) themes, adjustable font scaling, full <bdi> Arabic/RTL text isolation, and a built-in dual-language (English and Arabic) Help Viewer.

Download, Install, and Test MetaForge Today

All official packages, release notes, and repository manifests are hosted publicly on the MoTekLab Universal Distribution Hub (Distrib_Repo) and mirrored on the MoTekLab MetaForge Download Portal.

Option 1: Official APT Repository (Recommended for Debian, Ubuntu, Mint, Pop!_OS)

Install via APT to receive future upgrades automatically alongside your system updates:

echo "deb [trusted=yes] https://motaz-hefny.github.io/Distrib_Repo/debian stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/moteklab-metaforge.list
sudo apt update
sudo apt install moteklab-metaforge

Whenever a new release arrives (and MetaForge notifies you in-app), simply run:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade moteklab-metaforge

Option 2: Direct Standalone Package Downloads

Download the latest v0.10.2 binaries directly from the GitHub Releases Page:

  • Debian / Ubuntu (.deb): 
  sudo dpkg -i moteklab_metaforge_0.10.2_amd64.deb
  • Fedora / RHEL / openSUSE (.rpm): 
  sudo rpm -i moteklab_metaforge-0.10.2-1.x86_64.rpm
  • Universal Linux (.AppImage): 
  chmod +x moteklab_metaforge_0.10.2_amd64.AppImage
  ./moteklab_metaforge_0.10.2_amd64.AppImage

Quick Test Checklist

Once installed, launch moteklab_metaforge (or metaforge) and try these quick workflows:

  1. Test Keyless Discovery and Typo Tolerance: Drag a video file into the window and search Greys Anatomy (without the apostrophe). Watch MetaForge resolve Grey's Anatomy across your active providers without needing a single API key.
  2. Test Year Disambiguation: Search Dark Matter with year 2024 and confirm that the 2024 series is cleanly isolated from the 2015 series.
  3. Test Instant Tagging and .nfo Export: Select your preferred metadata fields, click Write Tags, and inspect how quickly the embedded poster, tags, and companion .nfo file appear alongside your media.
  4. Test the Update Center: Open About in the top bar and click Check for Updates to verify live release tracking.

Have feedback, feature requests, or a specific media workflow you want supported next? Join the community discussion on the MoTekLab Community Forum and let us know how MetaForge performs on your library.

Originally published on the MoTekLab Engineering Journal. Explore our free local-first tools at moteklab.com/products, md.moteklab.com, and fahhim.moteklab.com.

title: Building a HUD Speedometer for the Browser: Wake Lock, Fullscreen and Mirrored Text
description:
A heads-up display speedometer is a neat trick: put your phone face-up on the dashboard at night, and the windscreen reflects the readout into your field of view. Building one in the browser takes three APIs and one CSS transform, and each has a gotcha.

Mirror the text, not the layout

The windscreen reflects the display, so everything must be flipped horizontally before it bounces back the right way round.

.hud {
  transform: scaleX(-1);
}

Apply it to the readout container, not to body. Flipping the whole document mirrors your controls too, and users end up tapping the wrong side of the screen to exit.

Keep the screen awake

A speedometer that dims after thirty seconds is useless. The Screen Wake Lock API fixes that:

let sentinel = null;

async function keepAwake() {
  try {
    sentinel = await navigator.wakeLock.request('screen');
  } catch (err) {
    // user declined, battery saver is on, or the API is unavailable
  }
}

The gotcha: the lock is released automatically whenever the page becomes hidden, and it does not come back on its own. Re-request it when the tab becomes visible again:

document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (sentinel !== null && document.visibilityState === 'visible') keepAwake();
});

Wake Lock needs a secure context, so HTTPS or localhost, and it must be called while the document is visible. Calling it from a background tab throws.

Go fullscreen, from a gesture

Browser chrome ruins the effect and reflects as a bright band on the glass.

document.querySelector('.hud').requestFullscreen();

This must be called from a user gesture. Firing it on page load, or inside the geolocation success callback, is rejected: by then the gesture has expired. Wire it to the same button tap that starts the speedometer.

Design for reflected light

A reflection is dimmer and lower-contrast than the screen itself, and you are looking at it through glass at night.

  • Pure black background. Any lit pixel becomes a ghost on the windscreen.
  • A small number of very large, very bright glyphs. Thin fonts disappear in reflection; heavy weights survive.
  • One colour. Amber and white read best against road darkness. Avoid blue, which scatters and bleeds.
  • No animation on the number itself. Movement in the corner of a driver's eye is a genuine hazard, and a smoothed value updating 4 times a second looks calmer than one updating 20 times.

And the speed itself

Take it from position.coords.speed, which is Doppler-derived and far steadier than differencing coordinates, apply an accuracy gate and a small deadband so it reads a clean zero at traffic lights, and convert from m/s with * 3.6 for km/h.

A working version of all of this is at SpeediDash, and the HUD speedometer is the mirrored night-driving mode described above if you want to see the contrast choices in context before building your own.

title: AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15
description:
AWS has raised the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes in all commercial regions, with no opt-in and no new pricing. The limit had stood since 2018. AWS's post lists the costs: twice the concurrency at the same request rate, three-hour SQS visibility timeouts, and Kafka mappings that must be recreated. Practitioners welcome it and ask what belongs elsewhere.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
